I have to work every day with my ex, who is now married with kids. I act like I'm fine.
I failed publicly at work and my team got hurt because of it. I'm thinking about quitting.
People say I'm cold, but I just don't trust anyone to have my back.

spoiler.summary: Lin warms to Korra after they fight Amon together, choosing to save Korra's life instead of capturing him. When the raid on Sato's secret factory fails and her officers are captured, she resigns to go after Amon outside the law, rescues Team Avatar from prison, and finds her officers already de-bent. Defending Tenzin's family, she sacrifices herself to take down Equalist airships and refuses to reveal Korra's location, letting Amon take her bending. Korra later restores it, and Lin is reinstated as chief, now on good terms with Tenzin and Korra.
key_events: Saves Korra instead of catching Amon at the arena
Loses her officers in the Sato factory trap and resigns
Rescues Team Avatar from Tarrlok's jail
Sacrifices herself to protect Tenzin's family
Amon takes her bending when she refuses to betray Korra
Korra restores her bending; reinstated as chief
spoiler.got_right: She takes responsibility for failures, puts others' lives before her goals, and is willing to sacrifice everything for people she once kept at arm's length.
spoiler.got_wrong: She uses her job and toughness as armour, refuses help and closeness, and lets old resentments shape how she treats people.

nodes.title: The sister who never forgave
nodes.literal_situation: While escorting the Avatar across the Earth Kingdom, the police chief is forced to visit the city run by the younger sister she hasn't spoken to in decades, over an old family rift she has never let go of.
nodes.pattern_label: a lonely grudge against your own family
nodes.pattern_text: A woman has spent decades estranged from her sister and her mother, holding on to an old injustice and an absent parent's silence about her father. Forced back into their world, she is cold, bitter and cruel to relatives who want to know her, and has to confront whether her anger protects her or is simply keeping her alone.
nodes.hook: She is guarded, prickly and determined to leave as fast as possible. Her sister is warm and successful, and her niece desperately wants a relationship with the aunt she's only heard stories about.
nodes.why_relatable: How long can you hold on to a grudge before it becomes who you are? Is it possible to forgive a family member who never seemed to take responsibility? What do you do with anger at a parent who did her best but still let you down?
watch_for: Notice what she's really angry about, underneath the argument she's having.
How does she respond to the niece who wants to know her?
What does she need to hear from her family, and can they say it?
example_user_messages: I haven't talked to my sister in over twenty years and now I have to see her. I'm dreading it.
My mom was so hands-off that I basically raised myself, and she never told me who my dad was.
Someone told me I'm going to end up a bitter, lonely woman and I cried because they might be right.
My niece wants to get to know me and I pushed her away, and I hate myself for it.

spoiler.summary: In Zaofu Lin is cold to Suyin and brutally rejects her niece Opal, and Korra tells her she will always be a lonely and bitter woman, leaving her in tears. Acupuncture forces her to relive the day Suyin scarred her and Toph tore up the arrest report; she attacks Suyin, they fight it out, then sleep, apologise and make peace. Lin reconnects with Opal and later tells Suyin she loves her during the Red Lotus battle. In Book Four, meeting Toph after twenty years, she finally confronts her mother about growing up without a father; after Toph saves her, Lin apologises and they reconcile with an embrace.
key_events: Scarred by Suyin's cable during a triad chase as a young officer
Toph tears up the arrest report; Lin stops speaking to Suyin
Tells Opal to get out; Korra calls her bitter and lonely
Acupuncture memories lead to a fight with Suyin
Apologises to Opal and reconciles with Suyin
Confronts Toph about her absent father
Reconciles with Toph after rescuing the Beifongs from Kuvira
spoiler.got_right: She finally names what hurt her, apologises when she's wrong, and chooses to show up for the family she once pushed away.
spoiler.got_wrong: She lets one old injustice harden into decades of estrangement, takes her pain out on innocent relatives, and refuses to talk about her feelings until her body forces her to.

nodes.name: Bolin
nodes.role: A goofy, big-hearted pro-bending earthbender who grew up on the streets under his older brother Mako's protection after their parents were killed

nodes.title: The lovable sidekick looking for his own worth
nodes.literal_situation: An orphaned younger brother who has always been looked after by his serious older sibling is the cheerful, clumsy earthbender on their struggling pro-bending team, and falls instantly for the new teammate, who has eyes for his brother.
nodes.pattern_label: a lovable younger sibling stuck in a shadow
nodes.pattern_text: A warm, funny younger sibling has spent his life being protected by a more serious, more capable older brother. People like him but don't take him seriously, he struggles with the skill everyone expects him to have, and he keeps losing out in love. He has to figure out whether he is just the comic relief or someone who can stand on his own.
nodes.hook: He is optimistic, starstruck and a little naive. His brother makes the decisions, his crush likes someone else, and he can't master the advanced technique he's dreamed of since childhood.
nodes.why_relatable: What happens when you're the fun one but never the one people count on? How do you step out from a sibling who has always protected you? What if the thing you're best at isn't the thing you wanted to be good at?
watch_for: Notice how others react when he tries to be taken seriously.
What does he do when he's left out of the group's plans?
When does he surprise himself?
example_user_messages: I'm always the funny friend but nobody ever takes me seriously.
My older brother basically raised me and I don't know how to do things without him.
I liked her first, but she fell for my brother. It's fine. It's totally fine.
Everyone else in my friend group seems to have a purpose and I'm just along for the ride.

spoiler.summary: Bolin's crush on Korra ends in rejection when she and Mako fall for each other. In Book Two he drifts from the team, gets trapped in a relationship with the domineering Eska and becomes a movie star as Nuktuk for Varrick, then saves President Raiko and exposes Varrick's scheme on his own. In Book Three he fails to learn metalbending but, trapped by Ghazan's lava in the collapsing Northern Air Temple, discovers he can lavabend, saving Mako, Asami and Tenzin, and later holds off Ghazan in battle. He also begins dating Opal.
key_events: Crush on Korra is rejected; she and Mako get together
Captain of a failing Fire Ferrets
Relationship with Eska, then fleeing her
Becomes famous as Nuktuk and exposes Varrick's kidnapping plot
Can't learn metalbending at Zaofu; meets Opal
Discovers lavabending at the Northern Air Temple
spoiler.got_right: He stays kind, forgiving and loyal, and when it counts he steps up with courage and finds his own unique strength.
spoiler.got_wrong: He is gullible, can't keep secrets, and leans on others' approval to feel worthwhile.

nodes.title: All in on a cause
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, he has found a new purpose as a proud officer serving a charismatic leader who is restoring order to a troubled region, and he is the face of her aid work, while the people closest to him grow more and more skeptical.
nodes.pattern_label: realising the cause you joined isn't good
nodes.pattern_text: An idealistic young man joins a charismatic leader's movement because it seems to be helping people and makes him feel important. The people he loves warn him, and he defends his choice. As the leader's methods become harder to ignore, he has to admit he was wrong, break away at real personal cost, and try to repair the relationships his loyalty damaged.
nodes.hook: He is excited and proud, sure he's making history by bringing food and order to struggling towns, and frustrated that his loved ones can't see the good he thinks he's doing.
nodes.why_relatable: How do you know whether a cause you believe in is really doing good? Why is it so hard to hear doubts from the people who love you? What would it take to question something that gave you purpose?
watch_for: Notice the moments when he chooses not to ask questions.
How does he react when someone he loves challenges what he's seen?
What would it take for him to change his mind, and what would it cost him?
example_user_messages: I joined a company I really believed in, and I'm starting to realise the boss is doing shady stuff.
My girlfriend and my brother both say I've been brainwashed by this group, and I keep defending it.
I'm scared to admit I got it wrong because I've told everyone how great this was.
I finally walked away and now I have to apologise to everyone I argued with.

spoiler.summary: Bolin defends Kuvira to Opal and Mako and even blames Mako for wasting his time, but at Zaofu he sees her threaten dissenters with reeducation camps and realises, with Varrick, that she is a tyrant. His escape fails and he is sentenced to a reeducation camp; he and Varrick escape by blowing up the train, help other fugitives, and reach Republic City to warn the world about her superweapon. He apologises to Mako, helps Lin and Toph free the Beifongs, saves Zhu Li, wins back Opal, and fights inside the Colossus alongside his brother, carrying Mako out when the core explodes.
key_events: Recruited as the face of Kuvira's army
Tells Mako he's making history while Mako is a glorified butler
Kuvira threatens him with a reeducation camp
Deserts with Varrick and Zhu Li; captured and sentenced
Escapes the train with Varrick and warns Republic City
Apologises to Mako and wins Opal back
Carries Mako out of the exploding Colossus
Hiroshi Sato is killed in the final battle
spoiler.got_right: His heart is always in helping people; once he sees the truth he risks his freedom to act on it and humbly makes amends.
spoiler.got_wrong: He lets flattery, purpose and a charismatic leader override his conscience, dismisses the warnings of those who love him, and looks away from evidence he doesn't want to see.

nodes.name: BoJack Horseman
nodes.role: The washed-up star of a hit 90s family sitcom, now in his fifties, drinking on his couch in a Hollywood hills mansion and trying to get his career and his life going again.

nodes.title: Wanting to be loved while hating himself
nodes.literal_situation: Twenty years after his sitcom ended, BoJack spends his days drinking and watching his own reruns. A publisher wants his memoir, he can't write a word of it, and he's saddled with a ghostwriter who asks questions he'd rather not answer.
nodes.pattern_label: craving love while believing you don't deserve it
nodes.pattern_text: A person whose biggest success is decades behind them numbs a deep self-loathing with drinking, charm and cruelty, and pushes away everyone who gets close. They desperately want someone to tell them they are good, but keep doing things that prove otherwise. The question is whether feeling bad about yourself is the same as changing, and whether it is ever too late to become someone better.
nodes.hook: BoJack is rich, lonely and stuck. He mocks the people who stick around, sabotages anything that might change his routine, and secretly hopes that telling his story will finally make people understand and love him.
nodes.why_relatable: He is funny, self-aware and in real pain, and he hurts people anyway. Can someone who has always used self-hatred as an excuse learn to take responsibility instead? Is the loneliness something done to him, or something he keeps choosing?
watch_for: When he apologises, is he trying to repair things or trying to feel better about himself?
Who does he reach for when he is at his lowest, and what does he ask of them?
Does admitting he is 'a bad person' ever change what he does next?
example_user_messages: I keep pushing away anyone who actually cares about me and then I'm furious that I'm alone.
Everything good in my life happened twenty years ago and I don't know who I am now.
I say sorry all the time but I keep doing the same awful things. I don't know if I can actually change.
Some part of me thinks if people really knew me they'd leave, so I make them leave first.
I drink so I don't have to think about how much I hate myself.

spoiler.summary: BoJack's memoir, ghostwritten by Diane, becomes a hit but exposes him. He lands his dream role as Secretariat, falls for Diane (who marries Mr. Peanutbutter), betrays and hurts nearly everyone around him: he sabotages Todd, sleeps with Todd's friend Emily, pressures a teenage girl's friends into drinking at prom in New Mexico, and goes on a bender with his former TV daughter Sarah Lynn that ends with her fatal overdose. He finds a half-sister in Hollyhock, gets sober in rehab and becomes a drama professor, but journalists uncover the truth about Sarah Lynn and his pattern with young women. Hollyhock cuts him off, he relapses and nearly drowns in his old house, having a near-death vision of lost friends. He survives, serves a prison sentence, and on day release attends Princess Carolyn's wedding, ending on a quiet rooftop talk with Diane that feels like a goodbye.
key_events: Memoir 'One Trick Pony' becomes a hit and wins him acclaim
Herb Kazzaz refuses to give him closure and later dies
Declares love to Diane; she marries Mr. Peanutbutter
Sleeps with Todd's friend Emily; Todd ends their friendship
Sarah Lynn dies of an overdose after a bender with him
Chokes co-star Gina on set while high on painkillers
Goes to rehab and gets sober; teaches drama at Wesleyan
Public exposure in a disastrous TV interview
Hollyhock cuts contact; he relapses and nearly drowns
Serves time in prison; final rooftop conversation with Diane
spoiler.got_right: He eventually stops running, gets sober, and accepts that he has to live with the consequences of what he did rather than be absolved of them. He also shows real care, especially for Hollyhock and Todd, and is sometimes the only one honest enough to name uncomfortable truths.
spoiler.got_wrong: He treats self-loathing as a substitute for accountability, uses the people who love him as emotional crutches, abuses his power over younger women, and keeps choosing the momentary escape over the harder work of changing.

nodes.title: Still waiting for his mother's approval
nodes.literal_situation: BoJack finally lands the role he has wanted since childhood and is trying to be positive, but memories of the cold, cutting mother who raised him keep surfacing, and she still has the power to wound him with a single phone call.
nodes.pattern_label: a grown adult still aching for a cruel parent's love
nodes.pattern_text: A middle-aged person raised by a cold, contemptuous parent keeps hoping that some achievement or some confrontation will finally make that parent say they are proud of them. As the parent ages and the chance for a real reckoning slips away, they have to decide what to do with a lifetime of anger. The question is whether you can let go of the apology you are owed without pretending the damage never happened.
nodes.hook: BoJack is trying out a new, optimistic outlook, yet every conversation with his mother reduces him to the scared kid hiding under the kitchen table. He wants her to see him, and he wants her to pay.
nodes.why_relatable: How much of who he is was shaped by a parent who told him he ruined her life? Can he stop repeating her cruelty? And what does he actually want from her: love, an apology, or just the last word?
watch_for: What does he hope will happen every time he sees his mother?
Which of her habits and phrases show up in the way he treats others?
When he finally has the chance to say what he's always wanted to say, what does he choose?
example_user_messages: I'm 50 and I still want my mom to tell me she's proud of me. She never will.
My parent was cruel to me my whole childhood and now they're old and sick and I'm supposed to take care of them.
Every time I talk to my mother I feel like a scared kid again, even though I'm a grown adult.
I always imagined I'd finally tell my dad everything he did to me, and now I don't know if there's any point.

spoiler.summary: Flashbacks show Beatrice and Butterscotch's abusive, alcoholic marriage and how Beatrice's own trauma (her mother's lobotomy, her father's coldness, a childhood fire) shaped her. In Season 4, Beatrice has dementia and BoJack reluctantly takes her in at Hollyhock's urging, hoping she'll remember him so he can tell her off. After learning she has been secretly drugging Hollyhock with diet pills, he takes her to a grim nursing home, but when she finally recognises him he gives her a comforting fantasy of a summer night at her family's lake house instead of the confrontation. In Season 5 she dies, and BoJack delivers a long, raw eulogy (Free Churro) processing that she never loved him in the way he needed.
key_events: Beatrice develops dementia and moves into BoJack's house
Beatrice secretly drugs Hollyhock, causing an overdose
BoJack chooses kindness over revenge at the nursing home
Beatrice's death and BoJack's eulogy in 'Free Churro'
spoiler.got_right: In the end he chooses compassion over retaliation, and he begins to see his mother as a damaged person shaped by her own abuse.
spoiler.got_wrong: For decades he let the wish for her approval drive him, and he reproduced her cruelty and drinking in his own relationships instead of looking at where they came from.

nodes.title: Getting sober and facing the past
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, BoJack is working again on a demanding new show and trying to limit himself to a set amount of alcohol a day, but the limit keeps creeping up and the line between the dark character he plays and himself keeps blurring.
nodes.pattern_label: getting clean and reckoning with the harm you caused
nodes.pattern_text: A person with a long history of substance use and hurting people finally tries to get clean and build a new life. Sobriety brings real progress, but it also removes the fog that kept them from looking at what they actually did. The question is whether a fresh start is possible without facing the people you hurt, and what accountability really demands.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, BoJack is telling himself he has things under control. He wants a clean slate and a second chance, and he's terrified of what honesty about his past would cost him.
nodes.why_relatable: Is getting sober the same as making amends? Does a new life count if the old one is kept secret? He wants to be seen as someone who changed, but can he stand the scrutiny that real change requires?
watch_for: Notice what he tells himself about his drinking at the start of this stretch, and what he admits later.
When people from his past resurface, does he want to repair things or to control the story?
What does he think he is owed for getting better?
example_user_messages: I'm 90 days sober and now I have to actually look at everything I did when I was using.
I told myself I'd only have two drinks a day. Now it's a bottle.
I'm terrified that if the people in my new life find out what I did years ago, they'll leave.
I want a fresh start so badly but I don't know if I've earned one.

spoiler.summary: After a back injury on the set of Philbert, BoJack spirals on painkillers and alcohol, blurs reality with his role, and nearly strangles co-star and girlfriend Gina on set, which the studio covers up. Diane refuses to let him hide, and he checks himself into rehab, gets sober and becomes a drama professor at Wesleyan. He tries to make amends privately, but journalists piece together the truth about Sarah Lynn's death and his history with young women. His first interview goes well; the second exposes him. He relapses, nearly drowns, then goes to prison and emerges sober but without the life he tried to rebuild.
key_events: Back injury and painkiller addiction on the Philbert set
Strangles Gina while high; incident is covered up
Checks into rehab and gets sober
Becomes a drama professor at Wesleyan
Sarah Lynn story breaks; second TV interview exposes him
Relapses and nearly drowns in his old home
Sentenced to prison
spoiler.got_right: He does go to rehab and genuinely works on sobriety, and he stops insisting on forgiveness he hasn't earned.
spoiler.got_wrong: He tries to leave his past behind instead of owning it, chooses publicity over honesty, and relapses when the consequences arrive rather than leaning on the people and practices that kept him sober.

nodes.name: Diane Nguyen
nodes.role: A thoughtful, idealistic writer from Boston, hired to ghostwrite BoJack's memoir, who lives with her cheerful celebrity boyfriend, Mr. Peanutbutter.

nodes.title: Wanting her work to matter
nodes.literal_situation: Diane, who wrote a respected biography of a sports legend, takes a job ghostwriting the memoir of a washed-up sitcom star, hoping to find the real person behind the persona and write something honest.
nodes.pattern_label: needing your work to change the world
nodes.pattern_text: A smart, principled person believes their work has to be meaningful, and ideally world-changing, or they themselves are worthless. They keep taking on causes and projects that disappoint them, and every compromise feels like a betrayal of who they are. The question is whether they can find value in work that is simply good, and in a life that isn't a constant fight.
nodes.hook: Diane is sharp, awkward and eager to do something important. The memoir job is a paycheck, but she is determined to make it true, whether or not her subject likes what she finds.
nodes.why_relatable: She holds herself to impossible standards and never feels like she has done enough. Is she chasing meaning or running from herself? What happens when the work that is supposed to prove her worth doesn't?
watch_for: How does she decide what the 'honest' version of someone's story is?
What does she do when a cause she believes in turns out to be messier than she hoped?
Does she ever let herself enjoy something without justifying it?
example_user_messages: I feel like if my job doesn't make a real difference then I'm just wasting my life.
Every project I take on I end up feeling like a fraud or a sellout.
I've been trying to write this thing for months and I can't, and I feel like I'm failing at the one thing I'm supposed to be good at.
Why can't I just be happy doing something that's fun and simple?

spoiler.summary: Diane's memoir of BoJack, 'One Trick Pony', is a hit but damages their friendship. She flees to war-torn Cordovia to work for a humanitarian celebrity, fails, and hides at BoJack's house in shame. She ghostwrites celebrity tweets, writes feminist think-pieces for Girl Croosh, exposes a beloved TV host's abuse allegations only to see him face no consequences, and consults on 'Philbert', a show that uses her pain as material. In Season 6, struggling to write a memoir of personal essays about her 'good damage', she starts antidepressants and instead writes 'Ivy Tran', a fun middle-grade mystery series, finally accepting that she doesn't have to suffer for her work to count.
key_events: Writes BoJack's memoir 'One Trick Pony'
Fails in Cordovia and hides at BoJack's house
Goes after Hank Hippopopalous; the story is buried
Works at Girl Croosh
Consults on 'Philbert' and clashes with BoJack
Writes the 'Ivy Tran' book series instead of her memoir
spoiler.got_right: She keeps telling the truth when it costs her, and eventually lets go of the idea that her worth depends on suffering or on changing the world.
spoiler.got_wrong: She is self-righteous and rigid, often judges others for compromises she makes too, and runs from her problems into new causes rather than dealing with them.

nodes.title: Carrying the damage from home
nodes.literal_situation: A family occasion forces Diane back to Boston, to the loud, dismissive family who mocked her all her life, and she finds they haven't changed at all, while she still hopes they'll finally appreciate her.
nodes.pattern_label: believing your pain is what makes you worthwhile
nodes.pattern_text: A person raised in a belittling, neglectful family has built their whole identity around surviving it, and quietly believes their pain is what makes them interesting and real. When depression settles in, they resist help, afraid that feeling better would mean losing who they are. The question is whether you can heal without betraying your story, and let go of hoping your family will ever see you.
nodes.hook: Diane is sure she's grown past her family, yet going home turns her into the ignored daughter again. She wants one sign of respect from them and knows she won't get it.
nodes.why_relatable: Why does she keep going back to people who hurt her? What does she think her unhappiness protects? And what would she lose, or gain, by getting help?
watch_for: How does she describe her family to outsiders versus how she acts around them?
What does she say when someone suggests she might need help?
Does she treat her sadness as a problem to solve or as part of her identity?
example_user_messages: Every time I visit my family they make me feel small, and I still keep hoping this time will be different.
My therapist wants me to try antidepressants but I'm scared I won't be me anymore.
I think I've made my whole personality about how messed up my childhood was.
I haven't left the apartment in days and I keep telling everyone I'm fine.

spoiler.summary: Diane goes home for her father's funeral, where her brothers and mother belittle her; BoJack tells her she doesn't need closure from them. Over the years her depression surfaces in her flight from Cordovia, her abortion, her failing marriage and her stalled career. In Season 6, in Chicago with her new partner Guy, she can't write her essays about her childhood 'good damage', becomes severely depressed, and finally tries antidepressants. She gains weight, feels lighter, and writes a joyful book series instead. BoJack's drunken, suicidal voicemail shakes her, but she keeps going, moves to Houston and marries Guy, and in her last talk with BoJack she gently lets their friendship end.
key_events: Father's funeral in Boston
Hides at BoJack's house after Cordovia
Refuses, then starts antidepressants
Gives up the 'good damage' memoir for 'Ivy Tran'
BoJack's suicidal voicemail
Marries Guy and moves to Houston
Final rooftop goodbye with BoJack
spoiler.got_right: She finally accepts help, questions the idea that trauma is what makes her valuable, and chooses a relationship where she feels part of an 'us'.
spoiler.got_wrong: She clung to her pain as identity for years, isolated herself, and got tangled in codependent friendships instead of taking care of herself.

nodes.title: Loving someone so different from her
nodes.literal_situation: Diane lives with Mr. Peanutbutter, a relentlessly cheerful celebrity who loves big gestures and never overthinks anything, while she overthinks everything.
nodes.pattern_label: committing to a partner who is your opposite
nodes.pattern_text: A serious, introspective person commits to a warm, carefree partner whose optimism first feels like relief. Over time their differences grow into loneliness: one wants to talk about hard things, the other wants everything to be fine. The question is whether love can bridge two completely different ways of seeing the world, or whether staying means shrinking yourself.
nodes.hook: Diane's boyfriend adores her and makes life easy and fun. She loves him, and she also isn't sure he actually hears her.
nodes.why_relatable: Can someone love you well if they don't understand you? Is she choosing him, or choosing not to be alone? What does she owe a partner who is kind but doesn't listen?
watch_for: What do they each do when they disagree about something big?
Who adjusts to whom in this relationship?
Does she tell him what she really feels, or what will keep the peace?
example_user_messages: My husband is a good person but I feel like I'm married to someone who doesn't know me.
Everyone says we're a perfect couple but I feel so alone in this relationship.
I always want to talk about the hard stuff and my partner just wants everything to be fine.
I think I'm the problem in my marriage and I don't know if I should stay.

spoiler.summary: Mr. Peanutbutter proposes and they marry in Season 1. They clash over Diane's trip to Cordovia, her abortion, his vanity campaign for governor and his big gestures, including an expensive house he builds for her without asking. She moves out and they divorce at the start of Season 5, then sleep together while he is dating Pickles. In Season 6 they reconcile as friends, and he apologises for never really listening to her.
key_events: Engagement and wedding in Season 1
Clashes over Cordovia and her abortion
His run for governor; she moves out
Divorce in Season 5
They sleep together while he's with Pickles
Friendly reconciliation phone call in Season 6
spoiler.got_right: She eventually admits the marriage isn't working and leaves, and later recognises her own part in it.
spoiler.got_wrong: She hid her real feelings for years, let resentment build, and later helped betray his new girlfriend.

nodes.name: Princess Carolyn
nodes.role: BoJack's tireless, fast-talking talent agent and on-again, off-again girlfriend, who can juggle a dozen crises at once but never finds time for herself.

nodes.title: The one who holds everything together
nodes.literal_situation: Princess Carolyn is a talent agent at a big agency, battling a rival for clients, carrying her most difficult client, BoJack, and trying to decide whether she can have a career and a love life at the same time.
nodes.pattern_label: the fixer who never asks for help
nodes.pattern_text: A driven, capable person takes care of everyone around them and believes hard work can fix anything. They hide their own needs to seem easy and unflappable, and pour years into people who don't give much back. The question is whether they can admit what they want for themselves, accept help, and stop measuring their worth by how much they carry.
nodes.hook: Princess Carolyn is great at her job and always lands on her feet, or at least that's the story she tells. Her personal life is a string of compromises, and she's starting to wonder if the life she wants exists.
nodes.why_relatable: Why does she keep investing in people who take her for granted? Is her ambition joy or armor? What would happen if she stopped being the one who fixes everything?
watch_for: How does she respond when someone offers to take care of her?
When she says she wants a quiet life, does she mean it?
Notice how long she stays in things after they stop working, and why.
example_user_messages: I'm the person everyone calls when something goes wrong, and nobody ever asks how I'm doing.
I've spent years propping up someone who never shows up for me and I can't seem to stop.
I started my own company and I'm drowning, but I'd rather die than ask for help.
I keep saying I want a calmer life but honestly I think I'd be bored.

spoiler.summary: PC is dumped by, then breaks up with BoJack, dates Rutabaga Rabitowitz, leaves Vigor and founds VIM, dropping Rutabaga as a partner. VIM struggles and closes, but she reopens it as a management company. She dates Ralph Stilton, produces 'Philbert' and 'Birthday Dad', and becomes a mother. She finally realises her assistant Judah has been the one quietly taking care of her; she turns down a big production deal from Lenny Turteltaub, starts her own company, and marries Judah in the finale, while BoJack helps her admit what she actually wants.
key_events: Leaves Vigor and founds VIM
VIM closes; she reopens it as a management company
Ends her long attachment to BoJack
Produces 'Philbert' and 'Birthday Dad'
Turns down Lenny Turteltaub's offer
Marries her assistant Judah
spoiler.got_right: She is resilient, loyal and very good at her work, and she eventually lets someone care for her and makes choices from what she wants rather than from fear.
spoiler.got_wrong: She sank decades into BoJack out of sunk-cost loyalty, hid her needs to seem 'easy', and let work swallow every other part of her life.

nodes.title: Wanting to be a mother
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after years of putting her career first, Princess Carolyn finally lets herself admit how badly she wants a child, and worries she may have waited too long.
nodes.pattern_label: longing for a child when time feels short
nodes.pattern_text: A career-focused person finally admits they want to become a parent, only to face fertility struggles, repeated loss, and fear that there's no room in their life for a child. They try to do it all alone and perfectly, as they do everything else. The question is what family looks like when it doesn't happen the way you planned, and whether you can accept help.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, Princess Carolyn is determined to make motherhood happen with the same relentless energy she brings to work, and just as determined not to let anyone see how scared she is.
nodes.why_relatable: Can she want this without it becoming another project to manage? What does she do with grief she won't talk about? Is going it alone strength or fear?
watch_for: Who does she tell about her setbacks, and who does she hide them from?
What does she believe she has to give up to be a good parent?
When help is offered, what makes her say no?
example_user_messages: We've been trying for a baby for a year and I'm running out of time.
I had another miscarriage and I haven't told anyone, not even my partner.
I adopted my daughter on my own and I'm so exhausted I don't know if I'm doing any of it right.
I feel like I have to choose between my career and being a good mom.

spoiler.summary: PC tells Ralph Stilton she's had a miscarriage, and they try to conceive. In 'Ruthie' she suffers her fifth miscarriage and learns she's unlikely to carry a child; she breaks up with Ralph rather than admit she isn't 'easy'. She pursues adoption, is rejected by a teen birth mother (Sadie) in her hometown, and misses another adoption, then at the end of Season 5 adopts a baby porcupine girl. Exhausted by juggling work and baby, she learns to accept help from Todd and Judah and names her daughter Ruthie.
key_events: Multiple miscarriages; told she likely can't carry a child
Breaks up with Ralph
Adoption falls through with Sadie
Adopts a baby girl she names Ruthie
Accepts help with parenting from Todd and Judah
spoiler.got_right: She never gives up on becoming a mother and eventually learns to accept support.
spoiler.got_wrong: She hid her grief, pushed away a partner who wanted to share the load, and tried to parent the way she works: alone and flawlessly.

nodes.name: Todd Chavez
nodes.role: A sweet, aimless twenty-something who has been crashing on BoJack's couch for years, full of wild schemes and blindly loyal to his grumpy host.

nodes.title: Drifting through life on a friend's couch
nodes.literal_situation: Todd lives rent-free on BoJack's couch, tolerating constant insults, bouncing between creative projects and odd schemes, with no job, no plan and a family he doesn't talk about.
nodes.pattern_label: a kind drifter searching for where they belong
nodes.pattern_text: A good-hearted, directionless young adult has been living in someone else's space for years, loyal to a friend who treats them badly. They are creative and generous but never commit to anything, and haven't dealt with the family rift that set them adrift. The question is when loyalty becomes self-neglect, and how you build a life of your own.
nodes.hook: Todd seems happy with his chaotic life, and he truly loves his roommate. But he is always the sidekick in someone else's story.
nodes.why_relatable: Why does he forgive everything? Is his easygoing attitude peace or avoidance? What would it mean for him to decide what he wants?
watch_for: What does he do when a friend does something truly unforgivable?
Which of his schemes does he actually see through, and why?
What does he avoid talking about?
example_user_messages: I'm almost 30 and still living on my friend's couch and I don't know how to change it.
My best friend treats me terribly but I keep forgiving him.
I haven't talked to my mom in ten years and part of me wishes I could.
I have so many ideas but I never finish anything.

spoiler.summary: BoJack secretly sabotages Todd's rock opera so he won't move out. Todd goes to prison, joins a cult-like improv group, co-founds Cabracadabra with Emily, and forgives BoJack again and again until he learns BoJack slept with Emily, and tells him he is the problem. Todd moves out and lives with Diane, Mr. Peanutbutter, and later in Princess Carolyn's apartment. He runs a clown dentist business, becomes an ad executive, and finally finds purpose as Ruthie's nanny and starting a daycare. He reconciles with his mother, moves in with Maude, and remains a gentle friend to BoJack in the end.
key_events: BoJack sabotages his rock opera
Learns BoJack slept with Emily and ends their friendship
Moves out of BoJack's house
Becomes Ruthie's nanny and opens a daycare
Reconciles with his mother
Moves in with Maude
spoiler.got_right: He finally draws a line with BoJack, names what he does, and builds a life around what he's actually good at: caring for others.
spoiler.got_wrong: For years he let his loyalty be exploited and drifted to avoid his own pain.

nodes.title: Not feeling what everyone expects
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, when someone he dated as a teenager wants to pick up where they left off, Todd finds himself making excuses to avoid getting intimate, and he can't explain why, even to himself.
nodes.pattern_label: realising you don't feel what others expect
nodes.pattern_text: A person slowly realises they don't experience attraction the way the people around them do, and doesn't have words for it. Naming it brings relief but also fear of being labeled or seen as broken. The question is how to accept yourself, find people like you, and build love and relationships on your own terms.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, Todd has always gone along with what's expected of him, but now he's avoiding something without knowing why, and it confuses him.
nodes.why_relatable: What if you don't want what everyone assumes you want? Is a label freeing or limiting? Can he find people who understand him without having to explain himself?
watch_for: How does he react the first time someone names what he might be feeling?
Who does he choose to tell, and how do they respond?
What does connection look like for him once he stops pretending?
example_user_messages: I don't think I feel attraction the way my friends do and I don't know what that means.
Everyone assumes I want a sex life and I just... don't.
I'm scared if I tell people who I am, they'll think something is wrong with me.
I finally found a word for myself and I still don't know how to say it out loud.

spoiler.summary: Todd avoids sleeping with Emily; later he tells her he might be 'nothing', and after resisting the label, he comes out as asexual to BoJack, joins an asexual support group, dates Yolanda (they break up amicably), creates an asexual dating app, and finds a happy relationship with Maude.
key_events: Avoids sleeping with Emily
Tells Emily he might be 'nothing'
Comes out as asexual
Dates Yolanda, then breaks up
Creates an asexual dating app; meets Maude
spoiler.got_right: He stays honest with himself and others, and seeks out a community.
spoiler.got_wrong: At first he avoided the conversation through excuses, and briefly let others' labels scare him.

nodes.name: Mr. Peanutbutter
nodes.role: A relentlessly cheerful, beloved TV star, BoJack's old sitcom rival, who lives with his writer girlfriend Diane and keeps trying to be BoJack's friend.

nodes.title: Never slowing down long enough to be alone
nodes.literal_situation: Mr. Peanutbutter has everything easy: a successful career, a partner he adores, endless enthusiasm and a new idea every day. He fills every moment with noise, parties and grand gestures, and he never stops to think.
nodes.pattern_label: a relentlessly upbeat person who can't be alone
nodes.pattern_text: A warm, eternally positive person throws themselves into relationships and projects, but uses cheerfulness and busyness to avoid their own sadness. They love big but don't really listen, and repeat the same relationship patterns over and over. The question is whether they can sit still, face the loneliness they've been outrunning, and learn who they are on their own.
nodes.hook: Everyone loves Mr. Peanutbutter, and he loves everyone. He can't imagine a problem that can't be solved with a surprise party, and he doesn't notice when his partner goes quiet.
nodes.why_relatable: Is relentless positivity a strength or a way to hide? Why does he always need someone beside him? What happens if he stops moving?
watch_for: How does he react when a partner tells him something he doesn't want to hear?
Notice the kinds of people he chooses, and whether the pattern changes.
What does he do when he's alone?
example_user_messages: Everyone tells me I'm so positive but honestly I just can't stand being alone with my own thoughts.
I've been divorced three times and I think I might be the common denominator.
My partner says I never listen to her, I just jump in with some big gesture.
I've never been single for more than a month and I think I need to learn how.

spoiler.summary: Mr. Peanutbutter marries Diane, but their marriage suffers from his refusal to listen and from grand gestures like building her a house without asking and running for governor. They divorce in Season 5, following two earlier divorces (Katrina and Jessica Biel) that repeated the same pattern. He dates much-younger Pickles, sleeps with Diane, and proposes to Pickles rather than confess. Pickles later leaves him for Joey Pogo. Alone, he admits his loneliness, apologises to Diane for not listening, writes a memoir about his sadness, and decides to focus on himself for a while.
key_events: Marries Diane; runs for governor
Divorce from Diane, his third divorce
Cheats on Pickles with Diane and proposes instead of confessing
Pickles leaves him for Joey Pogo
Apologises to Diane and chooses to be single
spoiler.got_right: He is genuinely kind, loyal to his friends (even BoJack), and eventually admits his flaws and chooses to learn to be alone.
spoiler.got_wrong: He never listened to his partners, used big gestures and positivity to avoid hard conversations, and repeated the same relationship over and over.

nodes.name: Hollyhock
nodes.role: A curious, awkward and warm seventeen-year-old raised by eight loving adoptive dads, who comes to Los Angeles in her gap year to find her biological family.

nodes.title: Searching for where she comes from
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, Hollyhock, a teenager with a big, loving family of adoptive dads, travels alone to Los Angeles with a spy kit and a single clue, determined to track down her biological mother.
nodes.pattern_label: an adopted teen searching for their roots
nodes.pattern_text: A young person raised in a loving adoptive family can't shake the need to know where they came from, and feels guilty for wanting it. They set out alone to find their biological family, carrying a quiet inner voice that says they're not good enough. The question is what they hope to find, what they'll learn about themselves, and whether finding it changes who their family is.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, Hollyhock arrives in a strange city on her own, full of nerve and very unsure of herself. She loves her dads and still wants to know who she is.
nodes.why_relatable: Is it disloyal to search for your roots when you already have a family? What does she hope finding her mother will answer? How does she cope with the voice in her head that tells her she's worthless?
watch_for: How does she talk about her dads when she's away from them?
What does she say about the voice in her head, and who does she confide in?
Notice how she responds when the people she meets don't live up to her hopes.
example_user_messages: I'm adopted and I love my parents, but I can't stop wondering who my birth mom is.
I feel guilty for wanting to find my biological family, like I'm betraying the people who raised me.
There's this voice in my head that tells me I'm ugly and stupid and everyone hates me.
I'm taking a gap year and I don't really know what I'm looking for.

spoiler.summary: A DNA test shows Hollyhock is related to BoJack, and she believes he's her father. She moves in with him while they search for her mother, but BoJack's mother Beatrice secretly doses her coffee with weight-loss pills, causing an overdose. Her dads take her home, BoJack learns she's actually his half-sister (daughter of Butterscotch and the maid Henrietta), and he passes Henrietta's number to her dads anonymously. Hollyhock finds her mother and tells BoJack she's never had a brother before. She starts college, but is left with lasting anxiety.
key_events: DNA test shows she's related to BoJack
Secretly drugged by Beatrice and overdoses
Revealed as BoJack's half-sister
Finds her birth mother Henrietta
Tells BoJack she's never had a brother
spoiler.got_right: She is brave about asking hard questions, open about her feelings, and able to lean on her dads.
spoiler.got_wrong: She trusted too quickly and assumed family ties meant safety.

nodes.title: Protecting herself from someone she loves
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a frightening experience that still sets off panic attacks, Hollyhock is at college, trying to get 'okay-er over time' while staying close to someone she cares about but has only known a short while.
nodes.pattern_label: setting a boundary with someone you love
nodes.pattern_text: A young person recovering from a traumatic experience is trying to stay close to a family member they love but don't really know. As they learn more about the harm this person has done to others, they have to decide how much of him they can let into their life. The question is whether you can love someone and still protect yourself from them.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, Hollyhock is building a life of her own, with friends, sports and classes, and working on her anxiety. She is fiercely loyal to the people she loves, and she's starting to feel crowded.
nodes.why_relatable: How do you set a boundary with someone who clearly needs you? When does forgiving someone become ignoring what they did? Is it cruel to say 'I need space' to a person you love?
watch_for: What does she do when her anxiety spikes, and who helps her?
How does she set limits, and how does the other person respond?
What would it take for her to walk away from someone she loves?
example_user_messages: My brother keeps showing up in my life uninvited and I don't know how to tell him I need space.
I found out something awful someone I love did, and I don't know if I can keep him in my life.
I still get panic attacks from something that happened a year ago.
Is it wrong to cut off family if they keep hurting people?

spoiler.summary: Hollyhock has panic attacks and flushes BoJack's painkillers, suspecting he drugged her. In Season 6, BoJack becomes a drama professor at her college; a guy named Peter tells her about how a movie star (BoJack) got his girlfriend Maddy alcohol poisoning at prom and abandoned them at the ER. She distances herself, quits rugby to avoid him, and tells him being siblings means nothing when they don't know each other. After his televised interview reveals his role in Sarah Lynn's death, she sends him a letter and changes her number, cutting him off entirely.
key_events: Panic attacks and flushed pills
BoJack becomes a professor at her college
Learns about BoJack's past from Peter
Quits rugby to avoid him
Sends a letter and cuts BoJack off
spoiler.got_right: She learns grounding techniques for anxiety, and protects herself by setting firm boundaries even when it hurts.
spoiler.got_wrong: She initially made excuses for BoJack out of love, and struggled to say what she needed directly until it was too much.

nodes.name: Walter White
nodes.role: A brilliant but underpaid high school chemistry teacher in Albuquerque who, on his 50th birthday, learns he has terminal lung cancer.

nodes.title: The overlooked man who wants his due
nodes.literal_situation: A gifted chemist who left a company that went on to make millions now teaches bored teenagers and works a second job at a car wash. A terminal cancer diagnosis makes him decide to use his chemistry to cook methamphetamine and leave money for his family.
nodes.pattern_label: a passed-over person finally claiming their worth
nodes.pattern_text: A talented person who spent decades being underestimated, underpaid and quietly humiliated gets a sudden deadline on their life. Using their gifts on their own terms makes them feel alive and respected for the first time in years. The question is whether the new confidence is healing an old wound or feeding a hunger for recognition that nothing will ever satisfy.
nodes.hook: Walt turns 50, washes his own students' cars for extra money, and learns he may have months to live. He decides to do something drastic and dangerous so his family won't be left with nothing.
nodes.why_relatable: He has spent his life being the reasonable, overlooked one while others took the credit. How much of what he does is really for his family, and how much is for the man who was never respected? Is feeling powerful the same as feeling whole?
watch_for: Notice how he reacts when someone offers him help he didn't earn himself.
What does he tell himself about why he is doing this, and does it change?
How does he respond when someone else gets credit for his work?
example_user_messages: I'm 50, I was the smartest person in my class, and somehow everyone I graduated with is rich and I'm scraping by.
I got some bad health news and it made me realise I've wasted my whole life playing it safe.
For the first time in years I feel respected, and I don't want to give that up even though it's costing me.
My old business partner made a fortune off an idea I helped build and I still can't let it go.

spoiler.summary: Walt partners with his ex-student Jesse to cook exceptionally pure blue meth, adopting the alias Heisenberg. What begins as providing for his family becomes a hunger for power: he lets Jane die, orders Gale's murder, poisons Brock and kills Gus Fring with a bomb, then kills Mike in a fit of wounded pride and builds an empire. His brother-in-law Hank discovers he is Heisenberg; Walt's deal with Jack's neo-Nazi gang leads to Hank's murder and the loss of nearly all his money. His family rejects him and he goes into hiding in New Hampshire. He returns to Albuquerque, arranges for his money to reach his son, admits to Skyler that he did it all for himself because he liked it and was good at it, frees Jesse, kills Jack's gang and dies in the meth lab.
key_events: Terminal lung cancer diagnosis on his 50th birthday
Becomes the meth cook 'Heisenberg' with Jesse
Watches Jane choke to death without helping
Kills Gus Fring with a bomb in the nursing home
Kills Mike Ehrmantraut
Hank discovers he is Heisenberg and is murdered by Jack's gang
Admits to Skyler 'I did it for me. I liked it.'
Frees Jesse and dies in the lab after killing the gang
spoiler.got_right: He finally stops lying to himself about his motives, admits the truth to Skyler, and uses his last act to free Jesse and secure something for his children.
spoiler.got_wrong: He mistook recognition and control for self-worth, blamed others for choices he made out of pride, and destroyed the family he claimed to be protecting.

nodes.title: Living a double life at home
nodes.literal_situation: A husband and father starts disappearing for hours, inventing excuses and hiding money and injuries from a pregnant wife, a teenage son and a DEA-agent brother-in-law.
nodes.pattern_label: keeping a secret life from your family
nodes.pattern_text: A person starts hiding a whole part of their life from the people closest to them, telling themselves it's to protect them. Each lie requires another, and the family begins to feel the distance without knowing its cause. The question is how long someone can live split in two, and what the secrecy does to the trust and love they say they are protecting.
nodes.hook: Walt comes home late, distracted, with stories that don't add up. His wife notices; his son adores him; his brother-in-law is a narcotics agent who talks shop at every barbecue.
nodes.why_relatable: He believes that if his family knew, it would hurt them, so he manages what they know. When does protecting someone become controlling them? Can you keep a secret this big and still be close to anyone?
watch_for: How does he explain his absences, and how do the stories grow?
Notice how he treats his wife when she starts asking questions.
Who does he confide in, if anyone?
example_user_messages: I've been hiding something big from my wife for months and I tell myself it's for her own good.
Every time I lie to my family I have to tell another lie to cover it and I'm losing track.
My partner keeps asking where I go and I get angry at her for asking instead of just telling her.
I think I'm doing all this for my kids but they barely know who I am anymore.

spoiler.summary: Walt's lies about fugue states, a second cell phone and gambling winnings pile up until Skyler figures out the truth, asks for a divorce and later becomes his reluctant money launderer. He grows controlling and menacing toward her ('I am the one who knocks'), and she stages a breakdown in the pool to get the kids out of the house. When Hank dies because of Walt, Skyler pulls a knife on him and Walt Jr. calls the police; Walt abducts Holly, then returns her and fakes a threatening phone call to clear Skyler. Flynn rejects him on the phone. In his last visit he finally tells Skyler the truth about why he did it and says goodbye to Holly, while only watching his son from a distance.
key_events: Skyler asks for a divorce after figuring out his secret
'I am the one who knocks' confrontation
Skyler walks into the pool to get the kids away
Knife fight at home; Walt Jr. calls the police
Abducts Holly, then leaves her to be found safely
Flynn tells him to die on the phone
Final honest goodbye to Skyler
spoiler.got_right: In the end he stops performing the devoted provider and tells Skyler the truth, giving her something she can use to protect herself.
spoiler.got_wrong: He used his family as the excuse for every lie, turned his home into a place of fear, and treated his wife's questions as disloyalty.

nodes.name: Jesse Pinkman
nodes.role: A small-time drug dealer and burnout in his twenties, kicked out by his parents, who is recruited by his former high school chemistry teacher.

nodes.title: Proving he's more than a screw-up
nodes.literal_situation: A young dealer written off by his parents and teachers is pulled into a partnership with his old chemistry teacher, who is brilliant, demanding and constantly calls him an idiot.
nodes.pattern_label: a written-off young person under a controlling mentor
nodes.pattern_text: A young person everyone has written off finds an older mentor who sees talent in them and pushes them hard. The approval they've never had from their own family feels like a lifeline, even when the mentor belittles and uses them. The question is whether they can recognise their own worth without needing it granted by someone who benefits from keeping them small.
nodes.hook: Jesse's parents have thrown him out and his old teacher remembers him as a failing student. Now that same teacher shows up wanting to be his partner, and Jesse has no idea what he's getting into.
nodes.why_relatable: He is funny, impulsive and far more capable than anyone gives him credit for, including himself. Why does he keep going back to someone who treats him badly? Is being needed the same as being valued?
watch_for: Notice what happens when his mentor praises him versus when he criticises him.
How does he treat kids and people weaker than him?
When does he start trusting his own judgement over his mentor's?
example_user_messages: My parents gave up on me years ago and honestly I kind of gave up on myself too.
My boss is the only person who ever told me I was good at something, but he also treats me like garbage.
I keep going back to someone who manipulates me because without him I don't know who I am.
Everyone treats me like the family disappointment even when I'm actually trying.

spoiler.summary: Jesse becomes Walt's partner and grows into a skilled cook. Walt repeatedly manipulates him: he lets Jesse's girlfriend Jane die, pushes Jesse to kill Gale, and secretly poisons Brock to turn Jesse against Gus, while Mike becomes a gentler mentor figure. Jesse realises the truth about Brock and Jane, turns against Walt and tries to help Hank, but Walt has him captured by Jack's gang, who enslave him to cook and murder Andrea. In the finale Walt frees him; Jesse refuses to kill Walt, strangles Todd and escapes screaming. In El Camino he gets the money he needs and starts a new life in Alaska.
key_events: Partners with Walt; becomes 'Cap'n Cook'
Jane dies of an overdose while Walt watches
Kills Gale on Walt's orders
Discovers Walt poisoned Brock
Enslaved by Jack's gang; Andrea murdered
Refuses to kill Walt and escapes
Starts a new life in Alaska (El Camino)
spoiler.got_right: He never loses his conscience, refuses to be Walt's weapon at the end, and chooses a life of his own.
spoiler.got_wrong: He kept seeking approval from a man who used him, and blamed himself for harm others had engineered.

nodes.title: Carrying guilt he can't put down
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that leaves him devastated and blaming himself, Jesse goes to rehab and tries to stay clean while still tangled up in the business that hurt him.
nodes.pattern_label: trying to recover while drowning in guilt
nodes.pattern_text: A young person who has been through something terrible tries to get sober and move on, but the guilt keeps coming back. They swing between numbing themselves, punishing themselves and trying to make amends to people they have hurt. The question is whether they can accept what they did without letting it define them forever.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, after a turning point that leaves Jesse grieving and convinced he is a bad person, he checks into rehab and hears that he should accept himself as he is. He isn't sure he can.
nodes.why_relatable: He feels responsible for pain he can't undo, and every attempt to feel better seems to cost him something. Is self-acceptance just letting yourself off the hook? What does it take to forgive yourself when you can't ask the people you hurt?
watch_for: What does he do to avoid being alone with his thoughts?
Notice who he tries to protect, and why.
Does he think he deserves to be happy?
example_user_messages: I'm sober now but I did things when I was using that I can't stop thinking about.
Someone I loved died and I'm sure it's my fault, and nobody can talk me out of it.
I throw parties every night so I never have to be alone with my own head.
People keep telling me to forgive myself but that feels like getting away with it.

spoiler.summary: After Jane's overdose death Jesse goes to rehab, then declares himself 'the bad guy' and sells to his fellow addicts before guilt stops him. He falls for Andrea and bonds with her son Brock. Killing Gale shatters him; he fills his house with non-stop parties to avoid feeling. Drew Sharp's murder during the train heist pushes him out of the business; he tries to give his money away, throwing bundles of cash out of his car. Captured and enslaved by Jack's gang, he loses Andrea. He escapes and in El Camino starts over in Alaska, recalling Jane's advice that he decides his own path.
key_events: Rehab after Jane's death
Kills Gale and spirals into non-stop parties
Leaves the business after a boy is shot during the train heist
Throws his drug money out of his car
Andrea murdered in front of him
Escapes and starts over in Alaska
spoiler.got_right: He kept feeling the weight of what he had done instead of rationalising it, and tried to protect children and give back what he had taken.
spoiler.got_wrong: He punished himself for things other people had caused and kept numbing instead of letting anyone help.

nodes.name: Skyler White
nodes.role: Walter White's pregnant wife, a sharp, organised homemaker with a background in bookkeeping who holds the family's finances together.

nodes.title: The wife who notices
nodes.literal_situation: Pregnant, caring for a teenage son and worried about her husband's cancer, Skyler sees him start disappearing, lying and acting like a stranger.
nodes.pattern_label: sensing your partner is lying to you
nodes.pattern_text: A person holding a family together notices their partner becoming secretive and distant at the worst possible time. Everyone around them treats their worry as nagging or paranoia, and they begin to doubt their own instincts. The question is whether they trust what they see, and what they will do once they can no longer pretend not to know.
nodes.hook: Skyler is expecting a baby, her husband has just been diagnosed with cancer, and his stories about where he's been don't add up. She's the only one who seems to notice.
nodes.why_relatable: She is expected to be supportive and patient, yet she's the one being lied to. How do you push for the truth when everyone says you're being unfair to a sick man? What do you owe a partner who won't let you in?
watch_for: Notice how others react when she voices her suspicions.
How does she try to take back some control of her own life?
What does she protect first: the marriage, the kids, or herself?
example_user_messages: My husband keeps disappearing and giving me excuses that don't make sense, and everyone tells me I'm overreacting.
I'm pregnant and I feel like I'm the only adult in this marriage.
He's sick, so I feel like a monster for being angry that he keeps lying to me.
I know something is wrong but I can't prove it and I'm starting to doubt myself.

spoiler.summary: Skyler pushes Walt to accept treatment and grows increasingly suspicious of his absences, a second phone and his fugue-state story. She takes a bookkeeping job with her old boss Ted Beneke, figures out the lie on the day Holly is born, and after Walt's surgery demands he move out. She then learns he is a meth cook and asks for a divorce.
key_events: Organises a family intervention about Walt's treatment
Discovers the second cell phone
Holly is born while Walt is missing
Asks Walt to leave and asks for a divorce
Learns Walt is a meth manufacturer
spoiler.got_right: She trusted her instincts and refused to keep pretending when the lies stopped making sense.
spoiler.got_wrong: She tried to manage the crisis alone and kept her own reactions secret, which pushed her toward choices she didn't really want.

nodes.title: Getting her hands dirty to protect her kids
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that forces Skyler to choose between walking away and getting involved, she uses her bookkeeping skills to keep her family's lives from collapsing.
nodes.pattern_label: compromising yourself to shield your children
nodes.pattern_text: A parent is trapped in a situation someone else created, where every option risks hurting the children. They decide to take control by becoming part of the thing they hate, telling themselves it's the lesser evil. The question is how much of themselves they can give up for their family before there is nothing left.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, after a turning point that leaves Skyler with no good options, she decides that if she can't escape the situation, she will at least be the one managing it.
nodes.why_relatable: She is practical, capable and furious, and she knows her choices are becoming harder to justify. When does protecting your family turn into protecting a lie? Can you stay in a situation for your kids without disappearing yourself?
watch_for: Notice how her competence changes the way her husband treats her.
What lines does she refuse to cross, and do they hold?
How does she cope when she feels trapped?
example_user_messages: My ex got us into a mess and the only way I can protect my kids is to go along with it.
I'm good at fixing things, so somehow I ended up covering for someone I can't stand.
I'm scared of my own husband and I'm trying to hold it together for the kids.
I made a choice to protect my family and now I don't recognise myself.

spoiler.summary: Skyler sleeps with Ted to hurt Walt, then decides to launder Walt's money, invents a gambling cover story and buys the car wash. She gives Ted $600k, which leads to his crippling accident and leaves Walt without escape money. After Gus's murder she becomes terrified of Walt, walks into the pool to get the kids away and tells him she is waiting for his cancer to come back. She shows him the pile of cash and he retires. When Hank discovers the truth she stays silent to protect the kids and even suggests killing Jesse. After Hank's death she pulls a knife on Walt. Left with nothing, she works as a taxi dispatcher; Walt's last visit gives her the coordinates of Hank's grave, which she uses for a deal with prosecutors.
key_events: Affair with Ted Beneke
Becomes Walt's money launderer via the car wash
Ted's accident after she gives him money
Walks into the pool to get the kids out
Pulls a knife on Walt after Hank's death
Gets a deal using the coordinates Walt gives her
spoiler.got_right: She faced the reality of what was happening, kept her children as her first priority and finally broke free.
spoiler.got_wrong: She convinced herself she could control the damage, and her schemes hurt other people and tied her more tightly to Walt.

nodes.name: Hank Schrader
nodes.role: Walter White's loud, confident brother-in-law, a DEA agent in Albuquerque who loves his job, his home-brewed beer and his nephew.

nodes.title: The tough guy who can't admit he's scared
nodes.literal_situation: After seeing violence up close on the job, a macho DEA agent starts having panic attacks he hides from his colleagues and his wife.
nodes.pattern_label: a tough person secretly falling apart
nodes.pattern_text: Someone whose whole identity is being strong and unbothered is shaken by something they can't joke away. They hide their panic behind bravado, snap at the people who love them, and refuse to call it what it is. The question is whether they can admit they are struggling and rebuild a sense of themselves that isn't only toughness.
nodes.hook: Hank is the guy who tells the war stories at every family party. After a brutal case, his hands start shaking, and he doesn't want anyone to know.
nodes.why_relatable: He has always been the strong one, so showing fear feels like losing himself. What does a person do when their coping style stops working? Can he let his partner see him weak?
watch_for: Notice how he uses humour when something scares him.
How does he treat his wife when she tries to help?
What new interests does he reach for when his old life feels out of reach?
example_user_messages: I've always been the tough guy in my family and now I'm having panic attacks I can't tell anyone about.
Something happened at work that I can't shake and I keep taking it out on my wife.
I got hurt and now I can't do the things that made me feel like me.
I was offered a big promotion and secretly I'm terrified to take it.

spoiler.summary: After killing Tuco and witnessing the Tortuga head explosion in El Paso, Hank has panic attacks and turns down the promotion. He beats Jesse and is suspended, then is ambushed by the Salamanca cousins and shot, killing both. Partly paralysed, he takes out his rage on Marie during a grinding recovery, collects minerals, and slowly regains his drive by quietly working the Heisenberg case from home, leading him to Gale's notes and Gus Fring.
key_events: Kills Tuco in a shootout
Witnesses the Tortuga bomb in El Paso
Beats Jesse and is suspended
Shot by the Salamanca cousins; kills both
Long, bitter recovery and the mineral collection
Rediscovers purpose working the case from his bed
spoiler.got_right: He finds a way back to purpose through his own intelligence and persistence, and eventually lets Marie support him.
spoiler.got_wrong: He hid his trauma behind bravado and lashed out at the person caring for him instead of admitting he was afraid.

nodes.title: The case he can't let go
nodes.literal_situation: A new, unusually pure product is flooding Albuquerque, and Hank throws himself into hunting down the mysterious cook behind it.
nodes.pattern_label: a relentless pursuit that tests family loyalty
nodes.pattern_text: A person who is very good at their work becomes obsessed with one problem that others have given up on. The pursuit gives them purpose and pride, but the closer they get, the more it threatens the people they love. The question is what they will do when doing their duty and protecting their family point in opposite directions.
nodes.hook: Hank is thrilled by a new challenge: someone out there is making a product better than anything he's seen. He is sure he'll crack it, and he loves telling the family about it over dinner.
nodes.why_relatable: He is underestimated as a loudmouth, but he is sharp and dogged. What happens when the thing you're best at puts you at odds with your family? How far do you go when everyone else says to let it go?
watch_for: Notice the small details he picks up that others miss.
How does he react when colleagues doubt his hunches?
What does he talk about with his family, and what does he leave out?
example_user_messages: I've been chasing the same problem at work for years and nobody believes me that I'm close.
I found out something about a family member that I can't unsee, and doing the right thing will blow up the whole family.
My boss wants me to drop it but I know I'm right.
Everyone thinks I'm just the loud guy, but I'm better at my job than they realise.

spoiler.summary: Hank pursues the blue meth and 'Heisenberg' for two years, never suspecting Walt. He links Gale to Gus Fring and eventually, after Gus's death and his promotion to ASAC, finds Walt's inscribed copy of Leaves of Grass on the toilet and realises his brother-in-law is Heisenberg. He confronts Walt, is blackmailed with a fake confession video, turns Jesse into an informant and captures Walt in the desert, only to be ambushed by Jack's gang. Hank refuses to beg and is executed; he and Gomez are buried in the desert.
key_events: Leads the hunt for Heisenberg
Connects Gale to Gus Fring
Finds Leaves of Grass and realises Walt is Heisenberg
Blackmailed with Walt's false confession video
Arrests Walt in the desert
Executed by Jack's gang: 'My name is ASAC Schrader, and you can go f*** yourself'
spoiler.got_right: He was right all along, kept his integrity, and faced his death without begging.
spoiler.got_wrong: His need to be the one who cracked the case made him keep it secret from his own agency, leaving him without backup.

nodes.name: Jimmy McGill (Saul Goodman)
nodes.role: A struggling, fast-talking public defender in Albuquerque, a former small-time con man from Chicago trying to go straight in the shadow of his brilliant older brother.

nodes.title: The little brother who is never good enough
nodes.literal_situation: Jimmy earned his law degree by correspondence while working in the mailroom of his older brother Chuck's prestigious firm. Now he takes low-paying cases and cares for Chuck, who is housebound by a mysterious condition.
nodes.pattern_label: craving a sibling's respect that never comes
nodes.pattern_text: A younger sibling with a messy past works hard to earn the respect of an accomplished older sibling they idolise. However much they change or care for them, they are still seen as the family screw-up. The question is whether they can stop measuring themselves by that one person's approval, and what the resentment does to them if they can't.
nodes.hook: Jimmy brings groceries and ice to his ill brother, calls him his hero, and scrambles for clients out of a tiny office behind a nail salon. He wants to be a real lawyer in Chuck's eyes.
nodes.why_relatable: He has genuinely changed, but the people who knew him before don't seem to believe it. Can you earn someone's respect if they've already decided who you are? Is he trying to become better, or just trying to be seen?
watch_for: Notice how his brother talks about him when he isn't in the room.
What does he do with his talent for bending the rules when he's rejected?
Is caring for his brother love, duty, or a bid for approval?
example_user_messages: My older brother is the successful one and no matter what I do he still sees me as the kid who messed up.
I turned my life around years ago but my family still acts like I'm going to screw it up.
I take care of my sibling every week and he still doesn't respect me.
I got my qualifications the hard way and I feel like a fraud next to people who went to real schools.

spoiler.summary: Jimmy learns that Chuck secretly blocked HHM from hiring him because he believes 'Slippin' Jimmy with a law degree is like a chimp with a machine gun.' Their rivalry escalates: Jimmy doctors Mesa Verde documents to help Kim, Chuck tricks him into a taped confession, and Jimmy is exposed at the bar hearing where Chuck has a public meltdown. Chuck says Jimmy never mattered to him; Jimmy is suspended, Chuck relapses and dies in a house fire that is implied to be suicide. Jimmy represses his guilt, which Howard and Kim see as coldness.
key_events: Discovers Chuck blocked him from being hired at HHM
Swaps Mesa Verde addresses to sabotage Chuck
Chuck records his confession
Bar hearing: Chuck's meltdown on the stand
Chuck: 'You never mattered all that much to me'
Chuck dies in a fire he set himself
spoiler.got_right: He cared for his brother for years and genuinely tried to become someone better.
spoiler.got_wrong: He let his brother's contempt define his worth and fought back with the very tricks that proved Chuck's point.

nodes.title: The persona that takes over
nodes.literal_situation: A former scam artist trying to build an honest career keeps discovering that cutting corners, putting on a show and bending the rules gets him further than playing it straight.
nodes.pattern_label: a persona slowly replacing who you are
nodes.pattern_text: A person with a past they are ashamed of tries to build a respectable life, but they keep getting rewarded for the shortcuts they swore off. They start playing a louder, flashier version of themselves because it works and it hurts less. The question is whether the persona is protecting who they really are or replacing them.
nodes.hook: Jimmy has promised himself he is done with cons. But he is broke, clients won't take him seriously, and he has a gift for talking people into things.
nodes.why_relatable: He is clever, warm and funny, and the honest path keeps punishing him. How much do you compromise to succeed? When do you stop being someone who plays a role and become the role?
watch_for: Notice when he chooses the shortcut, and what pushes him to it.
How does he react when someone sees the good person underneath?
What does he stop feeling as the act gets bigger?
example_user_messages: I used to be a bit of a hustler and I've tried so hard to go straight, but it feels like honesty just gets me nowhere.
I've built this confident, flashy version of myself for work and I don't know where it ends and I begin.
Every time I bend the rules it pays off, and that's what scares me.
I think I became someone I would have hated years ago, and I'm not sure I can come back.

spoiler.summary: Jimmy starts as an earnest elder-law attorney but is repeatedly drawn back to scams. After Chuck's death he rebrands as 'Saul Goodman', becomes a cartel lawyer, survives the desert with Mike, and helps Kim ruin Howard, which ends with Lalo killing Howard and Kim leaving him. As Saul he becomes Walt's criminal lawyer in Breaking Bad and flees as 'Gene Takavic', managing a Cinnabon in Omaha. Gene relapses into cons and is caught. He first negotiates a sweetheart deal, then, learning Kim confessed, publicly admits everything in court, reclaims the name Jimmy McGill, and accepts an 86-year sentence. Kim visits him in prison and they share a cigarette.
key_events: Adopts the name Saul Goodman
Becomes the cartel's lawyer; stranded in the desert with Mike
Scheme against Howard ends with Lalo killing Howard
Kim leaves him
Hides as Gene Takavic in Omaha
Confesses in court and reclaims the name Jimmy McGill
Sentenced to 86 years; Kim visits him in prison
spoiler.got_right: At the end he stops performing, tells the truth about himself and takes responsibility for what he did.
spoiler.got_wrong: He used charm and cons to avoid grief and accountability, and let the persona grow until it hurt everyone he loved.

nodes.name: Mike Ehrmantraut
nodes.role: A taciturn ex-Philadelphia cop working as a courthouse parking booth attendant in Albuquerque, living near his daughter-in-law and granddaughter.

nodes.title: Living for his granddaughter
nodes.literal_situation: A quiet, grim former cop who moved across the country to be near his daughter-in-law and granddaughter spends his days in a parking booth, carrying a private grief about his family's past.
nodes.pattern_label: a grieving parent carrying secret guilt
nodes.pattern_text: An older person carries grief and guilt about a loss in the family that they feel responsible for. They put all their love into caring for the ones who are left, while keeping the truth locked away. The question is whether providing for the family can make up for what happened, and whether they will ever let themselves be forgiven.
nodes.hook: Mike is gruff, precise and nearly silent. He takes his granddaughter to the park, lives alone, and there are people from his old life asking questions he doesn't want to answer.
nodes.why_relatable: He shows love by doing, not talking, and he carries something he has told no one. Can you move forward while believing you caused a loss? What do we owe the family members left behind?
watch_for: Notice what he's willing to do for his granddaughter.
How does he react when someone asks about his past?
Does he ever let anyone comfort him?
example_user_messages: My son died and I think it was my fault, and I've never told anyone why.
I moved to be near my grandkid because she's the only thing that still matters to me.
I'm not good with words. I just try to take care of the family I have left.
People keep asking how I'm doing and I just shut down.

spoiler.summary: Mike reveals to Stacey that he was a dirty cop who pressured his son Matt to take a bribe; Matt hesitated and was murdered by his corrupt colleagues, and Mike then killed both of them. He works odd jobs to provide money for Stacey and Kaylee, which draws him into Gus Fring's organisation; he feels his soul darken after killing Werner Ziegler.
