spoiler.summary: April becomes Ron's assistant and finds a kindred spirit and mentor in him. She falls for Andy, Ann's ex, and breaks up with Derek. She agrees to date Andy, then storms off when she learns Ann kissed him; spends the shutdown in Venezuela and returns with a boyfriend to make Andy jealous; then forgives him. After dating for a few weeks they marry at a surprise 'fancy party'. Ben moves in and tries to teach them to be adults. Over time she softens toward her coworkers and even Ann, and during Leslie's campaign she takes over much of Leslie's work and turns out to be good at it.
key_events: Becomes Ron's assistant and protege
Falls for Andy
Leaves for Venezuela after Ann kisses Andy
Returns with Eduardo to make Andy jealous
Marries Andy at a surprise 'fancy party' after a few weeks of dating
Takes over Leslie's parks duties during the campaign
spoiler.got_right: She stays fiercely herself and shows her loyalty through actions, and she gradually lets the people who love her in.
spoiler.got_wrong: She uses cruelty and jealousy games, like freezing Andy out and parading a new boyfriend, instead of saying what she feels.

nodes.title: What do you want to do with your life?
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, April has become more capable at work than anyone expected, but she still has no idea what she actually wants to do, and none of the jobs in front of her feel like hers.
nodes.pattern_label: searching for work that feels like your own
nodes.pattern_text: A young adult who fell into their first jobs by accident realises they're good at things they don't care about and unsure what they do care about. Every obvious path feels wrong, and admitting that to the people who helped them feels like betrayal. The story asks how you find a calling after years of pretending not to want anything.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, after years of drifting through jobs she stumbled into, April starts to wonder whether she should be doing something that means something to her, and whether she even knows what that is.
nodes.why_relatable: She is capable but not fulfilled. How do you choose a direction when nothing clearly calls to you? Is it okay to walk away from a plan you worked hard for, or from a mentor who believes in you?
watch_for: What is she drawn to when nobody is watching?
How does she tell the people who helped her that she wants something different?
What role do the people closest to her play in her choices?
example_user_messages: I'm good at my job but I feel nothing about it.
I'm in my mid-twenties and I still have no idea what I want to be.
I got into the program I applied for and now I realise I don't actually want to go.
My boss has done so much for me. How do I tell her I want to leave?
Everyone else seems to have a calling and I just have a vague feeling that this isn't it.

spoiler.summary: April helps Andy find his own direction, works on Ben's campaign in Washington, and becomes deputy director of Pawnee Animal Control. She is accepted to veterinary school but realises at orientation that she doesn't want it. She works for Leslie at the National Parks Service, and by 2017 she wants out but is afraid to tell Leslie. When she finally does, Leslie helps her explore. April finds her fit at the American Service Foundation and moves to Washington, and later she and Andy become parents.
key_events: Deputy director of Animal Control
Accepted to vet school, then walks away at orientation
Works for Leslie at the National Parks Service
Confesses she wants to leave; Leslie helps her search
Chooses a job at the American Service Foundation in Washington
Becomes a mother
spoiler.got_right: She eventually trusts her own discomfort, tells the truth to people she loves, and chooses a path that is hers.
spoiler.got_wrong: She hides her doubts for a long time out of fear of disappointing others, and she sometimes dismisses options before really exploring them.

nodes.name: Andy Dwyer
nodes.role: Ann's sweet, lazy, unemployed boyfriend and the frontman of a going-nowhere band, recovering from breaking both legs in a construction pit.

nodes.title: Growing up after being left
nodes.literal_situation: Andy is Ann's easygoing, unemployed boyfriend and the frontman of a garage band. He broke both legs falling into the pit behind her house and is happily letting her wait on him while he plays video games.
nodes.pattern_label: a lovable slacker forced to grow up
nodes.pattern_text: A warm, fun-loving person has let someone else carry every adult responsibility in their relationship for years. When that partner finally runs out of patience, they have to learn to stand on their own. The story asks whether you can grow up without losing the joy that made people love you in the first place.
nodes.hook: Andy has two broken legs, a band that keeps changing its name, and a girlfriend doing everything for him. He's thrilled with this arrangement. She is starting to be a lot less thrilled.
nodes.why_relatable: He's sweet, but he's been coasting. What happens when the person who's been taking care of you stops? Can someone who has never had to try learn to show up for himself and for others?
watch_for: Who treats him like a kid, and who treats him like an adult?
What does he do when he really wants someone to take him seriously?
Which parts of his playfulness turn out to be strengths?
example_user_messages: My girlfriend dumped me and said I act like a child. She's probably right.
I've never had a real job and I'm starting to feel embarrassed about it.
I let my partner take care of everything and now she's gone and I don't know how to do anything.
I keep trying to win my ex back, but maybe I need to fix myself first.

spoiler.summary: Ann learns Andy delayed getting his casts off by two weeks so she would keep waiting on him, and she throws him out. He lives in a tent in the pit to stay near her and is hurt again when it is filled in; his settlement gets him a job running the City Hall shoeshine stand. He bonds with April, eventually lets Ann go, and falls for April. When Ann kisses him in the hospital April storms off, but he wins her back, and they marry in a surprise ceremony after a few weeks of dating. Ben moves in and tries to teach them how to be adults.
key_events: Ann dumps him after learning he delayed his cast removal
Lives in a tent in the pit
Gets the City Hall shoeshine job as part of a settlement
Lets Ann go; falls for April
Marries April at a surprise 'fancy party'
spoiler.got_right: He never loses his kindness, and he eventually accepts the breakup gracefully and starts growing up in real ways.
spoiler.got_wrong: He manipulates Ann by faking a longer recovery, camps outside her house instead of accepting the breakup, and for too long expects others to take care of him.

nodes.title: Looking for the thing you're actually good at
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, Andy is working a humble job at City Hall with little education and no real career, and the rock-star dream he has had forever isn't paying off.
nodes.pattern_label: a late bloomer searching for their calling
nodes.pattern_text: A good-hearted person who never took school or work seriously starts wanting a real career but has no idea where they'd fit. They chase a childhood dream, run into rejection, and have to decide which dreams to keep and which to let go. The story asks how you find work that uses who you really are, not who you think you should be.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, after years of odd jobs and a band that never breaks out, Andy starts to wonder what he's supposed to do with his life, and whether someone like him can have a real career at all.
nodes.why_relatable: He wants more but doesn't know how to get it. What do you do when the dream you picked doesn't pick you back? Can the qualities people dismiss as childish become the very thing you're good at?
watch_for: What is he doing when he seems happiest?
How does he handle it when a plan falls through?
Who helps him see his strengths, and how?
example_user_messages: I'm almost thirty with no degree and I have no clue what I'd even be good at.
I failed the test for the one job I've always dreamed about and I feel crushed.
People always say I'm like a big kid. Can that ever be a good thing at work?
I've held on to my music dream forever and I'm scared letting it go means I failed.

spoiler.summary: Andy takes a college class (Intro to Women's Studies) and passes. April notices that all his dream jobs involve law enforcement, and he trains hard for the police academy with Chris's help. He aces the written exam but fails the personality test. Ben hires him as an assistant at the Sweetums Foundation, sending him to London, where he gives up beer. Back home, a gig at a child's birthday party reveals a gift for children's entertainment; April becomes his manager and he becomes 'Johnny Karate', later hosting a local kids' TV show and being knighted by Lord Covington. He moves to Washington with April and eventually becomes a father.
key_events: Passes a college Women's Studies class
Aces the police written exam but fails the personality test
Becomes Ben's assistant at the Sweetums Foundation; works in London
Discovers a talent for children's entertainment
Becomes 'Johnny Karate' with his own kids' TV show
Knighted by Lord Covington
spoiler.got_right: He stays open and keeps trying after rejection, and he lets the people who love him point out strengths he couldn't see.
spoiler.got_wrong: He clings to fantasy versions of success and sometimes waits for others to hand him a direction instead of looking for one himself.

nodes.name: Tom Haverford
nodes.role: Leslie's sharp-dressed, scheming subordinate in the parks department, who cares far more about becoming a rich, famous mogul than about his government job.

nodes.title: The mogul in waiting
nodes.literal_situation: Tom works in the Pawnee parks department but has zero interest in government. He dreams of being a rich, famous entrepreneur, puts his energy into style, schemes and catchphrases, and uses his small bit of official power for perks.
nodes.pattern_label: a dreamer who loves the image more than the work
nodes.pattern_text: A person with big ambitions and endless ideas is more in love with the image of success than with the slow work it takes. They chase quick wins, flashy branding and the approval of cool people, while quietly doubting they're good enough. The story asks what it takes to turn hype into something real, and whether failure can teach them who they are.
nodes.hook: Tom has a thousand business ideas, a wardrobe his salary can't support, and a boss who praises him for doing no work. He's sure he's destined for greatness; he just hasn't started yet.
nodes.why_relatable: He wants to be somebody, and fast. Is ambition without follow-through still ambition? What happens when the persona you've built starts to crack, and what would it take to believe in yourself without the show?
watch_for: When is he performing, and when is he being himself?
How does he react when someone criticises his ideas?
Who believes in him, and does he listen to them?
example_user_messages: I have so many business ideas but I never actually finish any of them.
I spend way more money on looking successful than I actually make.
My side hustle just failed and now I have to crawl back to the boring job I quit.
I'm scared that if I stop acting confident, people will see I have no idea what I'm doing.

spoiler.summary: During the shutdown Tom works at Lady Foot Locker. He launches 'Snake Juice' at the Snakehole Lounge but is forced to sell his shares, and his cologne 'Tommy Fresh' is rejected. He quits the city to start Entertainment 720 with Jean-Ralphio; it burns through its money doing almost nothing and goes bankrupt, and Ron helps him return to his old job. His next idea, Rent-A-Swag, succeeds until Dr. Saperstein opens a copycat store and kills it. His friends help him launch Tom's Bistro, which becomes one of Pawnee's most successful businesses. In the flash-forward, an over-ambitious expansion fails, he turns that failure into bestselling self-help books, and he reacquires his bistros.
key_events: Forced to sell his Snakehole Lounge shares
Quits to found Entertainment 720, which goes bankrupt
Returns to the parks department
Rent-A-Swag succeeds, then is crushed by a copycat
Opens Tom's Bistro, a big success
Flash-forward: expansion fails; turns the failure into bestselling books
spoiler.got_right: He keeps getting back up, and eventually learns that consistency, humility and accepting help from friends matter more than swagger.
spoiler.got_wrong: He burns money on image, avoids hard work, and lets hype and unreliable partners steer his decisions.

nodes.title: Playing the field to avoid getting hurt
nodes.literal_situation: Tom is married but constantly hits on women, studies pickup-artist tactics like 'peacocking', and treats dating as a performance.
nodes.pattern_label: chasing attention instead of intimacy
nodes.pattern_text: A person who flirts with everyone and treats romance like a game keeps things shallow so nobody can really reject them. When real feelings show up, they have no idea what to do with them. The story asks what it takes for someone who performs confidence to let another person see them honestly.
nodes.hook: Tom is technically married, yet he flirts with every woman he meets and swears by pickup-artist tricks. The results are mostly embarrassing, and he acts like none of it bothers him.
nodes.why_relatable: He wants to be wanted, but only on his terms. Is all the flirting confidence or fear? What happens when someone he actually cares about isn't impressed by the act?
watch_for: What does he say about love when he thinks no one is taking him seriously?
How does he act around someone he genuinely likes compared with someone he's trying to impress?
What does he do when he's hurt?
example_user_messages: I flirt with everyone but I've never actually let anyone really know me.
I realised too late that I had real feelings for someone I was only supposed to be friends with.
I keep dating people I have nothing in common with because it's easier than getting serious.
My ex has moved on with someone I know and I can't stop thinking about it.

spoiler.summary: Tom's marriage to Wendy is a green-card arrangement. They divorce once she gets citizenship, and he realises he really had feelings for her. When Wendy dates Ron he gets jealous and brings Ron's ex Tammy as revenge, which backfires. He loses his girlfriend Lucy by talking about Wendy constantly. He has an on-and-off fling with Ann, a chaotic relationship with Mona-Lisa Saperstein, and a crush on Dr. Nadia Stasky. In 2017 he reconnects with Lucy, awkwardly hires her at his bistro rather than admit his feelings, finally tells her the truth, and proposes with a card trick at the Snakehole Lounge where they met. They marry.
key_events: His marriage to Wendy is a green-card arrangement; divorce leaves him heartbroken
Brings Tammy 2 to spite Ron, and it backfires
Loses Lucy by obsessing over Wendy
Short, messy relationship with Ann
Chaotic relationship with Mona-Lisa
Reconnects with Lucy and proposes with a card trick
spoiler.got_right: He finally drops the act, admits what he wants, and builds a relationship on honesty and shared history.
spoiler.got_wrong: For years he uses flirting and bravado to avoid vulnerability, and he chases people who feed his ego instead of those who know him.

nodes.name: Ann Perkins
nodes.role: A level-headed nurse who gets pulled into the parks department's world after demanding that something be done about the dangerous pit behind her house.

nodes.title: Finding herself outside a relationship
nodes.literal_situation: Ann is a nurse living with her long-term boyfriend, who broke both legs falling into the construction pit behind her house. She does all the caretaking at home, and her frustration with the pit brings her to a public forum where she meets the parks department's deputy director.
nodes.pattern_label: discovering who you are outside a relationship
nodes.pattern_text: A capable, caring person has spent years looking after a partner who never grew up. When they finally step away, they aren't sure who they are on their own, and they tend to absorb the tastes and lives of whoever they date next. The story asks how you build an identity that belongs to you rather than to whoever you're with.
nodes.hook: Ann is the responsible one in her relationship: she works hard, pays the bills and nurses her boyfriend while he plays video games. A chance meeting with an endlessly enthusiastic city employee opens up a friendship she never expected.
nodes.why_relatable: She is used to taking care of people. What happens when she starts asking what she wants? Why do some people lose themselves in each new relationship, and how do you find the person underneath?
watch_for: How does she change depending on who she's dating?
What does her new friendship give her that romance doesn't?
When does she stand up for her own needs?
example_user_messages: I've been taking care of my boyfriend for years and I'm exhausted.
Every time I date someone new I kind of turn into a version of them.
I just got out of a long relationship and I don't even know what I like anymore.
My best friend is the most intense person I know and somehow she's the one who makes me feel most like myself.

spoiler.summary: Ann dumps Andy after learning he delayed removing his casts to keep being pampered. She dates Mark but finds the healthy relationship boring and ends it. She kisses Chris, dates him, and then discovers he broke up with her so kindly she never noticed. She goes on a dating spree, dyes her hair, has her first big (drunken) fight with Leslie, reconciles, and takes a part-time job as the Health Department's public relations director. She has a short, mismatched relationship with Tom and briefly runs Leslie's campaign.
key_events: Dumps Andy over the cast deception
Dates Mark, then ends it out of boredom
Chris breaks up with her so gently she doesn't notice
Big drunken fight with Leslie, then reconciliation
Takes the Health Department PR job
Brief relationship with Tom
spoiler.got_right: She has the courage to leave a relationship that isn't working, and she invests deeply in her friendship with Leslie.
spoiler.got_wrong: She goes from partner to partner without asking what she wants, taking on each person's life instead of building her own.

nodes.title: Building a family on her own terms
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after years of relationships that never quite settled, Ann realises she badly wants a child and is tired of waiting for the right person to arrive first.
nodes.pattern_label: choosing parenthood without waiting for the one
nodes.pattern_text: A person in their thirties realises they want to be a parent and that waiting for the perfect partner could mean waiting forever. They decide to take matters into their own hands, which raises hard questions about who to ask for help, what might change, and what kind of life they really want. The story asks how you build a family on your own terms.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, after a string of short, unsatisfying relationships, Ann decides she doesn't want to wait for a perfect partner to start the life she wants.
nodes.why_relatable: She is ready for the next chapter, even without the traditional order of events. Is going it alone brave or reckless? How do you ask someone for help with something this big, and what if the answer changes things between you?
watch_for: How does she decide who to ask for help?
How do her friends react to her plan?
What does she want her whole life to look like, not just her family?
example_user_messages: I'm 35 and I want a baby but I'm not with anyone. Should I just do it myself?
I'm thinking of asking a friend to be a donor and I'm terrified it'll make things weird.
I'm done waiting for the perfect partner to start my life.
I have a gut feeling I need to move somewhere new to raise a family, but my best friend is here.

spoiler.summary: After babysitting Diane's daughters, Ann decides to have a baby on her own. She searches for a donor and asks Chris, who agrees; they take parenting-compatibility tests and then get back together romantically. She becomes pregnant, gets a strong gut feeling that she wants to raise the child away from Pawnee, and she and Chris move to Ann Arbor, Michigan, after a tearful farewell with Leslie. Their son Oliver is born, and years later they have a daughter named Leslie.
key_events: Decides to have a child without a partner
Asks Chris to be the donor
She and Chris get back together
Pregnant; decides to leave Pawnee
Moves to Michigan; tearful goodbye with Leslie
Son Oliver born; later a daughter named Leslie
spoiler.got_right: She stops waiting for permission and acts on what she wants, and she is honest with Chris about her needs.
spoiler.got_wrong: Her impulsive search for a donor (considering a string of acquaintances) is chaotic, and leaving means stepping away from the friendship that defined her.

nodes.name: Chris Traeger
nodes.role: An endlessly upbeat, fitness-obsessed state auditor who arrives in Pawnee with his more serious partner to fix the town's broken budget.

nodes.title: Literally the most positive person alive
nodes.literal_situation: Chris is a relentlessly upbeat state auditor who comes to Pawnee with his more serious colleague to cut the town's budget. He runs ten miles a day, eats only the healthiest food, calls everything 'literally' the best, and seems unable to say anything negative.
nodes.pattern_label: relentless positivity hiding real fragility
nodes.pattern_text: A person who has built their whole identity around being cheerful, healthy and in control can't admit when something is wrong, even to themselves. Small setbacks threaten to topple everything, and their niceness sometimes leaves others unsure where they stand. The story asks whether someone who treats their body like a machine can learn to care for their mind and let people see them struggle.
nodes.hook: Chris greets people by pointing at them and saying their full name. He was born with a rare blood disorder and wasn't expected to live three weeks, so he treats every day as a gift and seems to have no bad days at all.
nodes.why_relatable: He's everyone's biggest cheerleader, but who cheers for him? What happens when constant positivity stops working? Can you be kind without being fully honest?
watch_for: What happens when something small goes wrong for him?
How do people around him figure out what he's really feeling?
When does his niceness help, and when does it cause confusion?
example_user_messages: Everyone thinks I'm the happiest person they know, but lately I'm falling apart inside.
I'm obsessed with being healthy and in control, and one small injury sent me spiralling.
I'm so afraid of being negative that I never tell people how I really feel.
I tried to end a relationship so gently that the other person didn't even realise it had happened.
I've always taken care of my body, but I've never taken care of my mind.

spoiler.summary: Chris dates Ann, then breaks up with her so gently that she doesn't realise it. He returns to Pawnee as interim, then permanent, City Manager. A flu and a tendonitis diagnosis send him into existential crises. After Jerry's daughter Millicent dumps him, he spirals into depression; he starts seeing a therapist, Dr. Richard Nygard, and learns that working on his mind matters as much as his body. Ann asks him to father her child; they fall back in love, have a son, Oliver, and move to Michigan, with Chris handing his job to Ben. Years later they have a daughter.
key_events: Breaks up with Ann so kindly she doesn't notice
Becomes Pawnee's City Manager
Tendonitis triggers an existential crisis
Dumped by Millicent Gergich; falls into depression
Starts therapy with Dr. Nygard
Agrees to father Ann's child; they reunite and move to Michigan
spoiler.got_right: He eventually admits he needs help, goes to therapy, and learns emotional health is part of health.
spoiler.got_wrong: He hides behind cheerfulness, avoids hard truths (leaving them to Ben), and pushes his lifestyle on others instead of listening to them.

nodes.name: Johnny Rose
nodes.role: A self-made video-store tycoon whose family loses its entire fortune overnight, leaving them with nothing but a tiny rural town he once bought as a joke, where they move into two adjoining motel rooms.

nodes.title: Starting from scratch at sixty
nodes.literal_situation: His business manager embezzled the family's money and stopped paying their taxes, so the government has taken everything. The only asset left is a small backwater town he bought for his son as a gag gift, and the family is now living in its run-down motel.
nodes.pattern_label: losing everything you built late in life
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who spent decades building a successful life loses all of it through no fault of their own and has to start again with almost nothing. Their first instinct is to treat the setback as a temporary mess to escape as quickly as possible, and to lean on the status and methods that worked before. The real question is whether they can find purpose, pride and a new kind of work in the humble place they landed.
nodes.hook: He is in shock but determined to act like a CEO: making calls, trying to sell the town, and planning the family's exit. He is used to people returning his calls and taking his name seriously, and suddenly nobody does.
nodes.why_relatable: He asks himself who he is without the company, the money and the respect that came with them. He wonders whether taking small, unglamorous work means admitting defeat, and how long he can hold his family together on optimism alone.
watch_for: How does he treat the locals when he still believes he is above the town?
Which of his old business habits help him, and which hold him back?
When does 'getting out' stop being the only goal he talks about?
example_user_messages: I lost my business after thirty years and I honestly don't know who I am if I'm not running something.
We went bankrupt and had to move into a tiny place in a town I'd never have chosen. I keep telling myself it's temporary.
At my age I thought I'd be retiring, not starting over from nothing.
I feel embarrassed taking a small job when I used to be the boss of hundreds of people.
How do you rebuild your confidence when everything you worked for is just gone?

spoiler.summary: Johnny spends the early seasons trying to sell the town, chase old contacts and find a quick way back, while slowly softening toward the townspeople and the mayor who once took their doors off. When Stevie inherits the motel after her great-aunt Maureen dies, Johnny becomes her business partner, renames it the Rosebud Motel and revives it. The motel earns acclaim, Roland joins the team, and the trio pitches the idea of a motel franchise. His former assistant's New York hedge fund turns them down, but another investor funds the Rosebud Motel Group. Johnny sets up the company's office in Los Angeles so he can be with Moira, leaving town as an up-and-coming hotelier with his pride and purpose restored.
key_events: Business manager Eli embezzled the fortune
Johnny tries and fails to sell the town early on
Stevie inherits the motel and Johnny becomes her partner
The motel is rebranded as the Rosebud Motel
Former assistant's hedge fund rejects the franchise pitch
A different investor funds the Rosebud Motel Group
Johnny moves the headquarters to Los Angeles to be with Moira
spoiler.got_right: He never stops working or taking responsibility, treats his partners as equals once he respects them, and learns that a small, well-run business built with people he cares about can give him as much pride as an empire.
spoiler.got_wrong: At first he is condescending to the town and clings to the idea of a rescue from his old world; he often relies on outdated methods and underestimates the locals, especially Stevie, until they prove him wrong.

nodes.title: Getting to know his own family
nodes.literal_situation: After years of long hours running a company, he barely knows his adult son and daughter, who have no life skills. Now all four of them are crammed into two motel rooms with a connecting door.
nodes.pattern_label: a busy parent finally getting close to grown children
nodes.pattern_text: A parent who spent their children's childhood working and providing, rather than being present, is suddenly forced into close quarters with them as adults. They alternate between frustration at how unprepared their kids are and guilt about their own absence. The question is whether it's too late to become the steady, encouraging parent they wish they had been.
nodes.hook: He loves his family deeply but mostly knows how to fix problems with money, and the money is gone. His grown kids can't hold a job or do laundry, and his wife is falling apart over the loss of her old life.
nodes.why_relatable: He wonders how to push his kids to grow up without crushing them, and whether he contributed to their helplessness. He is also trying to be the calm one for everybody while quietly panicking himself.
watch_for: Notice how he talks to his children when they fail compared with when they try.
What does he do with his own fear so that nobody else sees it?
How does the way he supports his wife change over time?
example_user_messages: I worked nonstop when my kids were young and now they're adults and I feel like I don't really know them.
My grown kids moved back in and I'm torn between wanting them to stand on their own and wanting to protect them.
I'm the one holding everyone together and I'm terrified, but I can't let them see it.
Is it too late to be a better parent when your children are already in their thirties?

spoiler.summary: Johnny goes from exasperated reality-check to the family's biggest supporter. He pushes David and Alexis to work, then cheers on David's store, Alexis's diploma, degree and PR firm, and patiently backs Moira through her council seat, theatre directing and film comeback, even taking out a line of credit to fund her spending. By the finale the family is closer than it ever was when they were rich; Johnny watches David marry Patrick, sees Alexis off to a job in New York, and leaves for California with Moira.
key_events: Pushes David and Alexis to get jobs
Proudly supports Rose Apothecary and Alexis's business
Takes out a line of credit to fund Moira's spending
Attends David and Patrick's wedding
The family scatters: Alexis to New York, Johnny and Moira to Los Angeles
spoiler.got_right: His loyalty never wavers; he learns that encouragement gets more from his children than lectures, and that being present matters more than providing.
spoiler.got_wrong: He sometimes micromanages, loses his temper over his family's incompetence, and enables Moira's spending rather than having hard conversations.

nodes.name: Moira Rose
nodes.role: A dramatic former soap-opera star with an unplaceable accent and a closet of wigs, who is devastated to find herself stripped of her fortune and living in a small-town motel.

nodes.title: A star with no stage
nodes.literal_situation: A once-famous actress whose best-known role ended years ago has lost her mansion, her staff and her place in high society, and now lives in a motel in a town she finds unbearable.
nodes.pattern_label: holding on to who you used to be
nodes.pattern_text: Someone whose whole sense of self was built on being admired and important loses the status, the audience and the lifestyle that proved it. They keep performing the old identity loudly, partly as armour against grief and humiliation. The question is whether they can find new ways to matter, and a real community, without pretending the loss never happened.
nodes.hook: She stays in bed, mourns her lost wig collection's former home, and treats every local as beneath her. She insists her comeback is always around the corner.
nodes.why_relatable: She wrestles with whether admitting she's no longer at the top means disappearing entirely. She wonders if small, local ways of contributing count for anything, and whether she can accept kindness from people she has been dismissing.
watch_for: What does she do when someone in town offers her friendship she didn't ask for?
When does her grandness look like confidence, and when does it look like fear?
Which small-town roles does she scorn at first, and how does she treat them later?
example_user_messages: I used to be somebody. People recognised me. Now nobody here has any idea who I was and it's crushing.
Since I stopped working I feel invisible, and I keep acting bigger than I feel so no one notices.
I lost my house and my whole social circle and I refuse to accept this is my life now.
Is it pathetic to still be hoping for a comeback at my age?

spoiler.summary: Moira goes from sulking in the motel to joining the Jazzagals, winning a seat on the town council and directing the town's production of Cabaret. She lands a role in the low-budget horror sequel The Crows Have Eyes 3, which becomes a surprise success helped by Alexis's publicity work. Finally she is offered a return to Sunrise Bay in its reboot; after her conditions are met (including not casting Clifton Sparks), she accepts and moves to California with Johnny, having also let the town into her heart.
key_events: Joins the Jazzagals and befriends Jocelyn and Twyla
Wins a seat on the town council
Directs the town's production of Cabaret
Stars in The Crows Have Eyes 3
Signs on to the Sunrise Bay reboot and moves to California
spoiler.got_right: She never lets anyone tell her she's finished, pours real energy into the town's culture, and eventually lets herself love the people she once looked down on.
spoiler.got_wrong: Her vanity and snobbery hurt people, she resists accepting kindness for far too long, and she sometimes chases status at the expense of those around her.

nodes.title: A distant mother, up close
nodes.literal_situation: She was a largely absent parent who left her children to nannies; she can't remember her daughter's middle name. Now she shares a motel room wall with her grown son and daughter.
nodes.pattern_label: an emotionally distant parent learning to show up
nodes.pattern_text: A parent who was more focused on their own life and image than on raising their children is suddenly living in close quarters with them as adults. Their attempts at affection come out awkward, self-centred or theatrical, and the children don't expect much. The question is whether real closeness can grow late, and what it takes to become the parent your kids can actually lean on.
nodes.hook: She loves her children in theory but mostly relates to them through criticism, grand pronouncements and favouritism toward her son. Her daughter has spent years far away and they are practically strangers.
nodes.why_relatable: She is confronted with how little she knows about her own kids, and has to decide whether to face that guilt or perform her way around it. Can someone who never learned to nurture start now?
watch_for: How does she respond when her daughter needs comfort rather than advice?
Notice the difference between how she treats her two children.
When does she drop the performance and simply show she cares?
example_user_messages: I wasn't a very present mother and now my adult kids treat me like an acquaintance.
I don't really know how to comfort my daughter. Everything I say comes out wrong.
I was so wrapped up in my own career that I missed most of my children growing up. Can I fix that now?
My kids joke about how little I know them and it stings because it's true.

spoiler.summary: Moira slowly builds real relationships with both children, especially Alexis, whom she had long neglected. She comforts Alexis after her breakup with Ted, bonds with her over the film's publicity, and officiates David's wedding to Patrick in a pope-inspired outfit. Alexis ends the series telling her she's grateful they lost everything because it let her truly know her family.
key_events: Forgets Alexis's middle name early on
Grows closer to Alexis over the years
Alexis works as her publicist for The Crows Have Eyes 3
Officiates David and Patrick's wedding
Alexis says she is grateful they lost their fortune
spoiler.got_right: She keeps trying, and learns to show up with warmth instead of grand gestures; she is openly proud of her children's ambition.
spoiler.got_wrong: Her self-absorption repeatedly makes moments about her, and she plays favourites, leaving Alexis feeling second-best for a long time.

nodes.name: David Rose
nodes.role: The anxious, sarcastic, fashion-obsessed adult son of a formerly wealthy family, a former New York gallerist forced to move into a small-town motel with his parents and sister.

nodes.title: The guarded heart
nodes.literal_situation: Back in the city, his friends and lovers mostly wanted his money and status. Now broke and stuck in a tiny town, he is prickly, fearful and convinced nobody here could understand him.
nodes.pattern_label: learning to trust love after being used
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has been used and discarded by the people around them has learned to keep everyone at a distance with sarcasm and high standards. They expect every relationship to end badly and sabotage things before they can get hurt. The question is whether they can let themselves be seen and loved by someone kind, and believe they deserve it.
nodes.hook: He is miserable, lonely and anxious, hiding behind sharp jokes and black-and-white sweaters. The only person in town he clicks with is the equally sardonic motel clerk.
nodes.why_relatable: He wonders whether his old friends ever cared about him, and whether he can make real connections in a place where he feels like an outsider. When someone is kind to him, he isn't sure whether to trust it.
watch_for: How does he react when someone is straightforwardly nice to him?
Notice the ways he protects himself before he can be rejected.
What does his friendship with the motel clerk give him that nothing else does?
example_user_messages: Every relationship I've had, people wanted something from me. I don't know how to trust someone who's just nice.
I push people away with jokes before they can get close enough to hurt me.
I've never been in a relationship longer than a few months and I'm scared I'm just not built for it.
I moved somewhere I hate and the only friend I have is the one person as cynical as me.
Someone genuinely kind likes me and my first instinct is to find out what's wrong with them.

spoiler.summary: David has a brief fling with Stevie that turns into a deep best-friendship, gets hurt in a messy throuple with Stevie and Jake, and is manipulated by an old flame. Then he meets Patrick, his business partner at Rose Apothecary; they begin dating and it becomes the longest relationship of his life. A rough patch when Patrick's ex-fiancee Rachel shows up tests his trust, but they reconcile, Patrick proposes on a hike, and David chooses to stay in town, buy the cottage Patrick loves and marry him in the town hall, with Moira officiating.
key_events: Brief romantic fling with Stevie becomes best-friendship
Throuple with Stevie and Jake
Meets Patrick and starts dating him
Patrick's ex-fiancee Rachel appears
Patrick proposes on a hike
David decides not to move to New York and stays
David and Patrick marry in the town hall
spoiler.got_right: He eventually lets his guard down, forgives, communicates his fears, and makes a romantic gesture of his own instead of waiting to be pursued.
spoiler.got_wrong: He catastrophises, retreats when hurt, and tests people's loyalty instead of trusting it; his sarcasm often hurts those who care about him.

nodes.title: Taste looking for a purpose
nodes.literal_situation: He has an eye for design and curation but no practical skills with money, paperwork or inventory. Needing an income, he has to find work in a town that doesn't value anything he's good at.
nodes.pattern_label: turning a niche talent into a real livelihood
nodes.pattern_text: Someone with a strong creative eye but little practical experience has to earn a living for the first time in a place that doesn't seem to need what they offer. They must decide whether to compromise their standards or find a way to make their taste useful to others. The question is whether they can build something of their own, and accept help from people with the skills they lack.
nodes.hook: He is scornful of every job on offer and scared of failing at something that matters to him. His past career has left him with standards but no plan.
nodes.why_relatable: He asks whether he is actually good at anything that pays, whether working for someone else is a humiliation, and whether it's safe to risk failure publicly.
watch_for: What does he do when a job clashes with his idea of good taste?
How does he handle being told his numbers don't add up?
Notice when he lets someone else's strengths fill his gaps.
example_user_messages: I have great taste and zero business sense. How do I turn that into an actual job?
I'm terrified of opening my own shop because if it fails, it's my failure in front of everyone.
The only jobs around here feel beneath me and I hate that I think that way.
I'm creative but spreadsheets make me want to cry. I need a partner who's the opposite of me.

spoiler.summary: David first takes a job at the Blouse Barn and transforms it into an upscale boutique, then opens Rose Apothecary, which rebrands local products on consignment. Patrick, a practical business-minded newcomer, helps him with the licensing and becomes his business partner. The store thrives; David learns to trust Patrick's financial sense while supplying the vision, and ultimately chooses to keep running it in town rather than move back to New York.
key_events: Works at the Blouse Barn
Opens Rose Apothecary
Patrick becomes his business partner
Stays in town to keep running the store
spoiler.got_right: He commits to his vision, discovers he is genuinely brilliant at retail, and learns to share control with a partner who complements him.
spoiler.got_wrong: He is snobbish about honest work early on, avoids the unglamorous parts of business, and lets fear of failure make him defensive.

nodes.name: Alexis Rose
nodes.role: A globe-trotting socialite who has partied with celebrities and escaped absurd scrapes abroad, and who never finished high school, now broke and stuck with her family in a small-town motel.

nodes.title: The girl who was always rescued
nodes.literal_situation: She has always survived on charm, wealthy boyfriends and her parents' money. With all of that gone, she has no diploma, no job history and no plan beyond waiting for someone to whisk her away.
nodes.pattern_label: going from dependent to self-made
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has always been carried by charm, money or the people who wanted to take care of them suddenly has none of that safety net. They have to go back to basics, often feeling behind people much younger, and discover whether they can build a life on their own effort. The question is whether they can take themselves seriously before anyone else does.
nodes.hook: She is bored, oblivious and sure this is a brief detour. Her main strategy is finding a man who can get her out of town.
nodes.why_relatable: She wonders whether she is more than a pretty face with good stories, whether it's embarrassing to go back and finish what she skipped, and what she actually wants to do with her life.
watch_for: What does she do when she's the oldest person in a room of beginners?
Notice which of her party-girl skills turn out to be useful.
When does she start choosing things for herself rather than for a partner?
example_user_messages: I'm almost thirty and I never finished school. Going back feels humiliating but I don't see another way.
I've always relied on whoever I was dating to take care of me, and now I'm on my own and I don't know where to start.
People think I'm shallow and honestly I'm scared they're right.
I want to build a career that's actually mine, not something someone handed me.

spoiler.summary: Alexis finishes her high school diploma, earns an associate degree in public relations at Elmdale College, and starts Alexis Rose Communications, doing marketing for the motel and organising events for the town. After a heartbreaking breakup she throws herself into work as Moira's publicist for The Crows Have Eyes 3, impressing the streaming service Interflix, which hires her in New York. She even turns down Twyla's offer of money to make it on her own.
key_events: Earns her high school diploma
Studies PR at Elmdale College
Starts Alexis Rose Communications
Works as Moira's publicist for the film
Hired by Interflix in New York
Turns down Twyla's money to go it alone
spoiler.got_right: She commits to the unglamorous work of catching up, turns her social skills into a profession, and chooses independence even when help is offered.
spoiler.got_wrong: Early on she is self-absorbed and flaky, leans on men and her brother to bail her out, and underestimates herself for a long time.

nodes.title: Choosing between two kinds of love
nodes.literal_situation: Used to flings with celebrities, she quickly attracts attention from two very different local men: a laid-back, off-grid guy and the earnest town vet.
nodes.pattern_label: learning that love means sacrifice
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has always treated romance as fun, escape or rescue discovers that real love asks for honesty, patience and sometimes letting go. They bounce between partners without knowing what they truly want. The question is whether they can love someone generously, even when it costs them.
nodes.hook: She is enjoying the attention and treating romance as a way to pass the time or escape. She hasn't had to think about what a partner needs from her.
nodes.why_relatable: She wonders if she's ready for something serious, whether she's just attracted to being wanted, and what happens when a relationship clashes with her own goals.
watch_for: What draws her to each of the two men, and what does she avoid with each?
How does she react when someone asks for a real commitment?
Notice when she starts putting someone else's needs next to her own.
example_user_messages: I keep going back and forth between two people and I don't know if I actually love either of them.
My partner got an amazing opportunity far away and I don't know whether to follow or stay.
We love each other but our careers are pulling us in opposite directions.
I've always dated for fun. I don't know how to be in something real.

spoiler.summary: Alexis vacillates between Mutt and Ted, turning down proposals, then takes time to focus on herself. She reunites with Ted at the end of season four and they build a mature relationship. Ted gets a research job in the Galapagos; she hesitates to leave her family, agrees to go, but a mix-up means she never leaves. After a stretch of long-distance dating she ends it with him amicably because their careers are headed in opposite directions, a painful but selfless choice.
key_events: Dates both Mutt and Ted
Turns down marriage proposals
Reunites with Ted at the end of season four
Ted leaves for the Galapagos
Long-distance relationship with Ted
Amicable breakup with Ted
spoiler.got_right: She learns to love generously, supports Ted's dream even when it hurts her, and ends things with honesty and kindness instead of drifting.
spoiler.got_wrong: She strings both men along early on and uses relationships as escape routes before she knows what she wants.

nodes.name: Stevie Budd
nodes.role: The deadpan, cynical clerk at the town's run-down motel, a local who has never left and keeps most people at arm's length.

nodes.title: The loner behind the front desk
nodes.literal_situation: She has spent her whole life in a small town where she finds almost no one interesting, working a dead-end motel job and doing as little as possible. Then an eccentric, broke family moves into two of the rooms.
nodes.pattern_label: a stuck, guarded person letting others in
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who never left their hometown has settled into a small, safe routine and a protective cynicism, expecting little from life or people. When unexpected newcomers show up, they find a real friend and start being asked to take on more than they think they can handle. The question is whether they can let people close and believe they are capable of more.
nodes.hook: She is sarcastic, lonely and unimpressed by everything, especially the new motel guests. She would rather mock the family than admit she's curious about them.
nodes.why_relatable: She wonders whether she's already missed her chance at a bigger life, whether she will end up alone like her great-aunt, and whether she's worth taking seriously.
watch_for: How does she respond when someone treats her as an equal instead of a townie?
Notice how she handles moments where she's asked to take charge.
What does her humour protect her from?
example_user_messages: I've lived in the same small town my whole life and I've basically given up expecting anything to happen.
I don't really have friends. People bore me, or at least that's what I tell myself.
Suddenly I'm responsible for something big and I have no idea if I can handle it.
I'm scared of turning into the lonely relative everyone pities.

spoiler.summary: Stevie has a brief fling with David that turns into a lifelong best-friendship. When her great-aunt Maureen dies she inherits the motel, and with Johnny as her business partner she steps up, renames and renovates it as the Rosebud Motel, and learns marketing and management. She becomes part of the Rose family in all but name.
key_events: Brief fling with David becomes best-friendship
Great-aunt Maureen dies
Inherits the motel
Partners with Johnny to relaunch it as the Rosebud Motel
spoiler.got_right: She lets herself care about people, rises to responsibility, and learns from Johnny without losing her own voice.
spoiler.got_wrong: She hides behind cynicism and low self-esteem, and often assumes the worst about herself and others.

nodes.title: Wondering what else is out there
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that makes her life look more stable than ever, she suddenly starts questioning her future and whether she has settled for the town she grew up in.
nodes.pattern_label: questioning whether you've settled for too little
nodes.pattern_text: Someone whose life has finally become stable is hit by the worry that they never tested what else they could have done. Friends seem to be moving forward while they feel stuck. The question is whether they need to leave to prove themselves, or just need to know that they could.
nodes.hook: She is doing better than she ever has, but restlessness and a fear of being ordinary are creeping in, and she feels left behind by the people around her.
nodes.why_relatable: She wonders if staying close to home is a choice or a lack of courage, whether she should take risks that terrify her, and what happens if she tries and fails.
watch_for: What does she say yes to that surprises everyone, including herself?
How does comparing herself with her friends affect her choices?
Notice the difference between wanting to leave and wanting the option to.
example_user_messages: My life is fine, stable even, but lately I can't shake the feeling that I've settled.
Everyone around me seems to be moving on to bigger things and I'm still in my hometown.
I don't necessarily want to leave. I just want to know I could.
I said yes to something completely outside my comfort zone and now I'm panicking.

spoiler.summary: In season five Stevie has an existential crisis and pushes herself out of her comfort zone, accepting Moira's offer to play Sally Bowles in the town's Cabaret, and triumphing. In season six she briefly quits to work as a flight attendant for Larry Air, then returns to help Johnny and Roland land an investor for the Rosebud Motel Group. She stays based in town while travelling to open new locations, explaining to David she never needed to move to a big city, she just needed to know she could.
key_events: Plays Sally Bowles in Moira's Cabaret
Briefly leaves to work for Larry Air
Helps found the Rosebud Motel Group
Stays based in town while travelling for new locations
spoiler.got_right: She takes real risks, trusts mentors who believe in her, and defines success on her own terms.
spoiler.got_wrong: She compares herself to others and makes impulsive moves to prove something rather than figuring out what she actually wants.

nodes.name: Patrick Brewer
nodes.role: An earnest, practical, business-minded newcomer to town who helps with local business registrations and takes an interest in a new shop opening up.

nodes.title: The steady guy starting fresh
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, a calm, practical man arrives in town having left his previous life behind. He is drawn to helping launch a quirky new local shop and to the person running it.
nodes.pattern_label: realising the life you planned wasn't yours
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who did everything expected of them realises the life they were building never quite felt right, and leaves it behind without being sure what comes next. As they start fresh, they have to learn to name what they truly want and say it out loud, even to the people they love most. The question is whether they can stop avoiding hard conversations and live openly as themselves.
nodes.hook: He seems like the most well-adjusted person in town: kind, organised and confident about business. Beneath that, he is private about his past and unsure how to say what he really feels.
nodes.why_relatable: He wonders how to tell the people who know him best that he has changed, whether starting over this late means he wasted years, and how to be brave about feelings when he's always been the calm, sensible one.
watch_for: Notice what he leaves unsaid, and how that affects the people around him.
How does he handle it when someone reacts to him with insecurity rather than trust?
When does his calmness help, and when is it a way of avoiding something?
example_user_messages: I was engaged, I had the whole life planned out, and I walked away because something never felt right.
I'm in my thirties and only now figuring out who I actually am. Is that normal?
I'm terrified to tell my parents something about myself because I don't want them to see me differently.
I avoid the big conversations and then people get hurt because I didn't say anything.
I finally feel like myself and I want to do something romantic about it, but I've never been good at saying how I feel.

spoiler.summary: Patrick left his fiancee Rachel and moved to town, realising he had never felt the right way about the relationships he was in. He becomes David's business partner at Rose Apothecary, lets David make the first move, and they begin dating; it is his first relationship with a man and he finally feels 'what right feels like'. Rachel's surprise appearance causes a rift because he never told David about her, but they reconcile. He comes out to his loving parents, who accept him, stars in Moira's Cabaret, sets down roots in town, proposes to David on a hike and marries him, and they buy the cottage he dreamed of.
key_events: Left ex-fiancee Rachel before arriving
Becomes David's business partner
David kisses him and they start dating
Serenades David at the store's open mic
Rachel shows up unannounced
Comes out to his parents, who accept him
Proposes to David and marries him
spoiler.got_right: He is kind, patient and brave in his romantic gestures, and ultimately lives openly and joyfully as himself.
spoiler.got_wrong: He avoids rocking the boat on big things: he didn't make clear their first date was a date, hid his past engagement, and delayed telling his parents, which hurt people he loved.

nodes.name: Roland Schitt
nodes.role: The nosy, loud, fourth-generation mayor of the small town, who enjoys lording his local power over the newly broke family that just arrived.

nodes.title: The small-town big shot
nodes.literal_situation: As mayor of a town the newcomers technically own, he enjoys reminding the formerly rich family that they depend on his goodwill, and turns up uninvited to comment on everything they do.
nodes.pattern_label: a petty power player learning generosity
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has always been a big fish in a small pond uses the little power they have to feel important, especially over people who once looked down on them. They are loud, tactless and more interested in the title than the work. The question is whether they can become someone people rely on and grow into their responsibilities at work and at home.
nodes.hook: He takes the family's doors off their motel rooms after a spat, overshares constantly, and seems to embody everything they fear about the town.
nodes.why_relatable: Under the bluster he wants respect and friendship, and he is unsure how to earn them. He is also facing whether he takes his responsibilities, at work and at home, as seriously as he takes his title.
watch_for: What does he want from the newcomers underneath the teasing?
Notice the moments he goes out of his way for someone without making a show of it.
Which responsibility does he treat seriously first?
example_user_messages: I've always liked being the guy in charge around here, but I'm not sure anyone actually respects me.
I realise I've been kind of a bully to someone new and now I want to be their friend.
I'm becoming a dad again later in life and I want to do it properly this time.
I talk big but honestly I've never done much with my position.

spoiler.summary: Roland's antagonism toward Johnny softens into an unlikely friendship; they help each other out and he eventually takes a job at the motel with Johnny and Stevie. When Jocelyn has a baby, being a hands-on father becomes the first job he really takes seriously. He becomes a partner in the Rosebud Motel Group, stays to run the town location with a new income, and sends the Roses off with a prank tribute, putting their pictures on the town's welcome sign.
key_events: Removes the Roses' motel room doors early on
Becomes friends with Johnny
He and Jocelyn have a baby
Starts working at the motel
Partner in the Rosebud Motel Group
Puts the Roses on the town welcome sign
spoiler.got_right: He is fiercely loyal once he cares about someone, wants to do right by his town, and embraces fatherhood wholeheartedly.
spoiler.got_wrong: He uses petty power to feel important, is tactless and lazy about real change, and makes things about himself.

nodes.name: Twyla Sands
nodes.role: The endlessly cheerful waitress at the town cafe, who offers kindness to every newcomer and casually tells alarming stories about her chaotic family.

nodes.title: Sunshine from a stormy family
nodes.literal_situation: She waits tables at the local cafe, often gets orders wrong, and shrugs off stories about relatives in prison, cults and bad marriages as perfectly normal. The formerly rich family becomes some of her regulars.
nodes.pattern_label: staying kind when your family is chaos
nodes.pattern_text: Someone raised in a chaotic, dysfunctional family has chosen to be warm, generous and content with a simple life. Others underestimate them or overlook them, but they quietly show up for everyone. The question is what they really want for themselves, and whether they can let people see beyond their cheerful role.
nodes.hook: She is sweet, a little scattered and always ready to listen, while the people around her mostly talk about their own problems and rarely ask about hers.
nodes.why_relatable: She quietly faces the question of how much of her family's chaos she carries, whether being the kind one means being overlooked, and what she would do if her life suddenly offered more choices.
watch_for: Notice how others treat her stories, and how she tells them.
Who in the new family actually sees her, and when?
What does she seem to want for herself, when she's asked?
example_user_messages: My family is a total mess and I've just decided to be nice to everyone anyway.
People think I'm a bit of an airhead and never ask how I'm doing.
I'm happy with a simple life and people act like that means I lack ambition.
I always listen to everyone else's problems. I'm not sure anyone would listen to mine.

spoiler.summary: Twyla stays a warm presence throughout, befriending Moira in the Jazzagals and becoming close to Alexis. At the end of the series she reveals she won the lottery around the time the Roses arrived, keeping $46 million secret because she didn't want to be treated differently. She decides she already has what she needs, buys Cafe Tropical to run as her own, and offers Alexis money for New York, which Alexis declines, calling her the best person she has ever known.
key_events: Joins the Jazzagals with Moira
Close friendship with Alexis
Reveals she secretly won the lottery
Buys Cafe Tropical
Offers Alexis money for New York
spoiler.got_right: She defines a good life on her own terms and treats everyone with generosity, rich or broke.
spoiler.got_wrong: She keeps her own needs and secrets so hidden that even friends rarely see her fully, and normalises some genuinely troubling family history.

nodes.name: Otis Milburn
nodes.role: An anxious, awkward sixteen-year-old whose mother is a famous sex therapist, and who knows everything about sex in theory and nothing in practice.

nodes.title: The one who fixes everyone else
nodes.literal_situation: Otis has absorbed years of his therapist mother's language and can read people's intimate problems with uncanny accuracy, yet he is terrified of his own body and of getting close to anyone. When he accidentally talks a classmate through a crisis, the sharp, broke Maeve Wiley proposes they run a secret, paid sex-advice clinic for the whole school.
nodes.pattern_label: helping everyone while avoiding your own wounds
nodes.pattern_text: A person who is naturally gifted at listening and giving advice becomes the go-to helper for everyone around them, while quietly avoiding their own fears about intimacy and an old family hurt they have never processed. Being needed feels safer than being vulnerable. The question is whether they can take their own advice, and what happens to their relationships when helping others becomes a way of hiding.
nodes.hook: Otis is the kid nobody notices, carrying a secret: he is so anxious about intimacy that he cannot even touch himself. Suddenly his advice is in demand, he is earning money, and the girl he admires is his business partner. For the first time he feels useful and seen, as long as nobody looks too closely at him.
nodes.why_relatable: Why is it so much easier to understand other people's problems than your own? Can you be good at helping and still be bad at being honest about yourself? What does it cost the people closest to you when you are always the counsellor and never the one who needs help?
watch_for: What happens in Otis's body when things get close to intimate, and what might sit underneath it?
How does he behave when someone asks him for help versus when someone asks him how he feels?
Notice how he treats his best friend when the clinic starts going well.
example_user_messages: Everyone comes to me for advice but I can't sort out my own life at all.
I get panic attacks whenever things get physical with someone and I don't know why.
I'm really good at helping my friends but I never let anyone help me.
Something I saw as a kid with my parents still messes with how I feel about relationships.
I started something on the side that people love, but I feel like a fraud because I've never actually done what I'm advising on.

spoiler.summary: Otis's anxiety traces back to catching his father Remi having sex with a client as a child, and Jean's blunt explanation that sex can ruin lives. The clinic makes him popular and brings him close to Maeve, but it also feeds his arrogance: he neglects Eric, steals his mother's confidential notes to find out why Ola dumped him (leaking clients' secrets across the school), and drunkenly humiliates Ola and Maeve at a party he throws. He loses his virginity to Ruby that night. A frank talk with his father about not repeating his mistakes helps him own his behaviour. At Cavendish College he starts a new clinic and gets into a petty election war with rival therapist O, loses the support of students, and finally makes peace with her so they can run a clinic together.
key_events: Childhood memory of his father's affair revealed as the root of his anxiety
Steals Jean's therapy notebook; clients' secrets spread through the school
Drunken house party where he insults Ola and Maeve
Loses his virginity to Ruby after the party
Confronts his absent father and gets honest advice from him
Rivalry and election with O at Cavendish, ending in a partnership
spoiler.got_right: Genuine, non-judgemental listening; he really does help people, and he keeps coming back to apologise properly when he gets things wrong.
spoiler.got_wrong: Using the clinic as a place to hide and as a source of status, prying into private information, and treating his best friend and his mother as afterthoughts.

nodes.title: Needing space from a parent who analyses everything
nodes.literal_situation: Otis lives alone with his mother Jean, a brilliant, glamorous sex therapist who fills the house with anatomical art, brings home a string of one-night stands and cannot stop analysing her son. His father left years ago for America and mostly exists on video calls.
nodes.pattern_label: separating from a loving but intrusive parent
nodes.pattern_text: A teenager raised by a single parent who is warm, clever and utterly boundary-less feels smothered and exposed, while also being the person that parent leans on most. As the family changes shape around them, they have to work out how to become their own person without shutting out the parent who loves them. It is a story about boundaries, resentment and discovering that you still need each other.
nodes.hook: Otis wants one thing from his mother: privacy. She reads his moods like case files, talks openly about his development, and he suspects she is more interested in understanding him than in simply knowing him. He loves her and is quietly furious with her.
nodes.why_relatable: How do you set boundaries with a parent who thinks openness is always healthy? When is a parent's curiosity care, and when is it control? How do you stay close to someone while needing to pull away to grow up?
watch_for: What does Jean do with the things Otis tells her, and what does he stop telling her as a result?
How does Otis talk about his absent father compared with the parent who stayed?
Notice who looks after whom in this house when things get hard.
example_user_messages: My mum wants to talk about everything and I just want her to stay out of my business.
I found out my parent was writing about my private life without asking me.
My dad left when I was little and still acts like a fun uncle instead of a father.
We said awful things to each other and then she ended up in hospital, and I can't stop thinking about it.
My mum's struggling after having a baby and I've become the one holding the house together.

spoiler.summary: Otis discovers Jean has been writing a book about his sexual development and later that she has been secretly dating Jakob, the father of his girlfriend Ola. Jean's work at Moordale threatens his clinic, and he betrays her professionally by stealing her notes. When Jean becomes pregnant, Jakob and Ola move in and Otis struggles with a blended household. After a bitter fight, Jean goes into premature labour and nearly dies from a haemorrhage; Otis tells her he still needs her. The baby, Joy, turns out not to be Jakob's, and Jakob and Ola leave. In the final season Otis ends up parenting his mother as she battles postnatal depression, calls in her estranged sister Joanna, and by the end tells Jean he is proud of her.
key_events: Discovers Jean's book about him
Jean and Jakob's relationship revealed while he is dating Ola
Otis leaks Jean's confidential notes
Jean's pregnancy; Jakob and Ola move in
Premature birth and near-fatal haemorrhage
Paternity test shows Jakob is not the father; Jakob and Ola move out
Jean's postnatal depression; aunt Joanna arrives
spoiler.got_right: Eventually saying the vulnerable thing out loud, stepping up for his mother and baby sister, and letting a new father figure in.
spoiler.got_wrong: Punishing Jean with coldness and cruelty instead of stating his boundaries, and assuming there would always be time to make up.

nodes.title: Falling for the girl he works with
nodes.literal_situation: Otis starts running the clinic with Maeve Wiley, the sharp-tongued outsider everyone gossips about. She is dating the most popular boy in school, she seems out of his league, and he is falling for her anyway.
nodes.pattern_label: loving someone but never saying it in time
nodes.pattern_text: Two people who work closely together fall for each other, but fear, pride, bad timing and other relationships keep either of them from saying it at the right moment. Every missed chance creates new hurt and new partners caught in the middle. It asks what it really takes to be honest about your feelings, and whether loving someone is the same as being right for each other right now.
nodes.hook: Otis is quietly in love with his business partner and has no idea how to say it. He is also asked, for money, to help her boyfriend win her over.
nodes.why_relatable: What do you do when you have feelings for someone you work closely with? Is it more loyal to hide what you feel or to say it and risk everything? How many chances do you get to say the important thing?
watch_for: How does Otis handle being asked to help a rival with the person he likes?
Notice how often the important conversation almost happens, and what interrupts it.
How honest is Otis with the other people he dates about where his heart is?
example_user_messages: I'm in love with my best friend and colleague and I keep missing the moment to tell her.
I'm dating someone lovely but I think I'm still hung up on someone else.
Every time we get close one of us is with someone else.
We finally got together and now we're in a long-distance thing and I'm jealous of everyone she meets.
Is it possible to love someone and still not be right for each other yet?

spoiler.summary: Otis sabotages-by-advice Jackson's pursuit of Maeve, which backfires and makes them a couple; when Maeve learns he shared her private details with Jackson she freezes him out. By the time she is ready to confess, she sees him kissing Ola. He stays with Ola out of fear of becoming a cheater like his father, is dumped, humiliates Maeve at his party and sleeps with Ruby. His voicemail declaring love is deleted by Isaac. He dates Ruby but cannot say he loves her and they break up. On the France trip he tells Maeve what the voicemail said and they kiss; they finally get together, but Maeve leaves for a study programme in America. Long distance breeds jealousy, a night spent (platonically) in Ruby's bed becomes a secret, and when Maeve returns for her mother's funeral they finally sleep together but agree to break up so she can pursue her future. The creator has said she imagines them together about ten years later.
key_events: Otis's advice helps Jackson win Maeve
Maeve sees Otis kissing Ola just as she comes to confess
Isaac deletes Otis's love voicemail
Otis and Ruby date; he can't say 'I love you' back
Otis and Maeve kiss in France and become a couple
Maeve goes to America; long-distance strain
Otis and Maeve break up so she can chase her dreams
spoiler.got_right: He learns to say how he feels plainly and, in the end, to love someone enough to let them go.
spoiler.got_wrong: Manipulating a rival, staying in relationships he wasn't committed to, lashing out when hurt, and keeping secrets that eroded trust.

nodes.name: Maeve Wiley
nodes.role: A fiercely intelligent, sarcastic loner who lives alone in a caravan, writes other students' essays for rent money and carries a cruel nickname from an old rumour.

nodes.title: The girl who raised herself
nodes.literal_situation: Maeve's father walked out, her mother struggled with drugs, and the older brother who raised her has disappeared. At sixteen she pays her own rent on a caravan by selling essays and keeps everyone at a distance.
nodes.pattern_label: the child who had to parent herself
nodes.pattern_text: A young person who was let down by every adult in their family has built a hard shell of self-reliance: paying their own way, trusting no one, expecting to be left. When an unreliable parent reappears asking for another chance, they have to decide how much to give, how to protect a younger sibling, and whether they can grieve a parent they never really had. It is a story about loyalty, painful boundaries and letting a chosen family in.
nodes.hook: Maeve is alone, broke and determined never to need anyone. The school sees a 'bad girl'; the reality is a teenager doing an adult's job with no safety net, and a family that keeps leaving.
nodes.why_relatable: What do you owe a parent who wasn't there? How do you protect a younger sibling when the adults around them aren't safe? Can you let people help you without feeling weak? And what happens to someone who has learned that everyone leaves?
watch_for: How does Maeve react when someone does something kind for her without being asked?
What does she want from her mother, and does she ever say it?
Notice the moments she chooses responsibility over what she wants.
example_user_messages: My mum was never really there and now she wants back into my life and I don't know if I can trust her.
I've been looking after myself since I was a teenager and I don't know how to let anyone help.
I had to report my own parent to protect my little sister and I feel like a traitor.
My brother keeps disappearing whenever things get hard.
My mum died of an overdose and I don't know how to grieve someone who hurt me so much.

spoiler.summary: Maeve takes the fall for her brother Sean when he deals drugs at the school dance and is expelled; Sean leaves again. Her mother Erin returns claiming to be clean, with a toddler, Elsie. When Isaac helps prove Erin is using again, Maeve reports her to social services; Elsie goes into foster care with Anna and Erin says she'll never forgive her. Maeve moves in with Anna, later tracks down Erin after she takes Elsie, and the two reach a fragile reconciliation; Erin pays for Maeve's study trip. In the final season Erin overdoses and dies. Sean returns, fears becoming like her, and leaves again during the funeral, so Maeve organises it with Aimee and Otis and scatters the ashes with Aimee and Isaac over the caravan park.
key_events: Expelled after covering for Sean
Erin returns with half-sister Elsie
Maeve reports Erin to social services; Elsie fostered
Moves in with foster carer Anna
Erin's overdose and death
Sean leaves again; Maeve organises the funeral
spoiler.got_right: Protecting Elsie even when it cost her her mother, and eventually letting friends hold her up.
spoiler.got_wrong: Pushing away people who love her and assuming help always comes with strings.

nodes.title: Believing she's allowed to aim high
nodes.literal_situation: Maeve is the most talented writer at school, but she spends it ghost-writing other people's award-winning essays for cash. She acts as if school doesn't matter because wanting something that badly feels dangerous.
nodes.pattern_label: a gifted outsider afraid to want more
nodes.pattern_text: A brilliant person from a hard background has learned to hide their talent and pretend not to care, because hoping for more has only ever led to disappointment. When a mentor pushes them toward real opportunities, they face impostor feelings among more privileged peers, harsh criticism and the pull of the people who need them at home. The question is whether they can believe they deserve the future their talent could buy.
nodes.hook: Maeve reads feminist literature, writes brilliantly and tells herself the future is for other people. She is wasting her gift to survive, and part of her knows it.
nodes.why_relatable: Is it safer not to try than to try and fail? What does it feel like to be the only one in the room who had to fight to get there? When a mentor believes in you more than you do, do you trust them? And how do you choose between your ambitions and the people you love?
watch_for: What does Maeve do when a teacher tells her she could go somewhere?
How does she react to people who have had things easier than her?
Whose voice does she listen to when she's about to give up?
example_user_messages: I come from nothing and I keep sabotaging opportunities because I don't think I deserve them.
Everyone on my course has money and connections and I feel like a fraud.
A teacher told me my writing wasn't good enough and I want to quit.
I got an amazing opportunity abroad but it means leaving the person I love.
I'm scared that if I try properly and fail, it'll prove everyone right about me.

spoiler.summary: Maeve forces her way back into school by exposing who she wrote essays for, joins the Aptitude Scheme and the quiz team under Ms Sands, and learns to work with others. She is accepted onto a gifted study programme in America, nearly turns it down for Otis, and goes after Aimee (as her 'mum') talks her into it. At Wallace University she feels out of place among wealthy students, burns out, and is crushed when her tutor Molloy dismisses her novel. After her mother's death she almost drops out and enrols locally, but a heart-to-heart with Jean convinces her not to let one teacher decide her future. She returns to America, a publisher asks to read more of her novel, and Molloy apologises.
key_events: Re-enrols by exposing essay clients
Joins the quiz team and Aptitude Scheme with Ms Sands
Accepted to the US study programme
Molloy tears down her writing
Jean encourages her to go back
Publisher interest in her novel
spoiler.got_right: Fighting for her place and ultimately choosing her own future.
spoiler.got_wrong: Letting a single harsh critic almost end her dream, and shutting teammates out out of pride.

nodes.title: Letting someone in
nodes.literal_situation: Since an ugly rumour at fourteen, Maeve has been the school's favourite target. She sleeps with the popular swimmer but refuses to call him her boyfriend, and her only real friend won't be seen with her in public. Then she starts a business with Otis, who listens to her like no one else does.
nodes.pattern_label: learning to trust after being shamed
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has been judged and gossiped about for years protects herself by keeping romance casual and everyone at arm's length. When a kind, attentive person gets under her defences, and a thoughtful partner is also on offer, she has to weigh safety against real feeling, and learn to forgive people who hurt her out of fear. It is about trust, reputation and choosing love without losing yourself.
nodes.hook: Maeve doesn't do boyfriends, doesn't do feelings and doesn't expect anyone to see past her reputation. Working beside a boy who genuinely respects her is starting to make that harder.
