nodes.role: The Roy family company's long-serving general counsel, a calm, dry-witted insider who has quietly held things together for Logan for decades, and Roman's godmother.

nodes.title: Competent, overlooked and surviving
nodes.literal_situation: Gerri knows every secret in the company, including the huge debt Logan has hidden. When Logan falls ill and the family scrambles for power, she is the steady adult in the room, but nobody seriously considers her as more than the help.
nodes.pattern_label: the capable insider nobody considers for the top
nodes.pattern_text: An experienced, highly competent person has spent decades making a powerful family's problems disappear. Everyone relies on them and nobody sees them as a leader. When the family's infighting threatens everything, they have to decide how far to protect others, how far to protect themselves, and whether they want a turn at the top.
nodes.hook: Gerri is calm, careful and indispensable. As the family turns on itself she needs to keep her own position while everyone around her panics.
nodes.why_relatable: How do you survive in a workplace where power belongs to a family you'll never be part of? Is staying neutral wise or cowardly? Would you even want to lead, if everyone has already decided you're just the safe pair of hands?
watch_for: When she stays silent in a crisis, whose interests is she protecting?
Notice how she handles the young man who keeps testing her.
Does she want the top job, or just not to lose everything?
example_user_messages: I've been with this company thirty years and I'm still treated like the help.
I'm the one who cleans up everyone's messes and nobody thinks of me as leadership material.
The owners are fighting each other and I'm just trying not to get caught in the middle.
A younger guy at work keeps crossing lines with me and part of me enjoys the power.

spoiler.summary: Gerri reveals the company's hidden debt to Kendall, abstains in the no-confidence vote, and develops a strange, verbally dominant bond with Roman while mentoring him. She is named among those exposed by the cruise scandal but survives, and in Season 3 Logan makes her interim CEO. Roman then accidentally sends Logan an explicit photo meant for her, which undermines her position. Logan plans to fire her, and after his death Roman does fire her; she fights back with the threat of a harassment lawsuit and keeps her leverage through the sale.
key_events: Reveals the hidden debt to Kendall
Abstains from the no-confidence vote
Charged relationship with Roman
Named in the cruise scandal but survives
Becomes interim CEO in Season 3
Roman's explicit photo reaches Logan
Fired by Roman after Logan's death; threatens to sue
spoiler.got_right: She stayed level-headed, gave honest counsel, and protected herself when the family would not.
spoiler.got_wrong: She entangled herself with the boss's son and spent decades protecting a company whose crimes she knew about.

nodes.name: Ted Lasso
nodes.role: A relentlessly upbeat American college football coach hired, with no soccer experience, to manage a struggling English Premier League club.

nodes.title: The new boss everyone expects to fail
nodes.literal_situation: Ted arrives in London to manage AFC Richmond, a Premier League club, despite never having coached, played or even understood English football. At his first press conference the journalists mock him, the fans chant insults and the star players ignore him.
nodes.pattern_label: leading a group that expects you to fail
nodes.pattern_text: A person is dropped into a leadership role in an unfamiliar world where they don't know the rules, the language or the culture, and everyone is waiting for them to fail. Instead of faking expertise, they bet on kindness, curiosity and believing in people. The question is whether decency can actually win when the results, the critics and the pressure keep coming.
nodes.hook: Ted has crossed an ocean for a job he is not qualified for. He knows almost nothing about the sport, the locker room is divided and cold, and the press calls him a joke. He answers everything with jokes, biscuits and a hand-taped sign that says BELIEVE.
nodes.why_relatable: Can you lead people when you don't know the job better than they do? Is being kind a strategy or a weakness? What do you do when you are underestimated by everyone, and how much of the doubt do you let in?
watch_for: How does he respond when someone insults him to his face?
What does he care about more than winning, and does that ever cost him?
Who in the building starts to believe in him first, and why?
example_user_messages: I just got promoted to lead a team in a field I barely understand and I'm sure they all think I'm a fraud.
Everyone at my new job is waiting for me to mess up. How do I earn their respect without pretending to be someone I'm not?
I moved to a new country for work and I don't get half the jokes, rules or customs yet.
My management style is basically being nice to people and I'm scared that's not enough.
People keep underestimating me and part of me wonders if they're right.

spoiler.summary: Ted slowly wins over the club with unconventional coaching: he gives Roy a book to nudge him into leadership, benches star Jamie Tartt to teach teamwork, promotes kit man Nate to assistant coach and holds a ritual to 'break the curse' of the treatment room. Rebecca, who secretly hired him to fail, eventually confesses and he forgives her. Richmond is relegated at the end of season 1 but Rebecca keeps him. In season 2 they draw seven straight games, bring in a sports psychologist, and win promotion back to the Premier League, but Nate leaks Ted's panic attacks to the press and leaves for rival West Ham, tearing down the BELIEVE sign. In season 3 Richmond is predicted to finish last, signs superstar Zava who then quits, and reinvents itself with 'Total Football'; they finish second, beat Nate's West Ham in the final match, and Nate returns. Ted then decides to go home to Kansas to be near his son, leaving the club to Roy and the others; the team repairs the torn BELIEVE sign.
key_events: Rebecca secretly hired him to sabotage the club; she confesses and he forgives her
Richmond is relegated after losing the last match of season 1
Promotes kit man Nate to assistant coach
Nate leaks his panic attacks to the press and defects to West Ham
Richmond wins promotion in season 2
Total Football transformation in season 3; Richmond finishes second
Ted leaves Richmond to return to Kansas for his son; Roy takes over
spoiler.got_right: He treats people as whole humans, sees potential in the overlooked, forgives generously and builds a culture where players look after one another.
spoiler.got_wrong: He avoids conflict and his own feelings, sometimes laughs off people who need to be taken seriously (like Nate), and lets his aversion to confrontation leave problems festering.

nodes.title: Behind the relentless smile
nodes.literal_situation: Ted is endlessly cheerful and focused on everyone else's wellbeing. Back home in Kansas his marriage is in a rough patch, and part of the reason he took a job across the ocean is to give his wife some space. He is openly skeptical of therapy.
nodes.pattern_label: the helper who can't ask for help
nodes.pattern_text: A warm, funny person who is always there for everyone else uses constant optimism and busyness to keep old pain at arm's length. As their personal life strains, the feelings they have never faced start leaking out in their body and their sleep. They have to learn that asking for help is not weakness, and that you cannot outrun what happened to you as a child.
nodes.hook: Ted seems like the happiest man in any room. He bakes for his boss, remembers everyone's name and has a pun for every occasion, while his wife is growing distant on the phone and he is a very long way from home.
nodes.why_relatable: What happens when the person who always holds everyone up quietly starts to crack? Is relentless positivity strength or avoidance? Why is it so hard to accept the same care you give so freely to others?
watch_for: When does his cheerfulness seem like a genuine choice, and when does it look like a shield?
How does he react when someone refuses to be charmed by him?
What topics does he change the subject away from?
example_user_messages: Everyone says I'm the positive one but lately I have panic attacks and I don't know where they come from.
My marriage is falling apart and I keep telling everyone I'm fine.
I've always been the person who helps others and I really don't know how to let anyone help me.
I don't trust therapists but I think I need one.
Something that happened when I was a teenager still shapes everything and I've never really talked about it.

spoiler.summary: Michelle tells Ted she no longer feels the same way; he lets her go and they divorce. Signing the papers triggers a panic attack at a karaoke night, and he has a one-night stand and later an on-and-off casual relationship with Rebecca's friend Sassy. In season 2 the club hires sports psychologist Dr. Sharon Fieldstone; Ted resists her, then after a panic attack during a match he flees to her office asking for an appointment. After witnessing Jamie's abusive father, he tearfully reveals that his own father died by suicide when Ted was a teenager. Nate leaks his panic attacks to the press. In season 3 he struggles as Michelle begins dating Dr. Jacob, the couples counselor who had worked with them, and learns Jacob plans to propose. He keeps working with Sharon remotely, confronts his mother Dottie about how his father's death was handled, starts letting people see his pain, and ultimately chooses to go home to Kansas to be present for his son.
key_events: Michelle ends the marriage; divorce
Panic attacks at karaoke and during a match
Begins therapy with Dr. Sharon Fieldstone
Reveals his father died by suicide when he was a teenager
Nate leaks his mental health struggles to the press
Michelle dates their former marriage counselor
Confronts his mother about his father's death
Returns home to Kansas
spoiler.got_right: He eventually asks for help, lets Sharon challenge him, tells his friends the truth and forgives both himself and the people who hurt him.
spoiler.got_wrong: For a long time he masks everything with jokes, treats his own needs as last, avoids hard conversations and lets resentment toward therapy keep him from getting help sooner.

nodes.title: A dad on the other side of the world
nodes.literal_situation: Ted's young son Henry lives with his mother in Kansas while Ted works in London. He stays in touch through phone and video calls and a lot of goodnight messages across time zones.
nodes.pattern_label: parenting from far away while building a new life
nodes.pattern_text: A devoted parent takes an opportunity far from home, telling themselves it is the right thing for everyone. The new life becomes meaningful and full of people who need them, while their child grows up through a screen. Eventually they have to weigh the place and people they have built against being physically present for their kid.
nodes.hook: Ted adores his son but sees him mostly on a phone screen. He is building something that matters in a new country while his family life back home is uncertain.
nodes.why_relatable: Can you be a good parent from far away? When does chasing meaningful work start to cost your family too much? How do you choose between two places that both feel like home?
watch_for: How does he talk about his son to the people around him?
What happens to his mood after calls with home?
What does 'home' seem to mean to him as the seasons go on?
example_user_messages: I took a job in another country and I only see my kid on video calls.
I love my work but I feel like I'm missing my child growing up.
I finally built a life I love far from home and now I have to decide whether to give it up for my family.
Is it selfish to stay somewhere that makes me happy if my son is thousands of miles away?

spoiler.summary: Henry visits London with Michelle, and the visit reveals the marriage is over. As the divorce goes through and Michelle moves on with Dr. Jacob, Rebecca urges Ted to focus on being Henry's father rather than on his ex. Across season 3 the distance weighs more heavily, and after Richmond's final match Ted decides to leave the club and return to Kansas. The finale shows him coaching Henry's youth soccer team.
key_events: Henry and Michelle visit London
Divorce; Michelle moves on with their former counselor
Ted chooses to leave Richmond and go home
Coaches his son's youth team in Kansas
spoiler.got_right: He ultimately puts being present for his son above his own success and leaves gracefully, having set others up to carry on.
spoiler.got_wrong: He used the job partly to avoid his marriage's problems and spent a long time half-present in both places.

nodes.name: Rebecca Welton
nodes.role: The newly divorced owner of AFC Richmond, who won the club from her cheating billionaire ex-husband in the settlement.

nodes.title: Getting even with the one who hurt her
nodes.literal_situation: Rebecca has just come out of a very public divorce from Rupert, a charming, serially unfaithful billionaire, and been awarded the football club he loves. She hires an unqualified American coach, and tells no one except her assistant what she really hopes will happen to Rupert's beloved club.
nodes.pattern_label: turning heartbreak into a plan for revenge
nodes.pattern_text: After years of being humiliated and cheated on by a charming partner the world adores, a person is left with the one thing their ex truly loved. Their pain curdles into a quiet campaign to hurt them back, even if innocent people are caught in it. The real question becomes whether they can stop letting the ex define their life and let people who care about them in.
nodes.hook: Rebecca is sharp, glamorous and guarded. The tabloids call her 'the old Rebecca' now that her ex has a younger girlfriend with the same name. She feels that she alone sees who he really is, and she has decided the club will be her weapon.
nodes.why_relatable: What do you do with the anger when someone who hurt you seems to face no consequences? How much of yourself are you willing to lose to make them feel what you felt? Can you trust new people when trust has been used against you?
watch_for: How does she treat the people who are kind to her, and does it change?
Notice who she lets see her real feelings, and when.
How does her body language change when her ex walks into a room?
example_user_messages: My ex cheated on me for years and everyone still thinks he's wonderful. I can't stop wanting him to suffer.
Since the divorce I've been so bitter I barely recognise myself.
I did something petty and hurtful to get back at my ex and innocent people got caught in it.
I feel like I'm the only one who knows what he's really like.
How do I stop letting my ex live rent-free in my head?

spoiler.summary: Rebecca secretly hired Ted to run the club into the ground to hurt Rupert. She tries to discredit him with paparazzi photos and a hostile profile, but Ted's kindness, Keeley's friendship and Higgins quitting in protest wear her down. When Rupert announces his new partner Bex is pregnant and cruelly says he never wanted a child with Rebecca, she confesses everything to Ted, who instantly forgives her, and she apologises to Higgins. She keeps Ted after relegation and builds a real family at the club. In season 2 her father dies and she admits at the funeral that she hates him for his affairs and resents her mother for staying. Rupert buys rival West Ham and takes Nate. In season 3 she becomes obsessed with beating Rupert, then lets it go; when Bex leaves Rupert over his affair, Rebecca supports her, and she sells 49% of the club to its fans.
key_events: Secretly hired Ted hoping he would fail
Hires paparazzi to smear Ted; plan exposed by Keeley and Roy
Confesses to Ted, who forgives her immediately
Higgins quits over her revenge, then returns after her apology
Her father dies; she voices her anger at his infidelity
Rupert buys West Ham and lures Nate away
Rupert's marriage collapses; she comforts Bex
Sells 49% of the club to the fans
spoiler.got_right: She owns her wrongdoing fully when she finally confesses, apologises without excuses, and learns to put the people around her ahead of her grudge.
spoiler.got_wrong: She lets her pain justify manipulating innocent people, and for a long time measures her life by whether Rupert is winning.

nodes.title: Daring to want love again
nodes.literal_situation: In her forties, freshly divorced after a marriage in which her husband refused to have children with her, Rebecca is guarded about romance. She has a lot of power at work and very little softness in her private life.
nodes.pattern_label: daring to want love and family after a bad marriage
nodes.pattern_text: After a long relationship that left them feeling unwanted, a person in midlife isn't sure whether they still want love, whether they deserve it, or whether it is too late for the family they once hoped for. They date, settle, second-guess and sometimes fall for exactly the wrong person on paper. Slowly they learn to stop settling for 'fine' and to listen to what they actually want.
nodes.hook: Rebecca is elegant and in control, but lonely at home. She insists she is not ready to move on, while her friends keep nudging her back into the world.
nodes.why_relatable: Is it too late to start over in love? Should you settle for someone perfectly nice who doesn't make your heart race? What if what you want doesn't fit what people expect from someone your age and status?
watch_for: What does she say she wants in a partner, and what actually lights her up?
How does she respond when friends are honest about someone she's dating?
When does she protect her image, and when does she protect her heart?
example_user_messages: I'm in my forties, just divorced, and I have no idea how to date again.
The person I'm seeing is perfectly nice and I feel absolutely nothing.
I think I've fallen for someone much younger and I'm terrified of what people will say.
My ex never wanted kids with me and I'm scared I've run out of time.
I've spent so long being strong that I don't know how to be soft with someone.

spoiler.summary: Rebecca has a one-night stand in Liverpool, then dates the pleasant but dull John Wingsnight; Roy's speech that she deserves someone who feels like being struck by lightning makes her end it. On the anonymous dating app Bantr she unknowingly falls for Sam Obisanya, one of her own young players; they begin a secret relationship, which she pauses after her father's funeral. Sam turns down a lucrative transfer, telling her obliquely that he stayed for himself. A psychic tells her she will become a mother, reopening her grief about children. In Amsterdam she spends a magical night with a stranger on a houseboat, and at the end of the series she runs into him again by chance, leaving her love life hopeful and open.
key_events: Casual flings as she re-enters dating
Dates and breaks up with John Wingsnight after Roy's 'lightning' speech
Secret relationship with Sam, which she ends
Her father dies
A psychic predicts she will be a mother
Meets a stranger in Amsterdam and later reunites with him
spoiler.got_right: She refuses to settle for 'fine', listens to honest friends and allows herself to want things she had given up on.
spoiler.got_wrong: She lets fear of judgment and her own power at work drive decisions about love, hiding and cutting off relationships rather than being honest.

nodes.name: Roy Kent
nodes.role: AFC Richmond's gruff, ageing captain, a club legend whose best playing days are behind him.

nodes.title: When the thing you were best at starts to leave you
nodes.literal_situation: Roy is Richmond's captain and a former Champions League winner who is now noticeably slower than the young players around him. The fans still love him, but he knows the end of his career is coming, and he has no idea what he is without it.
nodes.pattern_label: losing the identity your career gave you
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has been exceptional at one thing their whole life starts to feel it slipping away as they age. Their pride makes it hard to admit, and they have no plan for who to be afterwards. They have to find out whether their worth was ever just their performance, and learn to try new things badly in front of people.
nodes.hook: Roy scowls, grunts and swears. He is proud and fiercely private, and he hears every 'old man' jibe from younger teammates as proof that his time is running out.
nodes.why_relatable: Who are you when you can no longer do the thing that made you you? How do you handle getting older in a field that worships youth? Can you start again as a beginner when you are used to being the best?
watch_for: How does he react when someone points out he is slowing down?
What does he refuse to try, and why?
Who is he gentlest with, and what does that show about him?
example_user_messages: I've been good at one thing my whole life and now I'm getting too old for it.
The younger people at work keep calling me a dinosaur and it really gets to me.
I retired and I have no idea who I am anymore.
Everyone says I should try something new but I hate being bad at things.
My whole identity was my career and it's ending.

spoiler.summary: Roy is benched as his form declines. In the season 1 finale he makes a desperate tackle on Jamie that injures his knee and ends his playing career, and he leaves the pitch to the fans chanting his name, crying afterwards with Keeley. In season 2 he is adrift: coaching his niece's under-9 girls team, avoiding a TV pundit job he despises, and doing yoga with older women. Keeley pushes him to try punditry, where his swearing honesty becomes a hit. He then returns to Richmond as a coach after helping captain Isaac rediscover joy, and by the end of the series he is set to lead the club.
key_events: Benched for declining form
Career-ending knee injury in the final match of season 1
Becomes a TV pundit
Returns to Richmond as a coach
Positioned to take over the club when Ted leaves
spoiler.got_right: He eventually lets people he trusts push him, tries new things and finds a role where his experience and honesty are valued.
spoiler.got_wrong: His pride makes him hide from new opportunities and lash out at people who remind him of what he is losing.

nodes.title: The hard man with the soft heart
nodes.literal_situation: Roy is emotionally shut down, mostly communicates in grunts and swearing, and keeps to himself outside training. The only person he is visibly tender with is his young niece Phoebe. He is drawn to the confident Keeley, who is dating his teammate and rival.
nodes.pattern_label: a guarded person learning to love out loud
nodes.pattern_text: A person who equates vulnerability with weakness falls for someone who sees straight through their tough exterior. Loving them means learning to talk about feelings, accept help and not pull away when things get real. When fear of being left creeps in, they have to decide whether to protect themselves or stay open.
nodes.hook: Roy is intimidating, blunt and very private. He looks after his niece with fierce love, but with everyone else he keeps a wall up, especially with the woman who seems to know exactly how to get under his skin.
nodes.why_relatable: What if showing feelings has always felt like losing? How do you let someone help you without feeling smaller? What do you do when you are scared the person you love will outgrow you?
watch_for: When he is hurt, does he speak up or go silent?
Notice what he does instead of saying how he feels.
How does he respond when someone he loves needs space?
example_user_messages: I'm terrible at talking about my feelings, and my partner says it's like dating a wall.
I fell for someone who was with a guy I can't stand.
My girlfriend's career is taking off and I'm scared she's going to leave me behind.
I pushed away someone I love before they could leave me.
The only person I'm soft with is my niece.

spoiler.summary: After Keeley dumps Jamie, Roy kisses her, then avoids her, and she sleeps with Jamie; he apologises and they start dating, a relationship that softens him. He struggles with jealousy, crowds her until she needs space, and learns to give it. At Rebecca's father's funeral they declare their love, but Jamie also tells Keeley he loves her, and Nate kisses her. When Keeley starts her own PR firm and is too busy for a holiday, Roy panics that she is leaving him and, at the start of season 3, breaks up with her pre-emptively. He regrets it, gets into a fistfight with Jamie over her, and she rejects them both. By the end he is opening up to the Diamond Dogs, admitting he messed up and needs to work on himself; his future with Keeley is left open.
key_events: Kisses Keeley, then avoids her
Dates Keeley; they say 'I love you'
Keeley launches her own firm; he feels left behind
Breaks up with Keeley at the start of season 3
Fights Jamie over her; she rejects them both
Opens up to the Diamond Dogs about his mistakes
spoiler.got_right: He learns to apologise, to be tender and to ask friends for help, and he is fiercely loyal to the people he loves.
spoiler.got_wrong: He expresses fear as anger or silence, crowds his partner and then ends the relationship to avoid the pain of maybe being left.

nodes.title: Reluctant leader
nodes.literal_situation: As captain, Roy watches the star striker bully the kit man and younger players, and he is furious when the new coach won't simply step in and fix it. Ted gives him a children's book about a girl who has leadership thrust upon her, and Roy is not amused.
nodes.pattern_label: stepping up to lead when you'd rather not
nodes.pattern_text: A respected but prickly veteran would rather keep their head down, yet the group keeps looking to them. They have to learn that leadership is not just toughness but taking responsibility for others, including people they can't stand. Over time they find themselves mentoring the very person who used to be their rival.
nodes.hook: Roy has the respect of the locker room but doesn't want the responsibility that comes with it. He has an arrogant young rival he'd happily headbutt, and a coach who keeps nudging him to be more than a hard man.
nodes.why_relatable: What if people look to you to lead and you don't want the job? Can you mentor someone who once drove you crazy? How do you pass on what you know without passing on your worst habits?
watch_for: How does he deal with people who aren't pulling their weight?
What does he teach his niece, on purpose and by accident?
How does his view of his younger rival change?
example_user_messages: Everyone at work looks to me to lead and I never asked for that.
I've been asked to mentor the one colleague I really can't stand.
I'm scared my niece is picking up all my worst habits.
I've gone from being one of the team to being their boss and it's weird.

spoiler.summary: Roy realises Ted's gift of A Wrinkle in Time is a nudge to lead, and he stops Jamie's gang bullying Nate. His rivalry with Jamie flares through season 1. As a coach in season 2 he initially refuses to coach Jamie, then teaches him to channel his aggression on the pitch; when Jamie punches his abusive father in the dressing room, Roy wordlessly hugs him. In season 3 he trains Jamie at 4am daily, teaches him to ride a bike and hears about his traumatic past, and they become best friends. He also worries he is passing his swearing and anger on to Phoebe. When Ted leaves, Roy becomes Richmond's manager.
key_events: Gets the leadership message from A Wrinkle in Time
Stops Jamie's bullying of Nate
Refuses, then agrees, to coach Jamie
Hugs Jamie after his father's abuse in the locker room
4am training sessions; becomes Jamie's best friend
Takes over as Richmond's manager
spoiler.got_right: He shows up for people consistently, is brutally honest in a way that helps, and learns to mentor with care rather than just intimidation.
spoiler.got_wrong: He is slow to let go of grudges and sometimes models the very anger he wants the young people around him to avoid.

nodes.name: Keeley Jones
nodes.role: A cheerful, savvy model and influencer, 'famous for being almost famous', dating Richmond's star striker.

nodes.title: More than a pretty face
nodes.literal_situation: Keeley is a glamour model and influencer best known for topless photos and being a footballer's girlfriend. She is clever, warm and brilliant at reading people, but nobody, sometimes including herself, thinks of her as a businesswoman.
nodes.pattern_label: proving you're more than your image
nodes.pattern_text: A person known mainly for their looks and charm realises they have real talent for building things and understanding people. Moving into a serious professional world means facing people who dismiss them, doubting themselves, and learning to lead others. Success brings new questions about whether they belong at the top and what it costs.
nodes.hook: Keeley has more instinct for marketing than most professionals, but her career so far is modelling and her public identity is 'someone's girlfriend'. She is about to meet a powerful older woman who notices her.
nodes.why_relatable: What if people only see one side of you? Can you reinvent yourself professionally without formal credentials? How do you lead people who don't take you seriously, and what happens when you are in charge and struggling?
watch_for: How does she respond when someone underestimates her?
Notice what she's naturally good at, even before she has a job title for it.
Who does she go to for advice, and who does she mentor in return?
example_user_messages: People only ever saw me as the pretty one and I want to be taken seriously at work.
I don't have a degree but I know I'm good at this. How do I get people to believe it?
I started my own company and I cry at my desk because I have no idea what I'm doing.
My employees don't respect me and I don't know how to be their boss.
My mentor offered me a huge opportunity and I'm scared it means leaving her behind.

spoiler.summary: Keeley befriends Rebecca, lands endorsements for players and is hired as Richmond's marketing head. She launches the dating app Bantr and is featured in Vanity Fair's business issue. With Higgins' advice ('a good mentor hopes you will move on, a great mentor knows you will') she accepts investors' offer to fund her own PR firm, KJPR. In season 3 she struggles to lead, clashes with her strict CFO Barbara, dates investor Jack, and suffers a humiliating leak of a private video she once sent to Jamie. Jack dumps her abruptly and pulls funding, and KJPR collapses. By the end, with Barbara's respect earned and Rebecca offering support, she is set to start again on her own terms.
key_events: Hired as Richmond's marketing head
Launches Bantr; featured in Vanity Fair
Leaves to start her own PR firm, KJPR
Clashes with CFO Barbara
A private video is leaked
Investor-girlfriend Jack pulls funding; KJPR fails
Prepares to start again with Rebecca's backing
spoiler.got_right: She trusts her instincts, champions other people (especially women written off like her), and refuses to shrink to fit other people's expectations.
spoiler.got_wrong: She mixes romance with business, hires friends without thinking it through, and hides how overwhelmed she is.

nodes.title: Between two men, and herself
nodes.literal_situation: Keeley is dating Jamie, Richmond's vain star striker, who treats her as an accessory. She keeps finding herself drawn into banter with Roy, his gruff rival on the same team.
nodes.pattern_label: learning what you deserve in love
nodes.pattern_text: A warm person in a relationship with someone self-absorbed begins to realise they deserve accountability and respect. They move on to someone better but face new tensions: jealousy, space, and whether their growing ambition fits the relationship. Eventually they have to decide whether to be defined by who they are with or to choose themselves.
nodes.hook: Keeley is fun, affectionate and generous, and she has been with Jamie long enough to excuse his worst behaviour. A conversation about accountability is about to make her look at him differently.
nodes.why_relatable: When do you stop excusing someone's selfishness? Can you stay friends with an ex? What happens when your career grows and your partner feels threatened? Do you have to choose between the people who love you?
watch_for: What does she want from a partner, and does she ask for it?
How does she handle it when someone wants more of her time than she has?
Notice how she treats the people she's broken up with.
example_user_messages: My boyfriend is gorgeous and popular but he never thinks about how I feel.
I think I'm falling for my boyfriend's rival and I feel awful about it.
I love my partner but he's smothering me and I need space.
Two people I care about both want me and honestly I just want to focus on myself.

spoiler.summary: After seeing Jamie flirt with Bex and mock people at the charity gala, Keeley breaks up with him. She and Roy kiss, he avoids her, she sleeps with Jamie, and then Roy and she start a loving relationship. She needs more space than he gives, and at Rebecca's father's funeral Jamie tells her he loves her while Nate kisses her during a shopping trip. As her firm takes off she can't take a holiday with Roy, and he breaks up with her at the start of season 3. She briefly dates investor Jack, a woman, who later dumps her. When Roy and Jamie arrive at her house after fighting over her and ask her to choose, she refuses both and throws them out, choosing herself.
key_events: Breaks up with Jamie over his lack of accountability
Starts dating Roy
Jamie declares his love; Nate kisses her
Roy breaks up with her in season 3
Brief relationship with Jack, who ends it
Refuses to choose between Roy and Jamie
spoiler.got_right: She walks away from people who don't respect her, asks for what she needs and ultimately refuses to let her worth depend on a partner.
spoiler.got_wrong: She sometimes uses one man to get at another, tolerates behaviour she shouldn't, and lets work and romance blur.

nodes.name: Jamie Tartt
nodes.role: Richmond's cocky, vain young star striker, on loan from Manchester City, who bullies teammates and plays only for himself.

nodes.title: Playing for a father who is never satisfied
nodes.literal_situation: Jamie is supremely talented, arrogant and the centre of attention. He hogs the ball, belittles teammates and seems to care only about himself. What drives him is not yet visible.
nodes.pattern_label: a harsh parent's voice in your head
nodes.pattern_text: A gifted young person has built their whole personality around never looking weak, because the parent whose approval they crave only respects toughness and winning. The arrogance hides deep insecurity, and the parent's voice drowns out everyone else's. They have to separate who they are from who they were raised to be, set boundaries, and decide what to do with the anger and hurt.
nodes.hook: Jamie is cocky, handsome and mean to anyone he thinks is beneath him. He calls himself the best, and he expects everyone to agree.
nodes.why_relatable: Where does arrogance come from? Can you want a parent's approval and still know they are hurting you? What happens when the voice in your head isn't really yours?
watch_for: Who is he trying to impress when he shows off?
How does he behave when he thinks nobody important is watching?
Notice how he talks about each of his parents.
example_user_messages: My dad only ever cared whether I won. Nothing I did was ever good enough for him.
People think I'm arrogant but honestly I'm terrified of being seen as weak.
My father is cruel to me and I still want him to be proud of me.
I finally stood up to my dad and now I don't know how I feel.
Is it possible to forgive a parent who hurt you without letting them back in?

spoiler.summary: At the treatment-room ritual Jamie burns boots his mother bought him and vows to make her proud rather than act tough like his father. After Richmond's final match of season 1, his father James berates him for passing instead of scoring and throws a shoe at him; Ted witnesses it. In season 2 Jamie reveals he quit Manchester City partly because he was fed up with his father. When a drunk James storms the dressing room after an FA Cup semi-final loss and mocks the team, Jamie tells him to stop, then punches him; Roy embraces him as he sobs. In season 3 he reveals his father coerced him into sex at 14, confides his depression to his loving mother Georgie, and panics about his father being in the crowd at a Manchester match. Ted tells him forgiving his father is for himself; Jamie scores the winner and leaves the pitch in tears.
key_events: Burns his mother's boots and vows to make her proud
Father throws a shoe at him after season 1's final match
Punches his drunk, abusive father in the dressing room; Roy hugs him
Discloses sexual abuse his father arranged when he was 14
Visits his mother, admits depression
Chooses to let go of resentment for his own sake
spoiler.got_right: He eventually sets boundaries with his father, lets people comfort him and chooses forgiveness as something he does for himself.
spoiler.got_wrong: For years he passes on his father's cruelty to weaker teammates and mistakes arrogance for strength.

nodes.title: The star who has to learn to pass
nodes.literal_situation: Jamie is Richmond's best player and knows it. He ignores the coach, bullies the kit man and newer players, won't pass to teammates and treats his girlfriend as an accessory.
nodes.pattern_label: from self-centred star to team player
nodes.pattern_text: The most talented person in the room has always been rewarded for being selfish. When they are held accountable, they lose the relationships, jobs and admirers they took for granted, and have to earn their way back with people who have every reason to dislike them. They discover that being part of something bigger than yourself can feel better than being the star.
nodes.hook: Jamie is the club's most gifted player and its biggest problem. He believes he doesn't need anyone, and he is used to getting away with everything.
nodes.why_relatable: What happens when being the best isn't enough? Can you win back people you treated badly? How do you apologise when your pride says you shouldn't have to?
watch_for: How does he react when he's benched or not the centre of attention?
Notice the first time he does something generous. Why then?
Who is willing to give him a second chance, and who isn't?
example_user_messages: I'm the top performer at work but nobody likes me and I'm starting to notice.
I burned a lot of bridges and now I want to come back and everyone hates me.
I used to bully people and I'm genuinely trying to be better now.
My old rival is now the one teaching me and it's humbling.
I always thought I didn't need anyone. I was wrong.

spoiler.summary: Ted benches Jamie for walking over a fallen Sam; Jamie rebels, loses Keeley and is sent back to Manchester City, where at the season 1 finale he makes the unselfish pass that relegates Richmond. He quits City for a reality dating show, is voted off, finds nobody wants him and asks Ted to come back. The squad greets him with fury; he apologises, starts therapy with Sharon, and joins the team's protest in solidarity with Sam. He gives a crucial penalty to Dani in the promotion match. In season 3 he trains with Roy at 4am, becomes a selfless playmaker in Total Football, leads the league in assists, supports teammate Colin coming out, and becomes Roy's best friend.
key_events: Benched for walking over Sam
Returned to Manchester City; his pass relegates Richmond
Voted off a reality TV show
Returns to Richmond; the team resents him
Tapes over the sponsor logo in solidarity with Sam
Gives the promotion penalty to Dani
Roy's protégé and best friend; league leader in assists
spoiler.got_right: He apologises honestly, keeps showing up despite hostility, accepts help and learns to share the spotlight.
spoiler.got_wrong: Early on he bullies people, treats others as props, and blames everyone else for consequences he earned.

nodes.name: Nate Shelley
nodes.role: AFC Richmond's timid, overlooked kit man, bullied by the players, whose name nobody bothers to learn.

nodes.title: Hungry to be seen
nodes.literal_situation: Nate washes the kits and tends the pitch at Richmond. The players mock him, and he is so used to being invisible that when the new coach asks his name, he doesn't know what to say. He has a sharp tactical mind that nobody has noticed.
nodes.pattern_label: the overlooked one who finally gets noticed
nodes.pattern_text: A person who has been invisible and belittled their whole life, including by a parent who never praises them, is suddenly noticed and lifted up by a kind mentor. Newfound recognition feels intoxicating, and the old hunger for approval turns into insecurity, envy and resentment towards the people who helped them. They have to figure out whether their worth comes from others' praise, and how to make amends when they hurt the people who believed in them.
nodes.hook: Nate is shy, anxious and bullied, wearing his father's too-big old suit. The new coach remembers his name, asks his opinion, and treats him like he matters. For Nate, that is completely new.
nodes.why_relatable: What happens when someone finally believes in you after a lifetime of being overlooked? Can praise ever be enough if you never got it from your parents? How do you handle it when a mentor's light starts to feel like a shadow?
watch_for: How does he treat people who have less power than him as he gains more?
Notice how he responds to compliments versus small slights.
What does his father say to him, and how does he carry it afterwards?
example_user_messages: I've been invisible at work for years, and now that I'm finally getting noticed I'm scared of losing it.
My dad has never once told me he's proud of me.
My mentor did everything for me and I've started to resent him and I don't know why.
I did something terrible to someone who believed in me. Can I ever make it right?
I got the promotion I wanted and I've turned into someone I don't like.

spoiler.summary: Ted makes Nate feel seen, buys him a suit, uses his tactical ideas and promotes him to assistant coach. Nate grows in confidence but also cruelty: he belittles the new kit man Will, is crushed by his father's coldness, feels sidelined when Roy joins the coaching staff and when Ted laughs off his offer to help Isaac, and resents Ted. He kisses Keeley, leaks Ted's panic attacks to journalist Trent Crimm, explodes at Ted that he never appreciated him, tears the BELIEVE sign in half and becomes manager of Rupert's West Ham. In season 3 he is praised but hollow under Rupert, finds love with the restaurant hostess Jade, earns his father's approval by playing violin, and quits West Ham when he sees who Rupert really is. He returns to Richmond humbly as kit man, apologises to Ted, who forgives him, and is welcomed back onto the staff.
key_events: Promoted from kit man to assistant coach
Bullies the new kit man; clashes with his father
Kisses Keeley
Leaks Ted's panic attacks to the press
Rips the BELIEVE sign and joins West Ham under Rupert
Falls for Jade
Quits West Ham and returns to Richmond; Ted forgives him
spoiler.got_right: His tactical instincts are real, and in the end he recognises what he has become, walks away from a toxic boss and apologises humbly.
spoiler.got_wrong: He needs outside approval so badly that he punches down, sees kindness as condescension and betrays the person who believed in him most.

nodes.name: Leslie Higgins
nodes.role: AFC Richmond's mild-mannered, long-suffering director of football operations, a loyal family man who has spent years doing whatever his bosses ask.

nodes.title: The yes-man who finds his spine
nodes.literal_situation: Higgins has spent years obeying the club's owners, including covering for the previous owner's affairs. The new owner makes him her accomplice in a plan he finds distasteful, sweetening it with a promotion he badly needs to support his wife and five children.
nodes.pattern_label: going along with a boss you know is wrong
nodes.pattern_text: A decent, conflict-averse employee has spent years keeping their head down and doing what powerful people ask, even when it made them complicit. When they are asked to help harm someone they have come to like, they have to choose between job security for their family and their own conscience. Standing up for once could cost them everything, but staying silent is costing them themselves.
nodes.hook: Higgins is kind, awkward, jittery around his boss and fond of the new coach. He has just been promoted, and the price is helping with something that makes him deeply uncomfortable.
nodes.why_relatable: What do you do when your boss asks you to do something wrong and your family depends on your paycheque? How long can you tell yourself you had no choice? What does it take for a people-pleaser to finally say no?
watch_for: How does he justify going along with things to himself?
Notice who he feels most at ease with at work, and why.
What is he like at home compared with the office?
example_user_messages: My boss keeps asking me to do things I know are wrong and I need this job to support my kids.
I've spent my whole career saying yes to people and I'm ashamed of some of the things I covered for.
I finally told my manager off and quit and I'm terrified.
I'm a people-pleaser and I think it's making me complicit.

spoiler.summary: Higgins reluctantly helps Rebecca sabotage Ted, including hiring a paparazzo, but becomes Ted's friend. He organises the ritual that unites the team, and Rebecca punishes him for it. When she orders him to sell home seats to rival fans to spite Rupert, he finally tells her to f*** off, tells her hurting others won't heal her pain, and quits. Rebecca later knocks on his window, apologises and asks him back, and he returns with dignity. Afterwards he becomes the club's quiet heart: a founding Diamond Dog, host of a Christmas dinner for players far from home, a happily married man who tells Jamie to love his father for who he is and forgive him for who he isn't, and a mentor who tells Keeley that 'a great mentor knows you will move on'.
key_events: Helps with Rebecca's sabotage against his conscience
Organises the ritual that unites the team
Tells Rebecca off and quits
Rebecca apologises and he returns
Becomes a mentor figure and gives Keeley his blessing to leave
spoiler.got_right: He finally draws a line, speaks the truth kindly but firmly, and becomes a wise, generous mentor.
spoiler.got_wrong: For years he let fear for his job make him complicit in cruelty to others, including his boss's marriage.

nodes.name: Sam Obisanya
nodes.role: A sweet, optimistic young Nigerian defender in his first season in the Premier League, far from his family and struggling for form.

nodes.title: A long way from home
nodes.literal_situation: Sam is a young player recently arrived from Nigeria, homesick and struggling on the pitch. The star striker belittles him and his family, and his confidence is slipping as his birthday approaches far from his loved ones.
nodes.pattern_label: a young person far from home finding their feet
nodes.pattern_text: A kind, hopeful young person moves far from their family and culture for a big opportunity, and quickly feels lonely, homesick and out of their depth. With the support of people who make them feel seen, they regain confidence and begin to thrive. As they grow, they face bigger choices about love, money and where they truly belong.
nodes.hook: Sam is gentle, polite and full of promise, but he misses home, his performance is dipping, and he is being picked on by the team's biggest ego.
nodes.why_relatable: How do you keep your spirit up when you are far from everyone who loves you? Can a little kindness really turn things around? When big opportunities come, how do you decide what is truly best for you?
watch_for: What small things help him feel at home?
How does he handle the teammate who bullies him?
Who does he call when he has a big decision to make?
example_user_messages: I moved abroad for a great opportunity but I'm so homesick I can't focus.
It's my birthday and I'm alone in a new country.
I fell for someone older and much more powerful and we're keeping it secret.
I got a huge offer somewhere else, and I need to figure out if staying is right for me or just about someone I love.
A little kindness from my new colleagues completely changed how I feel about this place.

spoiler.summary: Ted and the team throw Sam a birthday party with Nigerian treats, lifting his spirits; he scores the winner against Watford after Jamie is benched. In season 2 he is angry when Jamie returns but eventually becomes his friend. On the dating app Bantr he unknowingly falls for Rebecca, the club owner; they start a secret relationship, which she pauses after her father's funeral. Billionaire Edwin Akufo offers him a fortune to join his new African club; after asking his father and waiting for a sign, Sam turns it down, telling Rebecca and Ted he is staying because it is best for his own journey, not for her. He then buys a property to open a Nigerian restaurant named after his father.
key_events: Team birthday party boosts his confidence
Scores the stoppage-time winner against Watford
Secret relationship with Rebecca, which she ends
Rejects Edwin Akufo's lucrative offer
Opens a restaurant named after his father
spoiler.got_right: He is open-hearted, accepts support, and makes big decisions based on his own values rather than on romance or money.
spoiler.got_wrong: He sometimes defers to others' comfort, keeping a relationship secret and waiting for signs rather than trusting himself.

nodes.title: Speaking up when it costs you
nodes.literal_situation: Sam is excited about his first big advertising campaign for the club's airline sponsor, until his father tells him the airline's parent company is devastating the environment in his home country.
nodes.pattern_label: standing up for your values at a cost
nodes.pattern_text: A gentle, well-liked young person discovers that something they benefit from is causing harm to their home community. Speaking up could cost them money, relationships and their reputation, and invite abuse from powerful people. They have to decide whether to stay quiet and comfortable or use their voice, and how to keep going when the backlash is personal.
nodes.hook: Sam has finally found his feet at the club and is on the verge of a lucrative campaign. Now he has to decide whether to risk it all over something happening thousands of miles away.
nodes.why_relatable: Is it worth speaking up if it costs you your career? What do you owe the place you come from? How do you stay kind when people attack you for your beliefs?
watch_for: Who stands with him, and who hesitates?
How does his father influence his choices?
How does he respond when powerful people try to intimidate him?
example_user_messages: I found out the company I work with is harming my home country and I can't stay silent.
I spoke out publicly about something important and now I'm getting hate messages.
Someone vandalised my business because of where I'm from.
Doing the right thing might cost me my career. Is it worth it?

spoiler.summary: Sam refuses to promote Dubai Air because its parent company Cerithium Oil is polluting Nigeria. He tapes over the logo before a match, the whole team follows in solidarity, and at a press conference he confirms he is accusing the Nigerian government of corruption. Rebecca backs him despite pressure from the oil company's CEO. In season 3 he opens his restaurant, Ola's, and publicly challenges the anti-immigration Home Secretary; the restaurant is vandalised with racist graffiti. His father arrives unexpectedly and tells him not to fight back but to fight forward, and his teammates repair the restaurant. Edwin Akufo takes petty revenge, including paying to keep Sam off Nigeria's national team.
key_events: Taped-over sponsor logo protest; team joins him
Publicly accuses the Nigerian government of corruption
Opens a restaurant, Ola's
Restaurant vandalised by anti-immigration racists
Teammates rebuild it; his father visits
Edwin Akufo sabotages his national team call-up
spoiler.got_right: He acts on his values calmly, answers hatred with reasoned courage and lets his community support him.
spoiler.got_wrong: He sometimes swallows his hurt silently rather than sharing it, and has to learn that anger is allowed.

nodes.name: Eleanor Shellstrop
nodes.role: A sarcastic, self-serving saleswoman from Arizona who has just died and is welcomed into the Good Place, a paradise for the most virtuous people who ever lived, and quickly realises she is only there by mistake.

nodes.title: Faking it until she means it
nodes.literal_situation: Eleanor wakes up in the afterlife and is told by Michael, the neighbourhood's friendly architect, that she lived an exemplary life of human-rights work. Those memories are not hers: she was a selfish, rude saleswoman, and she has been let in by mistake. Terrified of being sent to the Bad Place, she begs Chidi, the ethics professor assigned as her soulmate, to secretly teach her how to be good.
nodes.pattern_label: a self-centred person trying to genuinely become good
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has always looked out only for themselves suddenly finds themselves surrounded by people who are better than them, and fears being exposed as a fraud. They start trying to be good for purely selfish reasons, to protect themselves. Slowly the question shifts from 'how do I not get caught' to 'what do I actually owe the people around me'.
nodes.hook: Newly dead and living a lie in paradise, Eleanor is a cynic who has never cared what anyone thought of her, now desperate to learn ethics fast enough to avoid being found out.
nodes.why_relatable: Can you become a better person if your first reason for trying is self-interest? Is it too late to change who you have been for thirty-odd years? And what does she do when being honest would cost her everything?
watch_for: Notice when her motives for doing good things start to change, and whether she notices it herself.
How does she react when being selfish would be the easy way out?
What does she seem to believe about whether people can really change?
example_user_messages: I've been a pretty selfish person my whole life and I'm only now realising it. Is it too late to change?
Everyone around me seems so genuinely good and I feel like a fraud who's going to get found out.
I started volunteering mostly to look good, and now I'm not sure if that makes me a bad person.
I want to be better but honestly I don't even know where to start.

spoiler.summary: Eleanor studies ethics with Chidi and slowly starts to care, eventually confessing she doesn't belong. At the end of season 1 she realises the 'Good Place' is actually the Bad Place: Michael is a demon and the four humans were chosen to torture each other. Michael reboots their memories hundreds of times, but Eleanor keeps figuring it out. The humans team up with Michael, plead with the Judge, and are sent back to Earth to see if they can improve without afterlife motivation. She then discovers the points system is broken, helps run a new test of whether people can improve, and helps design a new afterlife where people can keep growing after death. After finding peace, she eventually chooses to pass through the final door, becoming a spark that nudges a newly human Michael toward kindness.
key_events: Confesses to Tahani and Michael that she is the wrong Eleanor
Realises 'this is the Bad Place' at the end of season 1
Michael is revealed to be a demon; hundreds of memory reboots
Team works with Michael and pleads to the Judge; returned to Earth
Discovers no one has reached the Good Place in centuries because the system is broken
Helps design a new afterlife where souls can keep improving
Eventually walks through the door that ends her existence
spoiler.got_right: She never stops questioning, owns her mistakes once she sees them, and learns that being good is about what you owe other people rather than points or self-protection.
spoiler.got_wrong: For a long time she lies and manipulates to save herself, pushes people away before they can reject her, and uses sarcasm to avoid feeling anything.

nodes.title: A loner learning to let people in
nodes.literal_situation: Eleanor has been on her own since her early teens, after a childhood with neglectful parents. In the neighbourhood she is suddenly expected to be part of a community, go to parties, and share a home with a soulmate she barely knows.
nodes.pattern_label: a self-reliant loner learning to trust others
nodes.pattern_text: A person who learned as a child that nobody would take care of them has built a life around needing no one. Being pushed into close friendships and a serious relationship forces them to face how much they keep people at arm's length. They have to decide whether letting others matter is worth the risk of being hurt again.
nodes.hook: Eleanor prides herself on needing nobody and caring about no one, but she has just landed in a place where everyone expects her to be part of a close-knit community.
nodes.why_relatable: What happens when someone who has always been alone is surrounded by people who want to know her? Can she tell the difference between independence and fear? Does she believe anyone would stick around if they knew the real her?
watch_for: Notice how often she uses jokes to deflect when someone gets close.
How does she treat the people who are kind to her without expecting anything back?
What do her flashbacks to her childhood tell you about the walls she builds?
example_user_messages: I grew up basically raising myself and now I don't know how to let anyone get close.
Whenever someone is nice to me I get suspicious and push them away.
My parents were never there for me and I think it's why I act like I don't need anybody.
I'm falling for someone who is my complete opposite and it terrifies me.

spoiler.summary: Eleanor forms a found family with Chidi, Tahani, Jason, Janet and eventually Michael. She and Chidi fall in love across many memory reboots; they finally become a couple on Earth, before Chidi's memory is wiped for a new experiment and she must be near him without him knowing. His memories are later restored. She discovers her mother faked her own death and started a new family under a new name, and learns to accept her limits rather than wait for her approval. In the end Chidi decides he is ready to leave through the final door, and Eleanor learns to let him go before eventually going herself.
key_events: Her mother is alive, living under a false name with a new daughter
Eleanor and Chidi fall in love in multiple rebooted timelines
Chidi's memory is wiped, and she must work alongside him as a stranger
Chidi's memories are restored
Chidi chooses to walk through the final door; Eleanor lets him go
spoiler.got_right: She learns that loving people means showing up for them, and that letting someone go can be an act of love.
spoiler.got_wrong: She repeatedly assumes people will abandon her and tries to handle everything alone rather than asking for help.

nodes.title: The loner who has to take charge
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that puts other people's futures in her hands, Eleanor, who has always looked out only for herself, must guide a group of strangers who are counting on her and make hard calls under pressure.
nodes.pattern_label: a reluctant loner forced to lead
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has spent their life avoiding responsibility for anyone else suddenly has other people depending on them. They doubt they are the right person, clash with people they have to help, and struggle with carrying hard decisions alone. They discover whether they can lead without becoming someone they are not.
nodes.hook: Eleanor has never been responsible for anyone but herself, and now she is the one others turn to, with no idea whether she is up to it.
nodes.why_relatable: What if the person in charge feels like the least qualified one in the room? How do you help people you don't even like? Can someone lead while still privately struggling?
watch_for: How does she handle the people she finds hardest to care about?
Notice when she tries to carry everything alone, and when she asks for help.
What does she learn from her own past when dealing with someone who reminds her of herself?
example_user_messages: I just got put in charge of a team and I feel like the least qualified person there.
I've always been a lone wolf and now people are relying on me. I'm freaking out.
There's one person I'm supposed to help who is awful, and I'm not sure I even want to.
I'm trying to hold everything together while something personal is breaking my heart.

spoiler.summary: Eleanor becomes the architect of a new neighbourhood experiment to prove humans can improve, overseeing four new test subjects, including the unbearable Brent, while Chidi, whose memory has been wiped, is one of the subjects. She runs the project with Michael, cracks under the strain at times, and ultimately comes up with the idea for a reformed afterlife in which people are tested and can keep improving after death.
key_events: Becomes the architect of the new experiment
Must manage an amnesiac Chidi as a stranger
Tries to reform the stubborn, entitled Brent
Helps design the new afterlife system
spoiler.got_right: She leads with empathy, recognising her former self in the people she is trying to help.
spoiler.got_wrong: She tries to control every detail and hides her own pain, burning out instead of leaning on her friends.

nodes.name: Chidi Anagonye
nodes.role: A kind, deeply anxious moral philosophy professor, born in Senegal and raised in Australia, who is introduced as Eleanor's soulmate and reluctantly agrees to secretly teach her ethics.

nodes.title: The man who couldn't decide
nodes.literal_situation: Chidi has devoted his life to studying ethics, yet he can't pick a muffin without agonising. In the neighbourhood he is told Eleanor is his soulmate, learns she doesn't belong there, and has to decide whether to keep her secret, which goes against everything he believes about honesty.
nodes.pattern_label: overthinking every choice for fear of being wrong
nodes.pattern_text: A deeply conscientious person is so afraid of making the wrong choice that they barely make any choices at all. Their search for the perfect, ethically airtight answer leaves them anxious and physically sick with stress, and frustrates everyone around them. They have to learn to act, commit and live with uncertainty.
nodes.hook: Chidi is a gentle expert on right and wrong who can't make even small decisions, and he has just been handed a massive moral dilemma he can't research his way out of.
nodes.why_relatable: What do you do when there is no perfect answer? Is endlessly weighing every option really more ethical, or just a way to avoid responsibility? How does his indecision affect the people who depend on him?
watch_for: Notice what his stomach aches tell you about him.
How do his friends feel when he can't give them a straight answer?
Does knowing more about ethics make him happier, or more stuck?
example_user_messages: I overthink every single decision to the point where I literally feel sick.
I'm so scared of choosing wrong that I end up not choosing at all, and people are getting frustrated with me.
I keep waiting for a perfect answer that never comes.
My friends say my indecisiveness is exhausting and I don't know how to stop.

spoiler.summary: Chidi's indecision turns out to have caused real pain on Earth, and he died because of it when an air conditioner fell on him. In the afterlife, which is revealed to be the Bad Place, he teaches ethics to the humans and even to Michael. Back on Earth he meets neuroscientist Simone. After learning that nothing he does can earn points anymore, he has an existential breakdown and briefly rejects all rules. Later his memory is wiped to help the new experiment, and when his memories return, he finds a new calm: he realises there is no single perfect answer and makes decisions with clarity. In the end he chooses to walk through the final door, comparing it to a wave returning to the ocean.
key_events: His death was caused by his indecision (a falling air conditioner)
The neighbourhood is revealed to be the Bad Place
Teaches ethics to Michael
Existential crisis after learning the points system is rigged
Memory wiped, then restored with a new clarity
Chooses to leave through the final door
spoiler.got_right: He cares deeply about doing right by people and, at his best, gives others the tools to think for themselves.
spoiler.got_wrong: He hides behind theory and indecision, treating the absence of a perfect answer as a reason not to act.

nodes.title: Paired with someone nothing like him
nodes.literal_situation: Chidi is told that Eleanor, a brash, rule-breaking woman who is the opposite of him in every way, is his soulmate. He is torn between his loyalty to her and his disapproval of how she lived.
nodes.pattern_label: falling for your opposite and learning to let go
nodes.pattern_text: A cautious, principled person grows close to someone impulsive and rule-breaking whom they initially disapprove of. The relationship pushes them to loosen up, and forces them to face their fear of commitment and of losing control. In time it also raises the question of what it means to love someone when you can't hold on forever.
nodes.hook: Chidi is stuck sharing a life with someone who makes him deeply uncomfortable, and he isn't sure whether he is her teacher, her accomplice or something more.
nodes.why_relatable: Can someone who drives you crazy also be good for you? What happens when a careful person lets a chaotic person matter to them? Is loving someone about holding on or about wanting what is best for them?
watch_for: Notice how each of them changes the way the other one thinks.
When does his discomfort with her turn into something else?
How does he handle moments when his head and his heart disagree?
example_user_messages: I'm falling for someone who is my total opposite and I don't know if it can work.
My partner pushes me out of my comfort zone and I love it and hate it at the same time.
I'm scared of committing because what if I choose wrong?
How do you love someone knowing it won't last forever?

spoiler.summary: Chidi and Eleanor fall in love in numerous rebooted timelines before becoming a couple for real on Earth. For the new experiment he volunteers to have his memory wiped and lives as a stranger to her, even briefly dating Simone; later his memories are restored and he and Eleanor reunite. In the final episode he realises he is at peace and ready to walk through the final door, and Eleanor, heartbroken, lets him go.
key_events: Falls in love with Eleanor across multiple reboots
Becomes a couple on Earth
Has his memory wiped to protect the experiment
Memories restored; reunites with Eleanor
Leaves through the final door before Eleanor
spoiler.got_right: He learns to open up, take risks and love without needing certainty.
spoiler.got_wrong: For a long time he lets fear and overthinking hold him back from saying what he feels.

nodes.name: Tahani Al-Jamil
nodes.role: A glamorous, gracious British socialite and philanthropist who raised billions for charity, and the neighbourhood's self-appointed hostess who can't stop name-dropping famous friends.

nodes.title: Always performing for approval
nodes.literal_situation: Tahani lives in a mansion in the neighbourhood and throws lavish parties for the other residents. She seems perfect: elegant, generous and endlessly accomplished. Beneath the polish, she has spent her life seeking the approval of cold parents who always preferred her celebrated sister.
nodes.pattern_label: chasing approval from a family who never gave it
nodes.pattern_text: A person has built their whole life around winning approval, from parents who favoured a sibling and from everyone watching. Their generosity and achievements are real, but they are also a performance for an audience that never applauds enough. They have to find out who they are when they stop competing and whether they can value themselves without outside praise.
nodes.hook: Tahani is the most admired person in the room and clearly needs to be, but she cannot quite stop comparing herself to a sister she can never outshine.
nodes.why_relatable: Who are good deeds for when you need to be seen doing them? Can you stop competing with a sibling who is always ahead? What would it take to feel enough without applause?
watch_for: Notice how she talks about her family, and what she leaves out.
How does she react when someone isn't impressed by her?
Is her kindness to others different from her need to be liked?
example_user_messages: My parents always loved my sister more and I've spent my whole life trying to prove myself.
I do a lot of good things but honestly I think I mostly want people to notice.
No matter what I achieve my family never seems impressed.
I'm tired of comparing myself to my sibling all the time.

spoiler.summary: Tahani learns she was actually meant for the Bad Place: her charity work was motivated by jealousy and a desire to beat her sister Kamilah, and she died when a statue of Kamilah fell on her. On Earth she gives away her fortune, tries a series of grand gestures, and eventually reconciles with Kamilah after discovering her sister had envied her too. She learns to let go of her parents' approval and finds real friendship with Eleanor.
key_events: Revealed to be in the Bad Place because of her selfish motives
Died when a statue of her sister fell on her
Gives away her fortune on Earth
Reconciles with Kamilah, who was also jealous of her
Credits Eleanor's friendship for her growth
spoiler.got_right: She is genuinely loyal and generous with her friends, and she eventually seeks her own worth rather than her parents' praise.
spoiler.got_wrong: She measures her value by applause and rivalry, and uses charity as a competition.

nodes.title: Finding a purpose of her own
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that strips away the stage she has always performed on, Tahani has to figure out who she is when nobody is watching, and what she might actually be good at beyond being impressive.
nodes.pattern_label: rebuilding an identity after losing the old one
nodes.pattern_text: A person whose identity was built on status and appearances loses the setting that gave it meaning. Without their usual role, they try one reinvention after another, looking for a purpose that feels truly theirs. They learn that real worth comes from doing work they care about, not from being admired.
nodes.hook: For the first time, Tahani can't lean on her status, and she is scrambling to prove, mostly to herself, that she has something real to offer.
nodes.why_relatable: Who are you once your old role is gone? How do you find work that feels meaningful rather than impressive? Can you start again at the bottom after a lifetime at the top?
watch_for: Notice which new pursuits she tries for show and which she tries for herself.
How does she cope with being bad at something?
Who helps her see herself differently?
example_user_messages: I've lost the job and lifestyle that defined me and I don't know who I am now.
I keep trying new things to prove myself but none of it feels like me.
I'm starting over from scratch after years of being at the top, and it's humbling.
I want to find work that actually means something to me.

spoiler.summary: After returning to Earth and later being thrust back into the afterlife, Tahani gives up her fortune and status, briefly lives off the grid, and learns a string of practical skills to prove herself. She becomes an essential part of the team building the new afterlife. In the finale, instead of walking through the door, she chooses to stay and become an architect alongside Michael, helping others as her true calling.
key_events: Gives away her fortune
Learns dozens of practical skills in the afterlife
Helps build the new afterlife
Chooses to become an architect instead of leaving
spoiler.got_right: She finds genuine joy in doing meaningful work and in helping others grow.
spoiler.got_wrong: At first every reinvention is still about proving herself to someone else.

nodes.name: Jason Mendoza
nodes.role: A sweet, impulsive young guy from Florida who has landed in the afterlife neighbourhood and is keeping a very low profile, saying as little as possible.

nodes.title: The quiet one everyone projects onto
nodes.literal_situation: In the neighbourhood he barely says a word, communicating only through calm gestures while the people around him talk for him and read their own meaning into his silence.
nodes.pattern_label: hiding who you are to fit in
nodes.pattern_text: Someone lands in a world where they are sure they don't belong and decides the safest option is to say as little as possible and let people see whatever they want to see. Keeping up the act is lonely and frightening. Eventually they have to find out whether the people around them will accept who they really are.
nodes.hook: He never says a word, and the neighbourhood treats his silence as wisdom, but nobody knows what is going on beneath the calm.
nodes.why_relatable: What is it like to be defined entirely by other people's assumptions? How long can someone keep quiet about who they are? What might a calm surface be hiding?
watch_for: Notice how other characters fill in the blanks about him.
What might his silence be costing him?
How does he react when someone treats him as a real person rather than a symbol?
example_user_messages: I'm in a place where I feel totally out of my depth so I just keep quiet and hope nobody notices.
Everyone thinks I'm someone I'm not and correcting them feels impossible now.
I'm scared that if people knew the real me they wouldn't want me around.
I've been pretending for so long I don't know how to stop.

spoiler.summary: 'Jianyu' is actually Jason Mendoza, an amateur DJ and small-time criminal from Jacksonville, Florida, who died suffocating in a safe during a botched robbery. Placed in the neighbourhood as a silent monk, he kept quiet out of terror of being sent to the Bad Place. He reveals himself to Eleanor early on, and joins the other humans; it later turns out they were all in the Bad Place together.
key_events: 'Jianyu' is really Jason Mendoza from Jacksonville
Died locked in a safe during a botched heist
Reveals himself to Eleanor and Chidi
Part of the Bad Place experiment all along
spoiler.got_right: Once he opens up, he is loyal, warm and completely himself.
spoiler.got_wrong: Out of fear he lets a lie define him and isolates himself instead of asking for help.

nodes.title: The big-hearted guy learning to think things through
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that changes how everyone sees him, we get to know an impulsive, fun-loving guy who acts first and thinks later, and who must find out whether someone like him can grow up without losing what makes him lovable.
nodes.pattern_label: an impulsive, loyal person learning to grow up
nodes.pattern_text: A good-natured but reckless person has spent their life chasing fun and quick fixes, often dragging friends into trouble. They are fiercely loyal and surprisingly wise at moments, but struggle with consequences, responsibility and a parent who modelled the same chaos. They slowly learn to slow down and choose the people they love over their impulses.
nodes.hook: He is sweet, loyal and utterly impulsive, the kind of guy whose best ideas and worst ideas feel exactly the same to him.
nodes.why_relatable: Can someone who always chooses fun learn to take responsibility? How much of who we are comes from the parent who raised us? What does real loyalty look like when your friends deserve better choices from you?
watch_for: Notice the moments when he surprises everyone with real insight.
How does his relationship with his father shape his choices?
Who does he start putting ahead of his impulses?
example_user_messages: I always act on impulse and then regret it, and I'm starting to think I need to grow up.
My dad was kind of a mess and I'm scared I'm turning into him.
My friends love me but they say I never think things through.
I don't know how to be a responsible adult, I just want to have fun.

spoiler.summary: Jason's dream of success as a DJ was full of petty crimes with his best friend Pillboi and his father Donkey Doug. He falls for Janet and marries her in season 1, has a fling with Tahani after reboots, and on Earth tries to straighten out his dance crew and reconnect with his dad before sliding back. Over time he becomes a trusted part of the team and a devoted partner to Janet. In the end, after finding peace, he waits a long time in the woods to give Janet a necklace he made, then walks through the final door.
key_events: Marries Janet in season 1
Romance with Tahani in a rebooted timeline
Reconnects with Donkey Doug, who doesn't change
Recommits to Janet
Leaves through the final door after saying goodbye to Janet
spoiler.got_right: He is fiercely loyal and his simple, open-hearted instincts are often exactly right.
spoiler.got_wrong: He relies on impulse and 'Molotov cocktail' solutions and repeats his father's reckless patterns.

nodes.name: Michael
nodes.role: The warm, fussy and endearingly nervous architect who designed the neighbourhood, welcoming new residents to the Good Place in what is his very first neighbourhood.

nodes.title: Keeping his dream project together
nodes.literal_situation: Michael has just unveiled his first neighbourhood, a paradise he designed down to every frozen-yogurt shop. He is thrilled to welcome his residents, but soon strange malfunctions start disrupting everything, and he is desperate to keep it all from falling apart.
nodes.pattern_label: questioning the work that defines you
nodes.pattern_text: Someone has poured their entire identity into a career and a big project meant to impress their superiors. As things start going wrong, they are forced to spend time with the very people their work affects. Slowly they begin questioning what their work is for, and who they want to be beyond their role.
nodes.hook: Michael is a proud, anxious first-time architect whose perfect neighbourhood is starting to glitch, and his career may depend on fixing it.
nodes.why_relatable: What happens when your big project doesn't go according to plan? How much of your identity is tied up in your job? What do you owe the people your work affects?
watch_for: Notice how he responds when things go wrong in his neighbourhood.
How does he talk about the residents, and about his bosses?
What fascinates him about humans?
example_user_messages: My whole career is riding on this project and everything keeps going wrong.
I've started to wonder if the work I've been doing all these years actually hurts people.
I care way too much about impressing my bosses.
I'm realising the people I'm supposed to be managing understand things I don't.

spoiler.summary: Michael is actually a demon, and the 'Good Place' is his experimental Bad Place neighbourhood, designed for four humans to psychologically torture each other.
