When Eleanor figures it out, he reboots them hundreds of times, but they keep uncovering the truth. Facing retirement by his boss Shawn, he teams up with the humans, takes ethics lessons from Chidi, and gradually and genuinely becomes good, eventually betraying the Bad Place to save them.
key_events: Revealed to be a demon; the neighbourhood is the Bad Place
Reboots the humans more than 800 times
Teams up with the humans to avoid retirement
Learns ethics from Chidi
Turns against the Bad Place to save the humans
spoiler.got_right: He eventually lets himself be changed by the people he was meant to hurt and chooses to protect them.
spoiler.got_wrong: He puts his ego and career ambitions over the wellbeing of others and manipulates people who trust him.

nodes.title: Finding out what his existence is for
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that changes his relationship with the humans he oversees, Michael finds himself in unfamiliar territory: learning from them, fighting for them, and wondering what his own long existence is really for.
nodes.pattern_label: rethinking your life's purpose later in life
nodes.pattern_text: A person who has been around a long time and always defined themselves by their role starts learning from people they once looked down on. Friendship, loyalty and a newfound sense of mortality make them question what gives life meaning. They reinvent themselves and discover that being truly alive means accepting limits.
nodes.hook: Michael is used to being in charge, and now he has to learn to be a friend, a student and someone others can trust.
nodes.why_relatable: Can you change who you are after a very long time of being one thing? What does it mean to be a good friend when you have never had one? Would you give up your power for a more meaningful life?
watch_for: Notice how he reacts to the idea of endings and death.
How does he handle it when the people he cares about are in danger?
What does he envy about human beings?
example_user_messages: I've done the same thing for decades and I'm only now questioning if it means anything.
I'm realising I've never really had real friends until now.
I've always been the one in charge and it's strange to be learning from younger people.
I'm scared of getting older and running out of time.

spoiler.summary: Michael faces an existential crisis over death during his ethics lessons, then helps the humans reach the Judge and protects them on Earth. He discovers that nobody has made it into the Good Place in centuries because the points system is broken, runs a new experiment with Eleanor, and helps design a new afterlife. In the finale, instead of retiring, he asks to become human and lives out a mortal life on Earth, finding joy in small things; he is nudged toward kindness by a spark of Eleanor.
key_events: Existential crisis about death
Protects the humans on Earth
Discovers the points system is broken
Co-runs a new experiment with Eleanor
Becomes human and lives on Earth
spoiler.got_right: He embraces humility, friendship and the courage to change completely.
spoiler.got_wrong: He sometimes clings to control and grand schemes when simply trusting his friends would work better.

nodes.name: Janet
nodes.role: The neighbourhood's cheerful, all-knowing assistant, who appears whenever called and can provide anything the residents need, and who is quick to point out she is not a robot.

nodes.title: More than just the helper
nodes.literal_situation: Janet is the neighbourhood's helpful assistant, answering every question and fetching anything anyone needs with a sunny smile. Everyone treats her as part of the scenery rather than a person.
nodes.pattern_label: a helper discovering they have needs too
nodes.pattern_text: Someone whose whole identity is being useful to others has never asked what they want for themselves. As they begin to have feelings and preferences that don't fit their role, they are confused and embarrassed. They have to claim their own inner life and ask others to treat them as a full person.
nodes.hook: Janet exists to help, and does it perfectly, but nobody, not even Janet, has asked whether there is more to her.
nodes.why_relatable: What happens when the dependable helper starts wanting something for herself? Can someone defined by their usefulness discover who they are? How do others react when a person they took for granted changes?
watch_for: Notice how the residents talk to Janet compared with each other.
When does she start behaving in ways that surprise even her?
Who treats her as a person, and who treats her as a tool?
example_user_messages: I'm always the one who helps everyone and I've never really thought about what I want.
People treat me like I'm just there to be useful.
I've started having feelings that don't fit the role everyone expects me to play.
I want to be seen as a whole person, not just the reliable one.

spoiler.summary: After being rebooted (and nearly 'killed' by the humans, though she begs for her life only as a safety feature), Janet starts glitching and developing emotions. Each reboot makes her more human. She becomes a true friend and team member to the humans and Michael, even impersonating a Bad Janet and saving everyone by pulling them into her void, where they discover her inner world. By the end she is fully a person with her own feelings and choices.
key_events: The humans try to kill her by resetting her
Develops emotions and glitches after reboots
Poses as a Bad Janet
Pulls the group into her void to save them
Becomes a full member of the team and a person in her own right
spoiler.got_right: She learns to speak up for what she wants and embraces her growing personhood.
spoiler.got_wrong: She suppresses her feelings for too long, treating them as malfunctions.

nodes.title: Feelings she didn't expect to have
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that stirs unfamiliar feelings in her, Janet finds herself caught up in love, jealousy and heartbreak, emotions she has no experience handling.
nodes.pattern_label: navigating love for the first time
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has always been calm and composed falls in love for the first time and is thrown by the intensity of it. They struggle with jealousy, rejection and the pain of watching someone they love choose differently. They learn that deep feelings are not a malfunction, and that love can involve letting go.
nodes.hook: Janet has always been perfectly composed, and now her own feelings are making her behave in ways she can't explain.
nodes.why_relatable: What do you do with feelings you never expected to have? How do you handle jealousy when you're supposed to be fine? Can you love someone without controlling what they choose?
watch_for: Notice what happens to her surroundings when she's upset.
How does she try to handle heartbreak on her own?
Does she let herself be honest about what she wants?
example_user_messages: I've never felt this way about anyone before and it's scaring me.
I'm so jealous of the person my crush likes and I hate feeling like this.
I made a rebound mistake after getting my heart broken.
How do you let go of someone you still love?

spoiler.summary: Janet falls in love with Jason and marries him in season 1, but their marriage is erased by a reboot. She suffers when Jason pairs up with Tahani and builds a rebound boyfriend, Derek, who glitches. Eventually she confesses her love to Jason in front of the Judge, and they become a couple again. In the finale, Jason waits a long time to give her a handmade necklace before walking through the final door; Janet stays behind and lets him go.
key_events: Marries Jason in season 1
Marriage erased by a reboot
Builds a rebound boyfriend, Derek
Confesses her love to Jason
Jason leaves through the final door
spoiler.got_right: She learns to admit her feelings and let people make their own choices.
spoiler.got_wrong: She hides her heartbreak and copes by building a replacement instead of dealing with her pain.

nodes.name: Michael Scott
nodes.role: The attention-hungry, well-meaning regional manager of a small paper-company branch in Scranton who desperately wants his employees to be his friends.

nodes.title: The boss who wants to be everyone's friend
nodes.literal_situation: Michael runs a small paper-company branch in Scranton. He treats his employees as his family and best friends, stages jokes and events to get their attention, and can't understand why they mostly roll their eyes.
nodes.pattern_label: a lonely leader who needs his team to love him
nodes.pattern_text: A person put in charge of others confuses being liked with doing the job well. Their need for approval makes them overshare, overstep and dodge hard calls, and every sign of rejection lands as a personal wound. The story asks whether they can earn real respect and real closeness without making everyone else responsible for their loneliness.
nodes.hook: Michael calls himself the world's best boss and bought the mug to prove it. His staff dodges his meetings, and a documentary crew is filming every awkward joke.
nodes.why_relatable: He wants work to feel like family because he doesn't have much of one outside it. Can you be close to the people you manage, or does the wish to be liked keep getting in the way of leading them? What happens when your loudest need is the one you can't admit?
watch_for: When does he choose being liked over doing the right thing, and when does he do the reverse?
Which coworkers start to see what's underneath the act, and what changes their minds?
What does he do when someone on his team is actually hurting?
example_user_messages: I just got put in charge of people I used to joke around with and I can't stand the thought of them not liking me.
My team never invites me to anything and honestly work is most of my social life.
I keep trying so hard to be fun at work and I can tell people find me exhausting.
I avoid giving hard feedback because I'm scared people will turn on me.

spoiler.summary: Across seven seasons Michael blunders through offensive meetings, pointless events and failed schemes, yet his branch keeps performing because he genuinely cares about his people. He sabotages Jim's shot at a promotion to protect his own job, clashes with corporate, quits to start a rival company, and slowly wins his staff's affection by showing up for them when it counts (buying Pam's painting, shielding the staff from layoff fears). When he falls in love with Holly and she has to move to Colorado to care for her parents, he chooses her over the job, secretly leaves a day early to avoid goodbyes, shares a tearful farewell with Jim, and Pam catches him at the airport. He returns in the finale as Dwight's best man, now a father.
key_events: Outs Oscar to the office and runs a disastrous Diversity Day
Gives Jim a bad recommendation to keep his own job, then agrees to co-manage with him
Buys Pam's painting at her art show and tells her he's proud of her
Quits and founds the Michael Scott Paper Company
Leaves Scranton for Colorado with Holly a day early; Jim calls him the best boss he ever had
Pam says goodbye barefoot at the airport
Returns as Dwight's best man in the finale with children of his own
spoiler.got_right: He genuinely loves his people and shows up for them when it matters; his warmth turns a dull workplace into something like a family.
spoiler.got_wrong: He makes his loneliness everyone else's problem, crosses boundaries constantly, and puts being liked ahead of fairness, professionalism and other people's ambitions.

nodes.title: Longing for someone to come home to
nodes.literal_situation: Michael is a single man in his early forties who openly dreams of a wife and a houseful of kids. He throws himself into every crush and date, and keeps misreading who is actually interested.
nodes.pattern_label: a lonely romantic looking for love in the wrong places
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has wanted a family of their own since childhood keeps throwing themselves at relationships that can't give it to them, including ones where they are belittled or have to shrink. The story is about telling the difference between being wanted and being loved, and whether they can leave what's familiar long enough to recognise the right person.
nodes.hook: As a kid he said he wanted a hundred children so he'd have a hundred friends who couldn't say no. He's still waiting for the first one.
nodes.why_relatable: Why does he keep choosing people who don't treat him well? Is he in love with a person, or with the idea of not being alone? What would he have to change to be ready for something real?
watch_for: How does he act when a partner puts him down? Does he see it?
What does he give up of himself to keep a relationship going?
Who actually laughs at his jokes, and what does that tell him?
example_user_messages: I'm in my forties, I want a family so badly, and every relationship I get into ends with me feeling stupid.
My partner makes fun of me in front of people and spends my money, but I'm scared of being alone again.
I met someone who actually gets my weird sense of humor but the timing is terrible.
I keep falling for people who clearly aren't into me.

spoiler.summary: Michael starts an on-off relationship with his boss Jan that turns into a controlling, humiliating live-in relationship; it explodes at a dinner party and they break up, and Jan later has a baby without him. He dates Carol, Pam's mother Helene and a married woman, Donna, each a mismatch. He meets Holly, the new HR rep, who shares his goofy humor; she is transferred away and dates someone else, but she returns, they reunite, and he proposes in the office with the staff's help. He leaves Scranton to live with her in Colorado while she cares for her parents, and by the finale they have children.
key_events: One-night stand with Jan after closing a deal at Chili's
The Dinner Party blowup ends the Jan relationship
Falls for Holly; she is transferred to Nashua
Dates Pam's mother and gets slapped by Pam
Discovers he is 'the mistress' of a married woman and ends it
Holly returns; he proposes with candles in the office
Moves to Colorado with Holly and later has children
spoiler.got_right: He never stops believing in love and eventually recognises the person who accepts him exactly as he is.
spoiler.got_wrong: He clings to relationships that diminish him, ignores red flags, and treats partners as the cure for his loneliness rather than as people.

nodes.title: Fifteen years of loyalty and no respect
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, Michael has been with the company for fifteen years, and a new supervisor treats him like a relic. His anniversary party gets cancelled and the people upstairs stop returning his calls, and he starts wondering whether his loyalty was ever returned.
nodes.pattern_label: walking away from a job that stopped valuing you
nodes.pattern_text: After years of devotion to one employer, a person realises they are being taken for granted and quietly managed out. Walking away to bet on themselves means risking money, security and pride with little more than stubbornness for a plan. The story asks what self-respect is worth, and whether their scrappy instincts are enough to build something new.
nodes.hook: He has given the company fifteen years, and nobody upstairs will even pick up the phone.
nodes.why_relatable: Is it braver to stay and fight or to leave? Can he survive outside the only workplace he's ever known? Is his confidence real skill, or bluff?
watch_for: What does he actually do well, once everything else is stripped away?
Who is willing to follow him, and why?
How does he negotiate when he has almost nothing left to lose?
example_user_messages: I've been at my company for fifteen years and a new manager just walked in and treats me like dead weight.
I want to quit and start my own thing but I have no savings and I'm in my forties.
I gave everything to this job and they don't care whether I stay or go.
I started a business with a couple of friends and we're running out of money way faster than I expected.

spoiler.summary: When new VP Charles Miner arrives and cancels Michael's fifteenth-anniversary party, Michael drives to corporate, realises CFO David Wallace is only humoring him, and quits on the spot. He founds the Michael Scott Paper Company in a cramped office with Pam and Ryan, poaches clients with prices that turn out to be unsustainable, and soon realises they are going broke. Using the leverage of Dunder Mifflin's lost business, he bluffs his way into a buyout that brings all three of them back with full benefits instead of cash, and Charles is pushed out.
key_events: Charles Miner cancels his anniversary party
Quits in David Wallace's office
Recruits Pam and Ryan to the Michael Scott Paper Company
Discovers their pricing is bankrupting them
Negotiates his, Pam's and Ryan's rehiring instead of a cash buyout
spoiler.got_right: He finally stands up for his own worth, and his sales instincts and nerve at the negotiating table turn out to be real.
spoiler.got_wrong: He leaps without a business plan, drags two people into financial risk, and only escapes disaster through a well-timed bluff.

nodes.name: Jim Halpert
nodes.role: A laid-back, quick-witted salesman at the Scranton branch who treats the job as temporary, pranks his deskmate, and is quietly close to the receptionist.

nodes.title: In love with a friend who's taken
nodes.literal_situation: Jim is a salesman who treats his job as a placeholder and spends his days pranking the deskmate who drives him crazy. His best friend at work is the receptionist, Pam, and she has been engaged to someone else for three years.
nodes.pattern_label: loving a close friend who is committed to someone else
nodes.pattern_text: A person has quietly fallen for their closest friend, who is in a long relationship with someone else. Saying nothing keeps the friendship safe but slowly hollows out their own life; speaking up could cost them everything. The story is about how long you can wait for someone, and when protecting a friendship turns into hiding from your own life.
nodes.hook: Jim's favorite part of the workday is making Pam laugh. Her fiancé works downstairs.
nodes.why_relatable: Should he say how he feels, or would that be unfair to her? What is he putting on hold while he waits? Is the job he shrugs off really just a job, or a place to hide?
watch_for: What does he do with his feelings when he can't act on them?
How does he treat the people he dates while his mind is elsewhere?
What would it take for him to risk the friendship?
example_user_messages: I'm in love with my best friend and she's engaged. I don't know if I should say anything.
I keep dating people just to distract myself from someone I can't have.
I told someone how I felt, they said no, and now I can't stand being in the same room.
My job is fine but I think the only reason I stay is one person.

spoiler.summary: Jim pines for Pam through two seasons, dates Katy, and at Casino Night confesses his love; Pam turns him down and he kisses her anyway. He transfers to Stamford and starts dating Karen. When the branches merge he returns with Karen as his girlfriend and keeps Pam at arm's length, even though Pam called off her wedding because of him. After Pam admits in front of everyone at Beach Games that she misses him, Jim interviews for a corporate job in New York, finds her note in his briefcase, withdraws, drives back and asks Pam out. They start dating, later marry and have two children.
key_events: Confesses his love at Casino Night; Pam says no; they kiss
Transfers to Stamford and dates Karen
Pam calls off her wedding to Roy
Returns to Scranton in the merger with Karen
Withdraws from the corporate job and asks Pam on a date
Dumps Karen off-screen
spoiler.got_right: In the end he is honest about what matters, choosing the person over the promotion.
spoiler.got_wrong: He hides behind jokes and indifference, runs away instead of facing rejection, and pulls Karen into a relationship while still in love with Pam.

nodes.title: Betting on a dream while others depend on you
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after years in which his life has become settled and comfortable, Jim is restless. An old friend offers him a stake in a risky new business in another city, doing work he's genuinely excited about.
nodes.pattern_label: chasing a late dream at a cost to the people at home
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has spent years being competent at a job they never loved gets a real shot at the work they dream of, but it means long absences, a big financial gamble and asking a lot of the people who share their life. The story is about whether ambition and a shared life can fit together, and what happens when you make a decision for two people on your own.
nodes.hook: He's been coasting for years and knows it. Now someone is offering him the thing he gave up on, and saying yes isn't really his decision alone.
nodes.why_relatable: Is it selfish to want more when your life is already good? How much risk is fair to take with money and time that aren't only yours? What does he owe the people who would carry the load while he's gone?
watch_for: Who does he tell about the opportunity, and when?
What does he assume the people around him will be fine with?
How does each side define what counts as a sacrifice?
example_user_messages: I've been offered a job doing what I actually love, but it means being away from my wife and kids half the week.
I put a chunk of our savings into my friend's startup and didn't tell my partner first.
My partner and I have been fighting constantly since I started this new venture.
I'm scared that if I say no to this I'll secretly resent my family forever.

spoiler.summary: Jim secretly invests in and joins Athlead, a Philadelphia sports-marketing startup, telling Pam only later and alarming her with how much money he put in. He splits the week between Scranton and Philadelphia; the strain grows until he misses Cece's recital and snaps at Pam, who breaks down. He turns down a lucrative three-month roadshow to stay with her, and Pam fears he'll resent her for it. Jim has the documentary crew show her a montage of their history and finally gives her the teapot letter. In the finale Pam has secretly put their house on the market so they can move to Austin, where Jim rejoins the company.
key_events: Secretly invests in Athlead and keeps it from Pam
Commutes to Philadelphia; marriage strains
Misses Cece's recital and blames Pam; Pam breaks down
Turns down the roadshow to stay with Pam
Gives Pam the teapot letter
Pam sells the house; they move to Austin
spoiler.got_right: He finally takes his own ambitions seriously, and when it matters he chooses his marriage and listens.
spoiler.got_wrong: He makes a huge shared decision alone, keeps it secret, and leaves Pam carrying the family while telling himself she's fine.

nodes.name: Pam Beesly
nodes.role: The shy, artistic receptionist at the Scranton branch, long engaged to a warehouse worker, who keeps her own wishes to herself.

nodes.title: Finding her voice
nodes.literal_situation: Pam answers the phones at a paper company, a job she took years ago as a stopgap. She has been engaged for three years to a fiancé who dismisses her art, and she answers most questions about her own life with a shrug.
nodes.pattern_label: a quiet person learning to ask for what she wants
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who has spent years going along with what everyone expects, a comfortable relationship, a job that was meant to be temporary, a talent they never pursue, slowly realises they are living a small, safe life by default. The story is about finding the courage to say what you want out loud, even when it disappoints people.
nodes.hook: Pam's life is on hold: the wedding date keeps slipping, her drawings stay in a notebook, and the only person who seems to notice she's unhappy is her friend at the next desk over.
nodes.why_relatable: What is she afraid will happen if she speaks up? Is safe the same as happy? Can someone who has always been the easygoing one start taking up space?
watch_for: When does she almost say what she means, and what stops her?
Who in her life encourages her art, and who shrugs it off?
What does courage look like for someone who isn't naturally bold?
example_user_messages: I've been engaged for years and I'm not even sure I want to get married anymore.
My boyfriend thinks my art is a waste of time and I've basically stopped doing it.
I'm the one who never makes a fuss, and I'm starting to feel invisible in my own life.
I have feelings for a friend and I'm scared to even admit it to myself.

spoiler.summary: Pam turns Jim down when he confesses at Casino Night, but calls off her wedding to Roy. With Jim gone to Stamford she gets her own apartment, a car and art classes. She briefly reunites with Roy, confesses the kiss, and ends it for good when he trashes a bar in a rage. Stung by overhearing that her art lacks courage, she walks across hot coals at Beach Games and tells Jim in front of everyone that he's the reason she called off the wedding. Jim asks her out, they start dating, and she is accepted to Pratt design school.
key_events: Turns Jim down at Casino Night, then kisses him back
Calls off her wedding to Roy
Moves into her own place and takes art classes
Ends it with Roy after he smashes up a bar
Coal walk and public confession at Beach Games
Starts dating Jim; accepted to Pratt
spoiler.got_right: She learns that small, honest acts of courage change everything, and she starts choosing her own life.
spoiler.got_wrong: For years she lets others decide for her, stays in a relationship out of inertia, and hides her feelings even from herself.

nodes.title: Testing the dream once it's real
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that gives her the confidence to take her ambitions seriously, Pam finally gets a real chance to train for a creative career and has to find out whether the dream holds up.
nodes.pattern_label: discovering your dream career isn't what you pictured
nodes.pattern_text: A person finally goes after the path they always said they wanted, only to find it doesn't fit the way they imagined. Stepping back feels like failure, and the next jobs they try are either not them or not something they're good at. The story is about separating what you're good at from what you think you should want, and shaping a role that fits.
nodes.hook: She spent years saying 'someday.' Now someday is here, and she's terrified it won't be what she hoped.
nodes.why_relatable: Does walking away from something you dreamed about make you a failure? What if you're bad at the sensible option too? Can you shape work around your real strengths instead of squeezing yourself into a job?
watch_for: Is she leaving something because it's wrong for her, or because it's hard?
What skills does she have that nobody has ever named?
How does she handle being the worst at something in front of colleagues?
example_user_messages: I finally went back to school for the thing I always wanted and I'm realising I don't actually like it.
I quit a program halfway through and I feel like everyone thinks I just gave up.
I switched careers and I'm the worst person on my team. Everyone else seems to know what they're doing.
I'm good at organizing people and reading a room, but that's not really a job, is it?

spoiler.summary: Pam goes to Pratt in New York (Jim proposes at a rainy rest stop), fails a class and, realising she hates graphic design, comes home. She becomes the first salesperson at Michael's scrappy startup and is rehired into sales when it's bought out, but she's one of the worst sellers in the office. She tricks Gabe into creating a salaried 'office administrator' role for her, where her people skills and knowledge of her coworkers make her genuinely effective. Per NBC's site, she later starts a mural business in Austin.
key_events: Starts at Pratt; Jim proposes at a rest stop
Fails a class and decides she hates graphic design
Joins the Michael Scott Paper Company as a saleswoman
Struggles as one of the worst salespeople
Invents the office administrator job and thrives
spoiler.got_right: She is honest with herself about what doesn't fit and builds a role around her real strengths.
spoiler.got_wrong: She sometimes avoids the hard middle of learning something new, and she gets her new role through a con rather than by asking directly.

nodes.title: Holding everything together while someone else chases a dream
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after years in which her life has settled into a steady routine, Pam learns that the person she shares her life with has quietly committed to a risky new venture in another city, leaving her to carry home and work on her own for long stretches.
nodes.pattern_label: the partner left holding everything together
nodes.pattern_text: When one partner goes after a big opportunity, the other absorbs the extra load at home, the loneliness and the worry, while trying hard to be supportive. Resentment and guilt build on both sides. The story is about saying what you need without crushing someone else's dream, and deciding together what a shared life should look like.
nodes.hook: She wants to be the supportive one. She's also exhausted, and she found out about the plan after it was already made.
nodes.why_relatable: How do you support someone's dream when it's costing you? Is it fair to ask them to give it up? What if you're afraid you'll never be enough to keep them happy?
watch_for: Who does she confide in when she can't say it at home?
What does she want for herself, separate from what she wants for them?
How do they each define giving something up?
example_user_messages: My husband took a job in another city without really asking me and now I'm doing everything with the kids by myself.
I want to support my partner's dream but I'm drowning and I feel guilty for even saying it.
I'm scared my partner will resent me forever if I ask him to stay.
We fight all the time since his new business started and I don't recognise us anymore.

spoiler.summary: Pam discovers Jim has secretly invested their money in Athlead in Philadelphia. While he commutes she handles work and two kids alone; after he misses Cece's recital and blames her, she breaks down and is comforted by Brian, the boom-mic operator. She interviews for a Philadelphia job but realises she doesn't want to move. When Jim turns down a big opportunity for her, she fears she isn't enough for him; he shows her a montage of their history and the teapot letter. In the finale she secretly sells their house so they can move to Austin together for his dream, and starts a mural business there.
key_events: Learns Jim hid his Athlead investment
Breaks down after the missed recital; Brian comforts her
Interviews in Philadelphia, then admits she doesn't want to move
Jim shows her the documentary montage and teapot letter
Secretly puts the house on the market; they move to Austin
spoiler.got_right: She eventually names her fear honestly and then makes a generous, active choice rather than a resentful sacrifice.
spoiler.got_wrong: For a long time she swallows her exhaustion to seem supportive, letting it build until it spills out.

nodes.name: Dwight Schrute
nodes.role: The branch's intense, rule-obsessed top salesman and beet farmer, who craves authority and worships his boss.

nodes.title: Desperate to be second in command
nodes.literal_situation: Dwight is the top salesman at a small paper-company branch and insists he is 'Assistant Regional Manager' (the real title is Assistant to the Regional Manager). He worships his boss, runs a beet farm on the side, and takes rules, rank and his own dignity extremely seriously.
nodes.pattern_label: craving authority before learning to lead
nodes.pattern_text: A fiercely loyal, hard-working person wants power and recognition so badly that they treat colleagues as rivals and rules as weapons. Their intensity makes them great at the work and terrible with people. The story asks whether they can earn the role they crave, and whether leading means commanding people or caring about them.
nodes.hook: Dwight would do anything his boss asked, and he keeps a mental list of everyone who might threaten his rank, starting with the prankster at the next desk.
nodes.why_relatable: What is he really chasing: the title, or the respect he thinks it brings? Can loyalty and ambition coexist when the person you admire is also in your way? What would it take for him to trust the people he sees as competition?
watch_for: What does he do when loyalty to his boss and his own ambition point in different directions?
When he gets a taste of power, how does he use it?
Who is quietly on his side even while he treats them as an enemy?
example_user_messages: I've wanted a management role for years and every time I get close someone else gets it.
People at work say I'm intense and hard to work with, but I'm just the only one taking the job seriously.
My mentor keeps passing me over and I'm starting to resent him.
I finally got some authority at work, it went to my head, and now my team can't stand me.

spoiler.summary: Dwight goes behind Michael's back to corporate, is forced to quit, and returns. His brief turns as acting manager are tyrannical ('Schrute Bucks'), and later he accidentally fires a gun in the office and loses the interim job. He schemes with Ryan to depose Jim as co-manager, buys the office building, and is set up to run the Sabre store in Florida, where Jim tackles him trying to warn him he's about to be cut, and Packer steals the promotion. Over the years his rivalry with Jim becomes a real, grudging friendship. In season nine, on Jim's recommendation, David Wallace makes Dwight Regional Manager; he appoints Jim his assistant, has Michael as best man at his wedding, and gives Jim and Pam generous severance.
key_events: Goes over Michael's head to Jan and is forced to quit
Tyrannical stint as acting manager
Teams with Ryan to get Jim demoted from co-manager
Accidentally fires a gun in the office as acting manager
Jim tackles him to warn him about the Sabre store
Named permanent Regional Manager on Jim's recommendation
Michael returns as his best man
spoiler.got_right: His loyalty, work ethic and love for the job are real, and he learns to value the people he once treated as obstacles.
spoiler.got_wrong: He confuses rank with respect, schemes against colleagues and bosses, and uses power to punish rather than to lead.

nodes.title: A love he's not allowed to show
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, Dwight is quietly involved with a coworker who insists that nobody at work can ever find out, and who sets every rule of the relationship.
nodes.pattern_label: loving someone who keeps you hidden
nodes.pattern_text: A person is devoted to a partner who wants the relationship kept secret and controls its terms. When things break down, both keep circling back through pride, jealousy and bad timing. The story asks whether two stubborn, guarded people can ever be honest enough to choose each other in public.
nodes.hook: He is loyal to a fault. She keeps him a secret.
nodes.why_relatable: What does it do to someone to be loved only in private? Is he being loyal, or just unable to let go? Can two people who both need to be in control ever meet in the middle?
watch_for: Who sets the rules of the relationship, and who follows them?
What does he do when he feels replaced?
What would a real grand gesture look like for someone this guarded?
example_user_messages: My partner won't let me tell anyone we're together and it's starting to feel like I'm her dirty secret.
We broke up months ago but we keep ending up back together and I don't know what we are.
I found out the person I love was also seeing someone else the whole time.
I think I still want to marry my ex, but we're both too proud to say it first.

spoiler.summary: Dwight and Angela date in secret until he mercy-kills her sick cat Sprinkles and she dumps him. She starts dating Andy but keeps sleeping with Dwight, even after accepting Andy's proposal; Dwight tricks her into a real wedding ceremony at his farm, which she voids. Phyllis exposes the affair and, at the duel, both men learn she lied to each of them and walk away. Angela later negotiates a contract to have Dwight's baby; he backs out for Isabel, then settles for five 'sessions'. Angela marries the Senator and has a son, Phillip, whom she claims is premature. After the Senator comes out, Dwight, now dating Esther, bonds with Phillip and proposes; Angela admits Phillip is his, and they marry in the finale.
key_events: Mercy-kills Angela's cat Sprinkles; she dumps him
Affair continues while Angela is engaged to Andy
Fake wedding at Schrute Farms turns out to be real; Angela voids it
The duel exposes Angela's lies; both men leave her
Baby contract and settlement
Angela has Phillip and claims he's the Senator's
Proposes; Angela admits Phillip is his son; they marry
spoiler.got_right: He stays devoted and, in the end, makes a real, public, vulnerable choice.
spoiler.got_wrong: He accepts being hidden, joins in the deception of Andy, and settles for transactional 'deals' instead of saying what he feels.

nodes.name: Andy Bernard
nodes.role: A preppy, Cornell-obsessed salesman from another branch of the company who badly wants to be liked and hides a quick temper.

nodes.title: Needing everyone to like him
nodes.literal_situation: Andy is a preppy salesman at another branch of the company who never stops mentioning Cornell and his a cappella group. He has a strategy for winning over any boss: mirror his personality, repeat his name, never break a handshake first. Under the confidence is a short fuse.
nodes.pattern_label: the overlooked child still chasing approval
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who grew up feeling second-best in their family has built a whole personality around being liked: bragging, people-pleasing, trying on whatever identity seems to impress. Beneath it is a temper and a fear of never being enough. The story asks whether they can stop performing for approval and discover who they are when nobody is clapping.
nodes.hook: He'll sing, name-drop his college and agree with anything the boss says, and he has no idea why people find him exhausting.
nodes.why_relatable: Why does he need everyone's approval so badly, and whose approval is he really after? What happens to the anger he keeps swallowing? Who is he when he stops trying to impress?
watch_for: What do his family members say to him, and how does he respond?
When he gets angry, what was really hurting him?
Who likes him for who he actually is?
example_user_messages: My parents always made it obvious my brother was the favorite and I'm still trying to impress them in my late thirties.
I overdo it at every new job trying to get people to like me and it always backfires.
I have a temper I'm ashamed of and it comes out whenever I feel humiliated.
I just want my dad to be proud of me once.

spoiler.summary: After the merger Andy sucks up to Michael, feuds with Dwight, and punches a hole in the wall when Jim hides his phone, landing in anger management. He falls for Angela, proposes and plans a lavish wedding while she keeps sleeping with Dwight; the duel exposes the affair and he is crushed. He dates Erin, loses her when she learns of the engagement, then loses her to Gabe and later rejects her out of hurt. Robert California makes him Regional Manager; at a garden party his father publicly belittles him in favor of his younger brother, who got Andy's original name, and his coworkers finally understand him and rally around him. He wins Erin back in Florida but returns to find Nellie in his job, refuses demotion and is fired, then gets David Wallace to buy the company and is reinstated.
key_events: Punches a hole in the wall and goes to anger management
Engaged to Angela, who is cheating with Dwight
The duel with Dwight in the parking lot
Dates Erin; she leaves him after learning of the engagement
Made Regional Manager by Robert California
Father humiliates him at the garden party
Fired after Nellie takes his job; reinstated when David Wallace buys the company
spoiler.got_right: Underneath the act he is kind, brave when it counts (blowing the whistle on the printers, defending the 'losers'), and loyal to his friends.
spoiler.got_wrong: He performs instead of connecting, lets anger and wounded pride drive his choices, and keeps seeking validation from people who can't give it.

nodes.title: Chasing a dream with nothing to fall back on
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a stretch of upheaval in his family and at work, Andy feels increasingly disconnected from the job he's doing. The performing career he wanted since college is still calling, and he's starting to feel it's now or never.
nodes.pattern_label: chasing a long-deferred dream at any cost
nodes.pattern_text: A person who spent years in a stable career they never cared about decides to go all in on the dream they put off, burning bridges and neglecting relationships along the way while everyone warns them it's a mistake. The story asks what it means to fail at your dream in public, and what is left of you afterwards.
nodes.hook: Everyone keeps telling him to be realistic. He's tired of being realistic.
nodes.why_relatable: Is it courage or escape to walk away from security? What does he owe the people he leaves behind? What if the dream doesn't want him back?
watch_for: How does he treat the people who care about him while his attention is elsewhere?
Is he running toward something, or away from something?
What does success mean to him by the end, compared to the start?
example_user_messages: I'm almost 40 and thinking of quitting my job to act. Everyone thinks I'm insane.
I went away for months to figure myself out and came back to find my relationship was over.
I went after my dream and failed in front of everyone, and I'm too embarrassed to face anyone.
I can't tell if I'm being brave or just running away from my real life.

spoiler.summary: Andy returns from manager training cockier and meaner. His father abandons the family, and Andy sails the family boat to the Bahamas for three months, leaving Erin behind; she breaks up with him for Pete. Vengeful, he hires their exes to make them miserable. Inspired by the documentary promos, he pays a dubious agent, quits, and deliberately gets himself fired by David Wallace, then says goodbye with a moving song. His reality-show audition collapses into a viral meltdown ('Baby Wawa'), but a mocking invitation to speak at Cornell goes so well that he is hired in Cornell's admissions office. At the finale he reflects: 'I wish there was a way to know you're in the good old days before you've actually left them.'
key_events: Father abandons the family; family boat must be sold
Sails to the Bahamas for three months, neglecting Erin and the job
Erin dumps him for Pete
Quits and gets himself fired to pursue acting
Viral audition meltdown
Hired by Cornell admissions after a successful speech
spoiler.got_right: He finally stops living for other people's approval and finds a place where he genuinely fits.
spoiler.got_wrong: He treats his partner and his job as disposable on the way to the dream, and mistakes running from his problems for bravery.

nodes.name: Ryan Howard
nodes.role: A business-school student working as a temp at the Scranton branch, who sees the job as a stepping stone and is the object of his boss's embarrassing admiration.

nodes.title: The temp in a hurry to be somebody
nodes.literal_situation: Ryan is a business-school student doing temp work at a paper company, sure it's just a stop on the way to something bigger. His boss has an embarrassing crush on him and keeps sending him on personal errands.
nodes.pattern_label: ambition outrunning character
nodes.pattern_text: A young person convinced they're meant for something bigger rushes up the ladder, taking credit and cutting corners. When success comes too fast, the pressure and the ego take over, and they cope in self-destructive ways. The story is about the gap between looking successful and being ready for it, and whether a hard fall teaches anything.
nodes.hook: Ryan keeps nothing personal on his desk. He doesn't plan on staying long enough to need it.
nodes.why_relatable: What is he actually good at, as opposed to what he looks good doing? Who does he step on to get ahead? What happens to someone who gets what they wanted before they're ready?
watch_for: How does he treat the people who helped him once he no longer needs them?
What does he do when he's in over his head but can't admit it?
Who is still in his corner at his lowest point?
example_user_messages: I got promoted way above my experience level and I'm faking it every single day.
I've been using to keep up with the pressure at my new job and I know it's getting out of hand.
I burned a lot of bridges on the way up, crashed hard, and now I'm back where I started.
I've always felt too good for my job and it's making me miserable and hard to like.

spoiler.summary: Ryan earns his MBA, takes over a sales desk, and then leapfrogs to corporate as Vice President, becoming Michael's boss and immediately dumping Kelly. In New York he grows a beard, launches the Dunder Mifflin Infinity website, develops a cocaine problem, tries to get Jim fired, and is arrested for defrauding shareholders. Released with community service and sober, he returns as a fill-in temp thanks to Michael, joins the Michael Scott Paper Company, and briefly matures there before sliding back to scheming.
key_events: Promoted to corporate VP and becomes Michael's boss
Dumps Kelly the moment he gets the job
Develops a drug problem under pressure
Targets Jim with a bogus warning
Arrested for fraud
Returns sober as a temp; joins the Michael Scott Paper Company
spoiler.got_right: At the bottom he gets sober, accepts help, and briefly discovers the satisfaction of honest work.
spoiler.got_wrong: He treats people as rungs on a ladder, lies to cover his failures, and never takes responsibility for the damage.

nodes.title: Reinventing yourself instead of growing up
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that knocks the shine off his big plans, Ryan is still at the branch in a vague role, cycling through trendy looks, hobbies and startup ideas while doing as little actual work as possible.
nodes.pattern_label: endless reinvention as a way to avoid growing up
nodes.pattern_text: Someone keeps trying on new identities, projects and looks, each one promising to be the thing that finally makes them special. Underneath is a person who has never committed to anything or anyone, and who leans on other people's goodwill to stay afloat. The story asks whether they will ever stop performing and take responsibility for a life.
nodes.hook: Ryan has a new look, a new side project and a new pitch every few months. None of them involve doing his actual job.
nodes.why_relatable: Why is committing to one thing so frightening to him? What does he take from the people who believe in him? What would it take for him to own his choices?
watch_for: How does he treat the one person who keeps investing in him?
What does he want from relationships: love, or an audience?
Whose problem does it become when things go wrong?
example_user_messages: I've started like five businesses and dropped every one. I keep thinking the next idea is the one.
I'm nearly 30, I still live with my parents and borrow my mom's car.
I keep going back to the same on-off relationship because at least someone wants me.
A friend put money into my idea and I let him down, and I don't know how to face him.

spoiler.summary: Ryan adopts a hipster persona, helps Dwight get Jim demoted from co-manager, and launches WUPHF.com with Michael's money, exploiting Michael's loyalty until the company fails. He lies to Deangelo about his job, panics and flees on a bus during the Sabre store presentation, loses Kelly to Ravi and keeps chasing her, then follows her to Ohio. In the finale he appears with a baby son, Drake, whose mother left; he deliberately triggers the baby's strawberry allergy to get time alone with Kelly, and the two run off together, leaving Drake behind with Ravi. Nellie takes the baby.
key_events: Helps Dwight get Jim demoted
Launches WUPHF.com with Michael's money; it collapses
Flees on a bus during the Sabre store presentation
Kelly leaves him for Ravi
Shows up at the finale with baby Drake
Runs off with Kelly, abandoning Drake; Nellie takes him
spoiler.got_right: Very little; in rare moments he admits he got away with too much and wanted real guidance.
spoiler.got_wrong: He mistakes image for identity, exploits people who love him, and dodges every responsibility right up to abandoning his own child.

nodes.name: Erin Hannon
nodes.role: An upbeat, naive young woman raised in foster care who joins the Scranton branch later in the series and wants desperately to belong.

nodes.title: Looking for a family at work
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that shakes up the staff, Erin arrives as the branch's cheerful new receptionist. She grew up in foster care, admires everyone around her, and badly wants the boss, who seems to resent her, to like her.
nodes.pattern_label: a person without family building one where they can
nodes.pattern_text: Someone who grew up without a stable family pours their warmth and loyalty into the people around them, desperate to belong and to be approved of. Their openness makes them easy to underestimate and easy to hurt. The story is about finding the people who choose you back, and learning that you can be loved without having to earn it.
nodes.hook: She's thrilled to be here. The boss barely acknowledges her, and she can't figure out what she did wrong.
nodes.why_relatable: What does a person who never had a family do with all that loyalty? Why does one person's approval matter so much to her? Can you belong somewhere without twisting yourself to fit?
watch_for: Whose approval does she chase, and why that person?
Who starts treating her like family, and how?
What does she do with the anger she almost never shows?
example_user_messages: I grew up in foster care and I think I get way too attached to my coworkers.
My boss doesn't seem to like me and it ruins my whole week. I don't know why it matters so much.
I don't have family, so my friends at work are basically everything to me.
An older guy at work gave me advice like a dad would and I kind of cried.

spoiler.summary: Michael initially freezes Erin out because she was hired while he was gone, but she wins him over after Scott's Tots and happily indulges his odd routines. At the Glee viewing party he realises she sees him as a father figure and embraces it, and before he leaves for Colorado he promises she can always call him for advice. Phyllis takes a DNA test to see whether Erin is the daughter she gave up; it's negative, but Phyllis keeps mothering her. In the finale Erin's birth parents, who saw the documentary, meet her at the Q&A panel.
key_events: Michael freezes her out, then warms to her after Scott's Tots
Michael realises she sees him as a father figure
Michael kisses her on the head and leaves his number before leaving
Phyllis DNA test comes back negative
Meets her birth parents in the finale
spoiler.got_right: Her openness and loyalty eventually earn her a real, chosen family.
spoiler.got_wrong: She seeks approval so hard that she tolerates being dismissed and struggles to stand up for herself.

nodes.title: Learning she deserves better in love
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, Erin has a sweet, awkward crush on Andy, a coworker who flirts back but never quite makes a move, and she has no idea how to ask for what she wants.
nodes.pattern_label: moving from people-pleasing to self-respect in love
nodes.pattern_text: An eager, forgiving person keeps waiting to be chosen: saying yes to whoever asks, staying through neglect, blaming themselves when something feels wrong. The story follows them learning to name what they need and to walk away when they are taken for granted, even when that means disappointing someone.
nodes.hook: She thinks he likes her. He thinks it's her move. Neither of them says a word.
nodes.why_relatable: Why does she say yes to people she doesn't really want? How long do you wait for someone to show up for you? Is kindness the same thing as putting up with anything?
watch_for: Who actually asks her what she wants?
What does she tolerate that she shouldn't?
Who makes her feel like herself rather than an audience?
example_user_messages: I said yes to a date with my manager because I didn't know how to say no, and now we're in a relationship.
My boyfriend left for three months without really asking me and now he acts like nothing changed.
I keep waiting for him to make the first move and it never happens.
Someone new actually listens to me and it made me realise how neglected I've been.

spoiler.summary: Andy and Erin miscommunicate for months before finally dating; she ends it when Michael lets slip that Andy was engaged to Angela. She dates Gabe mostly because he's her boss, breaks up with him publicly at the Dundies, confesses to Andy that she still likes him and is rejected. She drunkenly wishes Andy's girlfriend dead at Christmas, moves to Florida as a live-in maid, and Andy comes to win her back. When Andy leaves for three months on his boat trip she grows close to Pete, finally breaks up with Andy for good, and is still with Pete at the finale.
key_events: First kiss with Andy at the landfill
Dumps Andy after learning about his engagement to Angela
Dates Gabe; breaks up with him at the Dundies
Andy rejects her; she wishes his girlfriend dead
Andy wins her back in Florida
Andy's boat trip; she chooses Pete
spoiler.got_right: She eventually recognises neglect for what it is and chooses someone who simply wants her to be happy.
spoiler.got_wrong: She drifts into relationships out of politeness, stays too long, and struggles to say no until she's at breaking point.

nodes.name: Angela Martin
nodes.role: The strict, judgmental head of accounting and ruler of the party planning committee, who loves her cats and hides her feelings.

nodes.title: Keeping everything, and everyone, under control
nodes.literal_situation: Angela is the tiny, rigid head of accounting and the iron-fisted ruler of the party planning committee. She judges everyone's morals and outfits, lives with her cats, and never lets anyone see what she feels.
nodes.pattern_label: a rigid perfectionist hiding a messy heart
nodes.pattern_text: A person keeps others at a distance with rules, judgment and impossible standards, while privately living a life that contradicts everything they preach. Control feels safer than vulnerability, so they manipulate, lie, and push away the person they actually love. The story asks whether they can drop the armor, admit what they want, and let someone see them.
nodes.hook: Angela disapproves of nearly everything and everyone. Whatever she wants for herself, she keeps behind a locked door.
nodes.why_relatable: What is she protecting by being so hard on everyone? Why is it easier to judge others than admit what she wants? What happens when the image she's built can't hold the truth?
watch_for: How does she treat the people she looks down on, compared with the ones she quietly admires?
When her rules and her feelings collide, which one wins?
What does it cost her to apologise?
example_user_messages: People at work call me judgmental and cold, but I just have standards.
I'm seeing someone in secret and I refuse to let anyone at work find out.
I'm engaged to a nice man I don't love and I'm still seeing my ex behind his back.
I haven't spoken to my sister in years over something I can't even remember, and part of me is proud of that.

spoiler.summary: Angela rules the party planning committee tyrannically and secretly dates Dwight, then dumps him after he mercy-kills her cat Sprinkles. On the rebound she dates and gets engaged to Andy while continuing to sleep with Dwight, manipulating both. Phyllis blackmails her and then exposes the affair at the Christmas party, and after the duel both men leave her. She tries to get Dwight to father her child by contract, marries the closeted State Senator Robert Lipton, and gives birth to Phillip, lying that he's premature to hide that Dwight is the father.
key_events: Secret relationship with Dwight
Dumps Dwight after Sprinkles dies
Engaged to Andy while cheating with Dwight
Phyllis blackmails her and exposes the affair
Both men leave her after the duel
Marries the Senator; has Phillip and lies about his conception
spoiler.got_right: She is fiercely competent and, in rare moments (inviting Oscar to the committee, clearing Dwight's name), capable of real loyalty.
spoiler.got_wrong: She judges others for everything she does herself, lies to everyone including the men she's with, and chooses appearances over love.

nodes.title: Starting over from the bottom
nodes.literal_situation: Later in the series, after a turning point that humiliates her publicly and leaves her with nowhere to live, Angela has to accept help from a coworker she has treated badly for years.
nodes.pattern_label: humbled into letting people help
nodes.pattern_text: After a public humiliation strips away the respectable life they built, a proud person has to accept kindness from someone they once looked down on. Losing the image forces them to reckon with how they've treated people, and with the love they gave up for the sake of appearances. The story is about humility, second chances, and finally saying yes to what you actually want.
nodes.hook: She has always been the one looking down on others. Now she's sleeping on someone else's couch.
nodes.why_relatable: Can a proud person accept help without feeling destroyed? Is it too late to go back to a love you walked away from? Who shows up for you when your reputation is gone?
watch_for: How does she respond to kindness she hasn't earned?
What does she finally admit out loud, and to whom?
Is she willing to be vulnerable when there's no guarantee?
example_user_messages: My husband cheated on me with someone I know, and I found out in the most public way possible.
I lost my apartment and I'm staying with a coworker I used to be awful to.
I'm a single mom now and my life looks nothing like what I planned.
I think I'm still in love with my ex, but he's with someone else now.

spoiler.summary: Angela learns the Senator is having an affair with Oscar, plots revenge and then drops it. When the documentary airs, the Senator comes out and publicly leaves her; she loses her money and apartment and moves in with Oscar, with baby Phillip and her cats, and they rebuild their friendship. She realises she still loves Dwight, who is dating Esther. Dwight bonds with Phillip and proposes; she admits Phillip is his son. A year later she reunites with her estranged sister at her bachelorette party and marries Dwight in a traditional Schrute wedding.
key_events: Discovers the Senator's affair with Oscar
Senator comes out publicly and dumps her
Evicted; moves in with Oscar
Admits Phillip is Dwight's son
Reunites with her sister
Marries Dwight
spoiler.got_right: She finally lets go of pride, accepts help, forgives, and tells the truth about what and whom she wants.
spoiler.got_wrong: It takes losing everything before she stops hiding behind image and judgment.

nodes.name: Rick Grimes
nodes.role: A small-town sheriff's deputy who wakes from a coma into a collapsed world and sets out to find his wife and son.

nodes.title: Carrying everyone's survival
nodes.literal_situation: A deputy who went by the book before the collapse becomes the man a band of frightened survivors looks to for every life-or-death decision.
nodes.pattern_label: a decent person hardened by the weight of leading
nodes.pattern_text: A principled person ends up responsible for the safety of everyone around them, though they never asked for the job. Each hard call chips away at who they used to be, and they start to fear that protecting their people is turning them into someone they don't recognise. The question is whether you can carry that much responsibility without losing your humanity, and whether you can ever let others share the load.
nodes.hook: Rick wakes alone in a hospital to a world that has fallen apart. All he wants is to find his family, but his instinct to take charge and do the right thing quickly makes him the person everyone turns to.
nodes.why_relatable: He holds himself responsible for everyone and sets goals no one could meet. How much of yourself can you give up to keep others safe? When does being decisive turn into being ruthless, and who gets to tell you that you've crossed the line?
watch_for: What does each hard decision seem to cost him personally?
How does he react when someone in the group challenges his authority?
Who helps him remember who he was, and does he listen?
example_user_messages: I became the person everyone relies on and I don't know how to put it down. Every mistake feels like it's mine.
I've had to make so many harsh calls at work that I barely recognise myself anymore.
My team trusts me completely, and honestly that scares me more than anything.
I keep telling myself I'm protecting my family, but my partner says I've become cold.

spoiler.summary: Rick finds his family and becomes the group's reluctant leader. After killing his best friend Shane and losing his wife Lori in childbirth, he breaks down, then hardens into a ruthless protector who trusts no outsiders (the prison, Terminus, taking over Alexandria). He relinquishes and resumes leadership, embraces his brutality after the Claimers, and becomes Alexandria's leader and Michonne's partner. His overconfidence against the Saviors leads to Negan's line-up, where Glenn and Abraham are killed and Rick is utterly broken, before he rallies the communities to war. After Carl's death he is tempted toward pure vengeance, but Carl's letter moves him to spare Negan and build a peaceful coalition. Eighteen months later he blows up a bridge to stop a herd and is presumed dead, though he is secretly taken away by a helicopter.
key_events: Kills his best friend Shane in self-defence
Lori dies giving birth to Judith; Rick has a breakdown
Declares the group is no longer a democracy
Rips out Joe's throat with his teeth to save Carl
Becomes leader of Alexandria and Michonne's partner
Negan kills Glenn and Abraham; Rick submits, then rebels
Carl dies; Rick spares Negan to honour Carl's vision
Blows up the bridge and is presumed dead, taken away by helicopter
spoiler.got_right: He never stops caring for his people, and at his best he listens to the people who remind him of his conscience; sparing Negan to build a future is his hardest and wisest choice.
spoiler.got_wrong: He repeatedly lets fear and certainty turn into ruthlessness and arrogance, underestimating enemies and dismissing others' judgement, which costs lives.

nodes.title: Coming home to a family that kept going without him
nodes.literal_situation: Rick reunites with his wife and son at a survivor camp, where his best friend and fellow deputy has been looking after them while Rick was presumed lost.
nodes.pattern_label: returning to a family that moved on
nodes.pattern_text: A person comes back after a long absence expecting to pick up where they left off, only to find that the people they love have adapted without them. A marriage that was already strained and a lifelong friendship are quietly tested by everything nobody is saying. The question is whether honesty and forgiveness can hold a family together when everyone's place in it has shifted.
nodes.hook: It feels like a miracle: the family Rick feared was gone is alive. But his marriage had problems before the collapse, and his closest friend seems less relieved by his return than he expected.
nodes.why_relatable: What happens when you come back and everyone's roles have changed? Can a friendship survive when two people want the same place in a family? How honest can a couple be when both are hiding what they went through apart?
watch_for: What goes unsaid between Rick, his wife and his best friend?
How does Rick handle it when his friend disagrees with how he leads?
What does their son pick up on that the adults don't say out loud?
example_user_messages: I was away for a long time and when I came back my family had their own routines without me. I feel like a guest in my own home.
I think my best friend has feelings for my wife and I don't know how to bring it up.
My marriage was already rocky, and now something happened while I was gone that nobody will talk about.
My oldest friend and I have started competing over everything and I don't know how we got here.

spoiler.summary: Rick learns that Lori and Shane had an affair while he was in a coma and that Lori is pregnant, possibly with Shane's child. Shane grows jealous and unstable, challenging Rick's leadership, and tries to lure him into the woods to kill him; Rick kills Shane instead, and Carl puts down Shane's reanimated body. Rick's marriage stays strained until Lori dies giving birth to Judith, before they can fully reconcile. Rick raises Judith as his own and is haunted by hallucinations of Lori.
key_events: Lori and Shane had an affair during Rick's coma
Lori is pregnant and paternity is uncertain
Shane tries to kill Rick; Rick kills Shane
Carl shoots Shane's zombified body
Lori dies in childbirth before fully reconciling with Rick
Rick raises Judith as his own daughter
spoiler.got_right: He keeps choosing to be a father to both children and eventually understands that Lori's and Shane's choices came from fear and grief, not malice.
spoiler.got_wrong: He avoids emotional honesty with his wife just as he did before the collapse, and he lets the rivalry with Shane escalate instead of confronting it early.

nodes.title: Revenge or the future
nodes.literal_situation: In the middle of an all-out war between communities, Rick is fixated on killing the man who tormented his people.
nodes.pattern_label: choosing mercy after a devastating loss
nodes.pattern_text: After a devastating loss, a person has every reason to want the one they blame to suffer. But someone they love asked them to picture a life after the fighting, where old enemies have to live side by side. The question is whether you can let go of vengeance and build something, even when it means disappointing the people who share your anger.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, in the middle of a brutal conflict, a devastating personal loss leaves Rick burning to destroy his enemy, while a message from someone he loves asks him to imagine a future beyond the fighting.
nodes.why_relatable: Can you honour someone's hopes when your own grief is screaming for something else? Is mercy weakness or strength when others around you want blood? What does it take to lead people toward peace when they have every reason to hate?
watch_for: What does he see in himself that makes him hesitate?
How do his closest allies react to the choice he makes?
Can a peace built on one person's vision last without them?
example_user_messages: Someone took something from me I can never get back, and everyone expects me to want revenge. Part of me does.
My son always believed people could change. I'm trying to live up to that, but it's so hard.
I forgave someone who hurt us badly, and now some of my closest friends won't speak to me.
I'm trying to build something good out of the worst thing that ever happened to me.

spoiler.summary: Carl is bitten and takes his own life, leaving letters asking Rick to make peace. Rick first spirals, lying to and slaughtering surrendering Saviors, but after seeing what he has become he slits Negan's throat and then has Siddiq save him, imprisoning Negan for life and offering the Saviors a place in a new coalition. Maggie and Daryl resent the decision. Rick works to unite the communities by rebuilding a bridge, but the project fractures; he ultimately blows up the bridge to stop a herd and is presumed dead, leaving his vision as his legacy.
key_events: Carl dies after a walker bite and leaves letters
Rick betrays and kills Saviors who helped him
Rick cuts Negan's throat, then orders him saved
Negan is imprisoned for life; Maggie is furious
The bridge project to unite communities falls apart
Rick blows up the bridge and is presumed dead
spoiler.got_right: He chooses to honour his son's vision over his own rage and treats defeated enemies as future neighbours.
spoiler.got_wrong: He imposes his decision without bringing grieving allies like Maggie along, leaving wounds that almost tear the peace apart.

nodes.name: Daryl Dixon
nodes.role: A surly, gifted hunter living in the shadow of his volatile older brother on the edge of a survivor camp outside Atlanta.

nodes.title: The outsider who didn't think he mattered
nodes.literal_situation: A hunter raised in a neglectful, abusive home and used to following his older brother's lead finds himself part of a camp of strangers who need his skills.
nodes.pattern_label: an outsider discovering a chosen family
nodes.pattern_text: Someone raised in neglect and taught that they are worthless has always stayed on the margins, loyal to the one family member who at least showed up. When a group of strangers starts relying on them and treating them with respect, they have to decide who they really are and where they belong. The question is whether they can believe they are worth something, and choose the people who choose them.
nodes.hook: Daryl is angry, prickly and quick to lash out, and he mostly keeps to himself unless his brother is around. Nobody expects much from him, and he expects even less from himself.
nodes.why_relatable: What do you owe the family you were born into when they keep pulling you down? Can you trust people who seem to value you when you've never felt valued? How do you stop acting like the person everyone assumed you'd be?
watch_for: Who is the first person he goes out of his way to help, and why?
How does he behave differently when his brother is around?
What happens when someone thanks him or praises him?
example_user_messages: I grew up being told I was worthless and I still kind of believe it, even though people at my new job keep saying I'm good at what I do.
My older brother is a mess and he drags me into it, but he's the only family I've got.
I've always been the outsider. Now I have friends who actually care about me and I don't know how to handle it.
I have to choose between my family and the people who've actually been there for me.

spoiler.summary: Daryl's tireless search for Carol's missing daughter Sophia earns him respect and a deep bond with Carol, though he retreats when Sophia is found turned. He becomes indispensable at the prison and one of Rick's closest allies. When he rescues Merle from Woodbury he briefly leaves the group to follow his brother, but returns after seeing Merle's cruelty; Merle later sacrifices himself against the Governor and Daryl has to put down his reanimated brother. After the prison falls he bonds with Beth, who helps him face his past, and is devastated when she is killed. By Alexandria he is Rick's brother in all but blood and Carol's closest friend.
key_events: Searches relentlessly for Sophia; Sophia is found as a walker in the barn
Chooses to leave with Merle, then returns to the prison
Merle dies attacking the Governor; Daryl puts him down
Bonds with Beth, who is later shot at Grady Memorial
Rick calls Daryl his brother
Becomes Alexandria's recruiter
spoiler.got_right: He lets his actions show who he is and chooses the family that treats him with respect, even when it means breaking from his brother.
spoiler.got_wrong: He shuts down and lashes out when he's hurt, pushing away the people who care about him instead of letting them in.

nodes.title: The one who keeps running
nodes.literal_situation: Years into rebuilding, Daryl spends most of his time alone in the wilderness, uneasy with a settled life, while the people he loves keep needing him closer.
nodes.pattern_label: a lifelong runner learning to stay
nodes.pattern_text: A person who learned to survive by leaving has built real bonds, but a settled, peaceful life makes them restless and they keep drifting to the edges. When young people start looking to them as a parent figure, they have to decide whether to stay and be relied on, or keep running from the risk of losing more. The question is whether you can let yourself have a good thing when every instinct says to go.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, after a turning point that leaves him adrift, Daryl is more at home in the woods than among people. Yet a lost young person with a painful past sees in him someone who understands.
nodes.why_relatable: Why does a stable life feel harder than a crisis? Can someone who never had a real parent become one? What do you owe the people who depend on you when your heart is pulling you somewhere else?
watch_for: What does he recognise in the young people who look up to him?
When does he choose to leave, and when does he choose to stay?
How does he handle it when a friend's choices put people he loves at risk?
example_user_messages: Every time my life gets stable I get this urge to leave. I don't know why I can't just settle down.
My partner's kid has started treating me like a dad, and I'm terrified of letting them down.
I grew up in an abusive home and now I'm trying to help a teenager who went through the same thing.
My best friend made a reckless choice that hurt people I care about and I don't know if I can forgive her.

spoiler.summary: After Rick's apparent death Daryl searched for his body for years, then lived alone with Dog, and had a relationship with Leah before she left. He becomes a father figure to Lydia, who escaped her abusive mother Alpha, and later to Judith and R.J. Carol's revenge plan traps Connie and Magna in a cave, straining their friendship. Leah resurfaces with the Reapers; Daryl infiltrates them and ultimately kills her to protect Maggie. He reconciles with Carol, joins the Commonwealth army, helps overthrow Pamela Milton, then tells Carol he loves her and rides off to search for Rick, promising Judith he'll come back.
key_events: Spends years searching for Rick's body
Relationship with Leah in the woods
Becomes Lydia's protector and father figure
Rift with Carol after the cave collapse traps Connie
Kills Leah to protect Maggie
Leaves to find Rick after learning he is alive
spoiler.got_right: He shows up for kids who were hurt the way he was and ultimately gives them the steady care he never had.
spoiler.got_wrong: He isolates himself when grieving and lets bitterness toward Carol fester instead of talking it through.

nodes.name: Carol Peletier
nodes.role: A quiet, timid housewife at a survivor camp, trying to shield her young daughter from her controlling, abusive husband.

nodes.title: Finding the strength she was never allowed to have
nodes.literal_situation: At a camp outside Atlanta, a woman who has endured years of domestic abuse tries to protect her daughter while keeping her head down.
nodes.pattern_label: an abuse survivor reclaiming her own power
nodes.pattern_text: A person who spent years in an abusive relationship, making herself small to survive, is suddenly free of the one who controlled her. Grief and danger force her to discover how capable and clear-eyed she really is. The question is how to become strong without losing the tenderness that made her who she was, and whether others will accept the new version of her.
nodes.hook: Carol barely speaks above a whisper. She flinches when her husband raises his voice and has spent years convincing herself that enduring is the same as protecting her child.
nodes.why_relatable: Who are you once the person who defined your life is no longer in charge of it? Can you become strong without becoming hard? What happens when the people around you aren't ready for the stronger you?
watch_for: What small moments show her testing her own voice?
How do the others treat her as she changes, and does she care?
What does she keep of her gentleness, and what does she let go?
example_user_messages: I left an abusive marriage and I don't even know who I am on my own.
For years I made myself small to keep the peace. Now I'm realising I'm actually really capable.
Since my divorce I've become tougher, and some of my friends say they don't recognise me anymore.
I lost the person I was living for and I have to figure out how to keep going.

spoiler.summary: After Ed is killed by walkers, Carol pierces his skull herself. Her daughter Sophia goes missing and is later found turned in Hershel's barn, shattering Carol. She rebuilds herself, learning weapons and medicine, and becomes a pragmatic force at the prison, secretly teaching children to fight. She kills two sick members, Karen and David, to stop a flu outbreak and is exiled by Rick. Later she is forced to kill Lizzie, a disturbed girl in her care who murdered her sister Mika, and confesses the Karen killing to Tyreese, who forgives her.
key_events: Ed dies; Carol smashes his head with a pickaxe
Sophia is missing and later found as a walker in the barn
Secretly teaches the prison children to fight
Kills Karen and David to stop the illness; Rick exiles her
Kills Lizzie after Lizzie murders Mika
Confesses to Tyreese and is forgiven
spoiler.got_right: She refuses to be a victim again and becomes someone who acts decisively to protect the vulnerable.
spoiler.got_wrong: She makes life-or-death choices alone and in secret, becoming so pragmatic that she stops trusting others to share the burden.

nodes.title: When being the strong one becomes too much
nodes.literal_situation: Settled in a community at last, Carol is the group's most ruthless protector behind a harmless-housewife act, but the list of what she has had to do keeps growing.
nodes.pattern_label: burning out from always being the protector
nodes.pattern_text: Someone has spent years doing the hard, ugly things no one else would do to keep the people they love safe. They are good at it, and everyone relies on it, but the weight of it starts to crush them. The question is whether they can step back, grieve what it cost, and find a way to live that isn't only about enduring.
nodes.hook: Later in the series, after years of making the hardest calls for her group, Carol is starting to feel the weight of every one of them. She has found a gentle relationship and a quiet life within reach, and she isn't sure she deserves either.
nodes.why_relatable: What happens when the thing you're best at is slowly destroying you? Is it selfish to walk away from people who depend on you? Can you ever set down what you've done, or only learn to carry it differently?
watch_for: What does she keep count of, and why?
How does she respond to people who try to check on her?
What would make her pick up the fight again?
example_user_messages: I've always been the one who handles the hard stuff and I think I'm completely burnt out.
I keep replaying every tough decision I've had to make. I can't switch it off.
I want to walk away from all of it and live somewhere quiet, but people keep needing me.
I did things to protect my family that I'm not proud of, and I don't know how to live with them.
